## Introduction

Land revenue was the fiscal foundation of British rule, supplying close to half of British Indian revenue through the early 19th century. Three settlements — Permanent (Zamindari), Ryotwari and Mahalwari — were devised, and they differed on a single analytical question: whom does the state recognise as the owner and the revenue-payer? Beneath that difference lay one shared objective — a fixed, punctual, cash demand that the state could budget against. Every economic consequence that followed flows from that objective.

## The three systems
- Permanent Settlement, 1793 — the zamindar as proprietor. Introduced by Cornwallis on John Shore's assessment in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, and extended to the Northern Circars in 1802–03 and Banaras. Revenue was fixed in perpetuity; the Sunset Law of 1794 auctioned the estate of any zamindar who defaulted by sunset of the due date. The state secured predictable revenue but permanently forfeited any share of future agricultural growth — and the zamindar, whose income was rent-secure, had no reason whatever to invest in the land.
- Ryotwari — the individual cultivator as proprietor. Read and Munro, Baramahal 1792; extended to the Ceded Districts from 1800; standard across Madras and Bombay, later Berar and Assam, covering roughly half of British Indian territory. Assessment was made on the individual holding after survey, revised every 20–30 years, and Munro's original demand approached 50% of net produce (reduced towards one-third only after 1855). Removing the intermediary sounded progressive, but it left the ryot facing the collector directly, with no cushion in a bad year — so the moneylender simply replaced the zamindar.
- Mahalwari — the village estate as the unit. Holt Mackenzie's minute of 1819 → Regulation VII of 1822 → overhaul by Regulation IX of 1833. Applied in the North-Western Provinces, Punjab and Central India (in the modified Malguzari form). Settlement was made with the village mahal on the principle of joint responsibility. Village solidarity was preserved on paper; in practice joint liability meant the solvent cultivators paid for the insolvent, which accelerated the transfer of village land to moneylenders.

## Impact on the Indian economy
- Forced monetisation and distress sale. Revenue in cash on a fixed date compelled the peasant to sell immediately after harvest, at the seasonal price trough, to a buyer who was often his creditor. The terms of trade were structurally rigged against him.
- Rural indebtedness and land alienation. The moneylender became the effective landlord, aided by the new civil courts that enforced written contracts he alone could draft. The state was compelled to intervene — the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1879, and the Punjab Land Alienation Act, 1900 — which is itself an admission of systemic failure.
- Investment failure and stagnant productivity. Neither the rent-secure zamindar nor the capital-starved ryot had the means or motive to improve. Per-acre yields stagnated or declined across much of British India between 1890 and 1940.
- Famine vulnerability. With no storage buffer and a rigid cash demand, monsoon failure translated directly into starvation — the Great Famine of 1876–78 prompted the Famine Commission of 1880.
- Deindustrialisation of the village. As the rural economy monetised, the artisan lost his customary share of the grain heap; combined with the collapse of handicraft markets, this pushed labour back onto land and overcrowded agriculture.

## Andhra Pradesh anchoring — all three systems are visible in one state
- Coastal Andhra under Zamindari. The Northern Circars — Ganjam, Vizagapatam, Rajahmundry, Masulipatam and

Guntur — were brought under the Permanent Settlement in 1802–03, which is why coastal Andhra carried a dense estate structure (Bobbili, Vizianagaram, Pithapuram, Venkatagiri, Nuzvid) right down to 1948.

- Rayalaseema as Munro's Ryotwari laboratory. The Ceded Districts — Kadapa, Kurnool, Bellary and Anantapur — were where Munro, as Principal Collector from 1800, perfected the Ryotwari model. His suppression of the poligars and resumption of kattubadi and inam lands dispossessed an entire chieftain class. That dispossession produced the rebellion of Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy around Koilkuntla (1846–47), aided by Vadde Obanna and joined by thousands of peasants; Narasimha Reddy was publicly hanged in February 1847. Kurnool airport is named after him today. Earlier, between 1803 and 1805, the poligars of the Chittoor and Chandragiri palayams rose when deprived of their kaval rights.
- The Agency tracts. In the Eastern Ghats, the muttadari arrangement combined with new forest regulation to strip tribal communities of shifting cultivation and minor forest produce — producing the Rampa rebellion of 1879–80 and Alluri Sitarama Raju's Manyam revolt of 1922–24.
- Infographic (30-second reproduction): Draw an inverted tree. The trunk at the top reads “Colonial revenue demand: fixed, punctual, in cash”. Three branches descend: Zamindari → Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Northern Circars; Ryotwari → Madras, Bombay, Ceded Districts, Berar, Assam; Mahalwari → NWP, Punjab, Central India. Below all three, draw one common root line: “Same outcome — indebtedness, no investment, famine”.

## Conclusion

The three settlements were administrative variants of a single fiscal purpose, and their differences mattered less than their common design flaw: each guaranteed the state's revenue while leaving the risk of cultivation entirely with the cultivator. The result was an agrarian order that was highly monetised but chronically undercapitalised — commercially integrated and technologically frozen at once. Independent India inverted the logic: the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 dismantled the Andhra estates, and the state today transfers income to the farmer through PM-KISAN and Andhra Pradesh's own farmer-support scheme rather than extracting from him. The colonial system's true legacy is measured less in the revenue it collected than in the rural indebtedness and landlessness it institutionalised.

## Value addition
- Coverage (indicative): Zamindari roughly 19% of British Indian territory, Ryotwari roughly 51%, Mahalwari roughly 30%. Useful for a one-line quantification in the introduction.
- Terminology that scores: Sunset Law (1794); patni taluk and sub-infeudation in Bengal; kattubadi and inam resumption in the Ceded Districts; muttadari in the Agency tracts; Malguzari in Central India.
- The post-1857 revenue politics: Awadh's taluqdars, dispossessed in 1856, were restored as proprietors after the revolt and confirmed by the Oudh Estates Act, 1869 — land settlement was openly converted into an instrument for purchasing political loyalty.
- Nationalist critique to quote in substance: R.C. Dutt argued that a rigid, over-pitched revenue demand was the single greatest cause of Indian rural poverty; the Deccan Riots Commission (1875) itself conceded that the revenue demand, not merely the moneylender, lay at the root of agrarian distress.
- AP continuity point: Andhra Pradesh's Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973 and the abolition of estates in 1948 together completed the unwinding of the 1802–03 Circars settlement — a 170-year arc that an examiner will recognise as command over regional history.
P2-Q4b:
## Introduction

For Indian Muslims the 19th century was a century of successive losses: the extinction of Mughal sovereignty in 1858, the replacement of Persian as the language of the courts after 1837, exclusion from the new English-educated professions, and post-1857 official suspicion of the community as the revolt's prime movers. The reform responses that followed divided along a fault line that still frames Muslim political thought — purify and withdraw, preserve and educate, or modernise and engage.

## The purificationist stream — reform as return
- The Wahabi or Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya movement. Led in India by Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli (1786–1831), drawing on Shah Waliullah's reformist school and on Abdul Wahhab's Arabian teaching. It attacked shrine worship, saint veneration and syncretic custom as accretions, declared India dar-ul-harb, and launched armed jihad from the North-West Frontier, where Sayyid Ahmad fell at Balakot in 1831. Its Patna organisational base was systematically destroyed through the Wahabi trials of the 1860s and 1870s — making it the first reform movement the colonial state treated as a security threat.
- The Faraizi movement. Founded by Haji Shariatullah in eastern Bengal around 1818 and carried forward by his son Dudu Miyan, it insisted on the obligatory duties (faraiz) and rejected practices absorbed from Hindu custom. Its significance is that it did not stay religious: under Dudu Miyan it became an organised agrarian movement of Muslim peasants against Hindu zamindars and European indigo planters — showing how religious reform in colonial India absorbed and expressed class grievance.

## The orthodox-educational stream — reform as preservation
- Deoband, 1866. Darul Uloom was founded by Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi with a deliberate strategy: preserve Islamic learning through a self-financed madrasa network independent of state patronage, so that the community's intellectual life would not depend on a hostile government. It built a network of affiliated madrasas across northern India.
- Politically Deoband moved towards composite nationalism — Mahmud al-Hasan's Silk Letter Conspiracy during the First World War, and Hussain Ahmad Madani's Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind (1919), which opposed partition and argued that nationhood is constituted by shared territory, not shared religion. This makes Deoband the analytical counterweight to Aligarh's loyalism.

## Sayyid Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh movement — reform as modernisation
- Political rehabilitation of the community. In Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (1858) he argued that the revolt was caused by the absence of Indian representation in the legislature and by administrative ignorance of Indian sentiment — not by Muslim conspiracy. In The Loyal Mohammedans of India he directly countered the charge later given quasi-official form in W.W. Hunter's The Indian Musalmans (1871). This was the necessary precondition for everything else: a community under suspicion cannot bargain for opportunity.
- Institution-building. He founded the Scientific Society at Ghazipur (1864, moved to Aligarh in 1866) to translate Western scientific works into Urdu, and the bilingual Aligarh Institute Gazette. The MAO School (1875) became a College (1877) and finally Aligarh Muslim University (1920). The All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference (1886) carried the model outward to Bengal, Madras and the Deccan — converting one college into a national movement.
- Intellectual reinterpretation. Through Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq (1870) and his Quranic commentary he argued that revelation, being the word of God, cannot contradict nature, being the work of God — therefore no genuine conflict exists between faith and science. He rejected taqlid (blind imitation) and revived ijtihad (independent reasoning),

which is why conservative ulema denounced him. He also criticised polygamy and the extreme forms of purdah.

- Outcome. Within a generation Aligarh had produced a modern Muslim professional and administrative class — lawyers, civil servants, teachers — where almost none had existed in 1857.
- The limitation an examiner rewards you for naming. His loyalism was strategic but had costs. At Lucknow in 1887 he advised Muslims to stay away from the Indian National Congress, arguing that competitive representation would disadvantage a minority. This separated Muslim political development from the mainstream national movement at its formative moment, and his later “two nations” metaphor was put to uses he did not live to see. Badruddin Tyabji's Congress presidency in the same year (1887) is the direct counterpoint.

## Andhra Pradesh dimension
- The Deccan's Islamic culture was overwhelmingly shrine-centred and composite — the Ameen Peer Dargah at Kadapa and the Bara Shaheed Dargah at Nellore, whose Rottela Panduga draws Hindu and Muslim devotees together in large numbers. This is exactly the devotional practice that Wahabi and Faraizi purificationists sought to eliminate.
- The analytical payoff: purificationist reform found little purchase in the Telugu districts because it attacked the very tradition that gave local Islam its social depth, whereas the Aligarh model — education without doctrinal confrontation — travelled easily, spreading through Muhammadan Educational Conference sessions and Anjuman-run schools in the Telugu districts of the Madras Presidency. Reform movements succeed regionally to the extent that they work with, rather than against, established devotional culture.
- Infographic (30-second reproduction): Write one line at the top: “Muslim response to 19th-century decline”. Draw three downward arrows from it. Arrow 1 — PURIFY: Wahabi, Faraizi → armed resistance, agrarian militancy, state repression. Arrow 2 — PRESERVE: Deoband 1866 → madrasa network, composite nationalism. Arrow 3 — MODERNISE: Aligarh 1875–77 → English education, loyalism, Muslim professional class.

## Conclusion

The three streams were less rivals than competing answers to one question: how should a community relate to a power it can no longer defeat? Purification chose confrontation and was crushed; Deoband chose insulation and survived intellectually; Aligarh chose engagement and secured material advancement at the price of political separation. Sayyid Ahmad Khan's answer proved the most consequential, because he built institutions rather than merely arguments, and made rational enquiry religiously respectable at a moment when the community's confidence was at its lowest. The continuing life of that founding intent is visible in the Supreme Court's seven-judge ruling in Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (8 November 2024), which by a 4:3 majority overruled S. Azeez Basha (1967) and held that incorporation by statute does not by itself extinguish an institution's minority character under Article 30 — placing the question of who founded and animated Aligarh back at the centre of constitutional reasoning.

## Value addition
- Sir Syed's key texts, worth naming precisely:Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (1858); The Loyal Mohammedans of India; Khutbat-i-Ahmadiyya (his reply to William Muir's life of the Prophet); Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq (1870).
- Other reformers to name for breadth: Maulvi Abdul Latif's Mohammedan Literary Society, Calcutta (1863); Syed Ameer Ali's Central National Muhammadan Association (1877) and The Spirit of Islam; Justice Syed Mahmood, Sir Syed's son and the first Indian judge of the Allahabad High Court; Mirza Ghulam Ahmad's Ahmadiyya movement at Qadian (1889), which advocated rational interpretation and rejected violent jihad.
- Analytical frame that scores: present the three streams as purify – preserve – modernise rather than as a chronological list. It converts a descriptive answer into an argued one in a single sentence.
- Contemporary anchor: the AMU minority-status judgment of November 2024, which returned the question of Sir Syed's founding role to the Supreme Court; and Sir Syed Day, observed on 17 October, his birth anniversary.
- AP anchor: Ameen Peer Dargah (Kadapa) and Bara Shaheed Dargah (Nellore) with its Rottela Panduga as living evidence of the composite Deccani tradition that purificationist reform opposed and that shaped how reform was received in the Telugu country.
P2-Q5a:
## Introduction

Agrarian discontent in colonial India was continuous, but a movement is not the same as discontent. Between 1857 and 1947, scattered and localised rural revolts were gradually converted into organised, ideologically-articulated peasant politics. Explaining this transformation requires distinguishing the structural conditions that generated grievance from the political and organisational catalysts that gave that grievance direction — and the national movement was decisively reshaped by the result.

## STRUCTURAL FACTORS — the manufacture of agrarian distress
- Rigid and extractive revenue settlements. The Permanent Settlement (1793) fixed the state's demand but left the zamindar free to raise rent at will, creating a layer of intermediaries with no productive function. The Ryotwari and Mahalwari tracts placed the demand directly on the cultivator, in cash, revised periodically upward. In both, the burden of price fluctuation fell entirely on the peasant, which is why market crashes produced political revolts rather than merely economic hardship.
- Commercialisation without security. Peasants were pushed toward cotton, indigo, jute and oilseeds to earn the cash the revenue demanded. This tied subsistence to volatile world prices — so the Great Depression of 1929–33, which halved agricultural prices while revenue stayed fixed, converted a whole generation of cultivators into debtors almost overnight.
- Indebtedness and land alienation. With no institutional credit, the moneylender became indispensable and land became mortgageable property. The Deccan Riots of 1875 — where peasants burned debt bonds rather than attacked persons — showed the target was the legal instrument of dispossession, and forced the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1879.
- De-industrialisation and pressure on land. The collapse of handicrafts under machine-made imports drove artisans back into agriculture, raising the dependent population on a fixed land base, fragmenting holdings and depressing wages — deepening distress without any corresponding rise in output.
- Famines and wartime requisition. Recurrent famines, culminating in the Bengal Famine of 1943, exposed the administration's priorities; the Famine Inquiry Commission (1945) confirmed that policy failure, not absolute shortage, was decisive. Wartime levies and rationing abuse became the immediate trigger for both the Tebhaga and Telangana risings.

## CATALYTIC FACTORS — grievance becomes movement
- The Gandhian technique. Satyagraha gave the peasant a method that was legally defensible, morally unimpeachable and did not invite the massacre that armed revolt attracted. Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918) and Bardoli (1928) proved it worked.
- Institutional organisation. The UP Kisan Sabha (1918) under Gauri Shankar Mishra and Indra Narayan Dwivedi, the Oudh Kisan Sabha (1920) under Baba Ramchandra, and above all the All India Kisan Sabha, founded at Lucknow in April 1936 — with Swami Sahajanand Saraswati as President and Prof. N.G. Ranga of Guntur as General Secretary — supplied continuity, a manifesto and a national platform.
- Ideological input from the Left. Congress Socialists and communists brought a language of class, converting demands for relief into demands for rights — rent reduction, security of tenure and, ultimately, zamindari abolition.

## IMPACT ON THE NATIONAL MOVEMENT
- It converted nationalism into mass politics. Without the peasantry the Congress remained a body of lawyers and professionals petitioning for reform. Rural mobilisation gave it the numbers that made non-cooperation and civil disobedience credible instruments.
- It changed Congress policy in writing, not merely rhetoric. The AIKS and the Congress met at Faizpur in 1936 — the Congress's first rural session — and the agrarian sections of the Congress election manifesto of 1937 were directly shaped by the AIKS agenda. The 1937–39 Congress ministries marked the high watermark of peasant activity, with tenancy and debt-relief legislation across provinces.
- It supplied techniques of resistance. No-revenue and no-rent campaigns, social boycott of collaborators, and camp-based volunteer organisation were peasant innovations that the national movement adopted wholesale in 1930–34.
- It set the post-independence agenda. The anti-feudal thrust made zamindari abolition the first legislative priority of the new republic, and the constitutional protection of land-reform laws through Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule is the direct legatee of this pressure.
- Limits, honestly stated. Peasant militancy also strained the Congress: the Eka movement (1921–22) lost Congress backing when it turned violent, the Bihar Kisan Sabha broke with the Congress over the bakasht land issue in 1936–39, and the AIKS itself split during the War. The Congress absorbed peasant demands only to the extent they did not fracture its cross-class coalition.

## Andhra Anchor
- Prof. N.G. Ranga (Guntur) founded the India Peasants' Institute in 1933 and became the AIKS's first General Secretary in 1936 — making coastal Andhra a national laboratory of organised peasant politics. Acharya N.G. Ranga Agricultural University (Hyderabad, 1965; now headquartered at Guntur for AP) carries his name.
- Provincial ryot associations in the Andhra deltas linked anti-zamindar agitation to Congress electoral politics after 1937, while Rayalaseema, as a chronically drought-prone ryotwari tract, produced a distinct grievance of assessment relief rather than tenancy.

## Conclusion

The peasant movement was produced by a revenue system that made the cultivator the state's direct creditor, and was activated by a method and an organisation that arrived in the twentieth century. Its impact on the national movement was not additive but constitutive: it broadened the social base, rewrote the Congress's economic programme, supplied the repertoire of resistance and dictated the first legislative act of the independent republic. Nationalism in India became a mass force at the moment it became agrarian.

## Value addition
- Three-phase periodisation (retain from the original, it is sound): 1857–1921 sporadic and leaderless; 1923–1946 organised and class-conscious; post-1947 continuing agrarian struggles over unimplemented reform.
- Current data (PIB, June 2026): the 23rd instalment of PM-KISAN was released on 20 June 2026 — about ₹18,880 crore to 9.44 crore farmers, including 2.18 crore women; cumulative disbursal since 2019 exceeds ₹4.46 lakh crore, and Union Budget 2026–27 allocates ₹60,000 crore to the scheme. The contrast with a colonial state that extracted from the same cultivator is the sharpest possible closing line.
- Andhra current hook (NewsOnAir, June 2026): under PM-Kisan–Annadata Sukhibhava, Andhra Pradesh released ₹3,125 crore to 46.85 lakh farmers at ₹7,000 per farmer for the 2026 Kharif season, launched from Linganguntla village, Palnadu district — the same Palnadu that was a no-tax stronghold in 1921.
- Committees worth naming: Deccan Riots Commission (1875–76); Floud Commission (Bengal, 1938–40); Famine Inquiry Commission (1945).
P2-Q5b:
## Introduction

Communalism is the belief that people of one religion share identical secular — political, economic and cultural — interests that are distinct from, and eventually hostile to, those of another. It is a modern phenomenon, born of mass politics and competitive representation, not of medieval religiosity. Because it fragmented the very constituency that nationalism sought to unify, it functioned as the most useful unintended ally colonial rule ever possessed.

## How Communalism Served British Control
- Separate electorates institutionalised the division: The Indian Councils Act, 1909 created Muslim electorates; the 1919 Act extended the principle; the Communal Award (1932) stretched it to Depressed Classes and other groups, and the Government of India Act, 1935 carried it into provincial autonomy. The mechanism mattered more than the intent — once a candidate needed votes only from co-religionists, appealing across communities became electorally irrational. Classification created constituencies: The decennial Census from 1871 counted Indians by religion and caste, converting fluid identities into countable, comparable blocs. Numbers then became the currency of political claim-making — the essential precondition for majority-minority politics.
- Arbitration as leverage: Every deadlock — the Round Table Conferences, the Simla Conference of 1945, the Cabinet Mission of 1946 — allowed Britain to present itself as the indispensable neutral umpire. The League's veto after 1940 gave the Raj a standing reason to defer transfer of power.

## Indicative Traits of the Communalists
- Staged escalation of the ideology: Bipan Chandra identifies three stages — communal nationalism (co-religionists share secular interests), liberal communalism (the two communities have different interests but can bargain), and extreme communalism (the interests are irreconcilable, so coexistence is impossible). Recognising which stage an actor occupies is the sharpest analytical tool available on this topic; the shift to the third stage after 1937 made partition thinkable.
- Assertion of the community as a monolith: The Muslim League (1906) and, in reaction, the Hindu Mahasabha (1915) and RSS (1925) each spoke for an undifferentiated community, erasing the class, caste, regional and linguistic divisions that actually structured Indian society — a Bengali Muslim had far more in common with a Bengali Hindu than with a Punjabi Muslim.
- Selective history as grievance: Communal ideologues read the medieval past as unbroken conquest or unbroken oppression. This was reinforced by colonial historiography's Hindu–Muslim–British periodisation, which supplied communalism with an academic vocabulary.
- Middle-class social roots: The ideology was propagated by professional and clerical classes competing for a narrow pool of government jobs and legislative seats, dressing sectional economic anxiety as religious danger.

## Assessing the Impact
- Partition and its human cost: The most direct outcome — the displacement of more than fifteen million people and mass killing on a scale India had not previously witnessed. The Government of India now observes 14 August as Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, instituted in 2021, precisely so this cost is not forgotten.
- Weakening of mass movements: The League opposed and the Hindu Mahasabha boycotted the Quit India Movement, denying 1942 the united front that Non-Cooperation had briefly achieved in 1920–22. Constitutional counter-response: The Constituent Assembly's rejection of separate electorates in 1949 was a conscious repudiation of the colonial device. Articles 25–28 guarantee religious freedom and bar State religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions, and the 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted "secular" into the Preamble.

## Conclusion

The verdict is affirmative but qualified. Britain rarely manufactured communal sentiment outright; it created the institutional architecture — enumeration, separate electorates, weighted representation — within which communal politics became the rational strategy, then harvested the resulting deadlock as proof that Indians could not govern themselves. Communalism was thus less a British creation than a British instrument. Its legacy explains why the Constitution's commitment to secularism was not a borrowed abstraction but a considered answer to a lived catastrophe.

## Value addition
- Andhra Pradesh anchor: The Telugu districts of the Madras Presidency remained largely free of communal violence in 1946– 47, but the princely State of Hyderabad demonstrated the same logic in a different register — the Razakars mobilised a religious-linguistic elite against a Telugu-speaking peasantry, and integration followed only through Operation Polo on 17 September 1948.
- The Ministry of Home Affairs issued a gazette notification in March 2024 designating 17 September as Hyderabad Liberation Day; the Ministry of Culture and the Central Bureau of Communication mounted a fifty-panel photo exhibition on Operation Polo at Hyderabad's Parade Ground for the 2025 observance.
- Partition Horrors Remembrance Day (14 August), observed since 2021, is commemorated annually by the IGNCA under the Ministry of Culture — a citable, government-sourced marker of official memory politics.
- Quotable framing: Dr B.R. Ambedkar's warning in the Constituent Assembly that placing creed above country would put India's independence in jeopardy — the sharpest single line for the conclusion.
- Conceptual edge: Distinguish communalism (a political ideology of interest) from religious fundamentalism (a theological project) — examiners reward this distinction because most scripts conflate the two.

## Introduction

Satavahana rule over the Deccan and Andhradesa produced a society at once hierarchical and unusually open: a varna order overlaid by powerful merchant and artisan guilds, and a religious field in which Vedic sacrifice and Buddhist monasticism were patronised by the same court. Within this setting women appear in the epigraphic record with a visibility unmatched in contemporary India — as regents, as donors and as the source of royal names.

## Social structure
- Society was heterogeneous: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras coexisted with tribal groups such as Nagas and Medas, and with a substantial immigrant element (Sakas, Yavanas) absorbed into local guilds.
- Shrenis of weavers, potters, oil-pressers and corn-dealers functioned as bankers and endowment-holders, receiving permanent deposits whose interest funded monastic needs. This gave non-royal groups — including women — independent economic standing.

## Religious conditions
- Kings legitimised themselves through Vedic sacrifice — Rajasuya, Vajapeya and Ashvamedha — while simultaneously endowing Buddhist establishments at Amaravati, Bhattiprolu, Jaggayyapeta, Nasik and Karle.
- The coexistence was structural, not merely tolerant: Vedic ritual supplied royal legitimacy, Buddhist institutions supplied the moral and commercial infrastructure of trade routes. Amaravati's sculpture, with its Jataka narratives and donor panels, is the visual record of that bargain.

3. Prominence of women — the core of the answer Political authority: Naganika, queen of Satakarni I, acted as regent for her minor son Vedasri; the Naneghat cave carries her portrait relief and her record of sacrificial dakshinas — a woman publicly claiming the merit of Vedic sacrifice.

- Independent donative capacity: Gautami Balasri, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni, issued the Nasik Prasasti in the 19th regnal year of Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and made grants in her own name — the fullest Satavahana inscription, composed by a woman.
- Titles: elite women bore feminine forms of their husbands' offices — Mahabhoji, Mahasenapatini, Mahatalavari, Mahaaratini. This is status derived from marriage, not office held in their own right, and saying so precisely is what separates a 10-mark answer from a 6-mark one.
- Ordinary women: Amaravati and Nasik inscriptions record gifts by nuns (bhikkhunis), by merchants' wives and by female lay devotees acting without male mediation — the clearest proof that property rights and religious agency reached below the royal family.
- Metronymics: rulers styled themselves Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra, Kausikiputra. These derive from the mother's gotra, not her personal name, and most likely served to distinguish sons of different queens in a polygynous household. They indicate the high status of the mother, but do not by themselves establish matriliny — a qualification examiners reward.

## Conclusion

The Satavahana period thus combined a stratified varna order with genuine religious plurality and a striking public visibility for women. That visibility was real but bounded — grounded in donative wealth, maternal status and regency rather than in independent office. Measured against its own age, however, it made Andhradesa one of the few regions where women's names entered the permanent epigraphic record on their own account.

## Value addition
- Continuity into the Ikshvaku period: Chamtisri built the Nagarjunakonda Mahachaitya, and Bodhisri's inscription records endowments for monastic fraternities from Sri Lanka, Kashmir, Gandhara and China — women financing an international Buddhist network from Andhra soil.
- Literary corroboration: Hala's Gathasaptasati, itself said to include verses by women poets, portrays rural women in agrarian and domestic settings, supplying social detail no royal inscription contains.
- Prakrit became a Classical Language on 3 October 2024 (PIB / Ministry of Culture), taking India's total to eleven — a directly citable current hook, since the entire female donative record of this period is in Prakrit.
- Long AP arc for the conclusion: Naganika and Gautami Balasri → Rudrama Devi of the Kakatiyas → Molla and Tallapaka Timmakka → Durgabai Deshmukh — a continuous line of women's public agency in Andhra history.
- Site anchor: the ASI Amaravati Circle's site museums at Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda hold the relic caskets and donative inscriptions on which all of the above rests.
P2-Q6b:
## Introduction

The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (c. 624–1130 CE) governed the fertile Krishna–Godavari delta, a corridor open to the Deccan interior, the Kannada country and the Tamil south. That openness is the structural reason their five centuries reordered Andhra society: new communities arrived, occupational groups hardened into jatis, sectarian competition intensified, and the temple emerged as the institution that mediated all three.

## Immigration and the pluralisation of religious life
- Directed settlement, not random drift. The crown deliberately settled Brahmins, temple artisans and trading guilds in new villages and agraharas through copper-plate grants. Each agrahara became a node radiating Sanskritic ritual, temple architecture and literacy into its hinterland — state policy shaping the religious map.
- Named incoming communities. The Komatis, traditionally traced to Gaudadesa and settled at Penugonda, appear in Andhra for the first time as an organised mercantile community, introducing the worship of Kanyaka Parameshwari. Brahmin migration also ran outward, towards the Tamil country, producing the "Arama Dravida" group.
- Sectarian coexistence and competition. Saiva sects — Pasupata, Kalamukha, Kapalika — flourished at Srisailam, Tripurantakam, Alampur and Mahanandi, while Vaishnavism gained ground with Ramanuja's Visishtadvaita; Jainism survived on reduced patronage, as at the Nedumbi basadi at Bezawada endowed by Ayyana Mahadevi, queen of Kubja Vishnuvardhana. Buddhism, by contrast, faded.

2. Caste mobility: flexibility inside hierarchy

- Occupations froze into jatis. The ashtadasha (eighteen) professions of the Satavahana age became the eighteen jatis of the Chalukya age — the single most consequential social change of the period, because it converted a functional division of labour into a hereditary one.
- Yet upward movement was real. Sudra cultivators rose into a powerful landed community; the Brahmin order itself split functionally into Vaidiki (priestly) and Niyogi (administrative) and regionally into Kammanadu, Velanadu and Palanadu sub-groups — showing that even the topmost varna was being reorganised by occupation and locality rather than scripture.
- Tribal absorption by conquest and incorporation. Panduranga, commander of Gunaga Vijayaditya III, subdued the boyakottams (Boya tribal settlements) and brought the Boyas into the Brahmanical fold — the clearest documented instance of state-led assimilation in early medieval Andhra.

3. Social awakening: temple, vernacular and new publics

- The temple became the hub of social and economic life, managing land, irrigation and labour, and employing musicians, dancers and functionaries. Public processions (uregimpu) and jataras — the Bezawada inscription of Yuddhamalla records a jatara — drew artisans and cultivators into shared religious life for the first time.
- Learning was institutionalised through ghatikas and Jain sanghas at Bezawada and Ramatirtham, with Rajahmundry and Amaravati as Brahmanical centres, sustained by royal land grants.
- The costs were real too. The devadasi system appears in Andhra for the first time in this period, and prostitution was socially normalised — a reminder that "awakening" widened participation while entrenching new forms of subordination.

## Conclusion

Under the Eastern Chalukyas, Andhra's social order was not overturned but re-engineered: hierarchy was retained while its internal composition was rewritten by migration, occupation and patronage. The temple-and-agrahara complex was the machinery of that change. Its residue — the Vaidiki–Niyogi division, the Vaisya identity around Kanyaka Parameshwari, and the regional Nadu affiliations — remains legible in the community map of coastal Andhra today. Model Question: "Under the Eastern Chalukyas, the temple was less a place of worship than an instrument of social reordering." Critically examine with reference to agraharas, guilds and caste mobility.

## Value addition
- AP Tourism (aptourism.gov.in): the Bhimeswara temple at Draksharamam carries about 381 inscriptions dated between 1080 and 1434 CE — effectively a public archive of endowments, guild transactions and social claims across four centuries.
- ASI centrally protected monuments in Andhra Pradesh include the Bhimeswara temples at Draksharama and Samalkot and the Biccavolu temple group, protected under the AMASR Act, 1958.
- PIB (August 2026): Adopt a Heritage 2.0 (September 2023) had 30 MoUs by March 2026; PRASHAD has sanctioned 54 projects across 28 States and UTs worth Rs. 1,726.74 crore — the modern successor to temple-centred patronage.
- NMMA has documented 1.84 lakh monuments and 17.20 lakh antiquities (March 2026); ASI's LiDAR, GIS mapping and drone surveys are now used for heritage documentation.
- Continuity marker: the Kanyaka Parameshwari cult that began under the Eastern Chalukyas remains the principal community devotion of the Arya Vysya in Andhra Pradesh — a thousand-year-old social innovation still operating.

## Introduction

The Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE), founded by Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama dynasty, drew a remarkable succession of foreign observers across three centuries. Their value lies precisely in their externality: unlike court inscriptions and prasastis, which were composed to glorify patrons, these travellers were merchants, envoys and horse-traders with no stake in dynastic legitimacy. Read together with epigraphy, they allow a triangulated reconstruction of Vijayanagara society, and they are the single most important non-indigenous source for the period.

## Social Life
- Domingo Paes (Portuguese, c. 1520–22, reign of Krishnadevaraya) gives the fullest social portrait. He described Vijayanagara as a city as large as Rome, with well-laid bazaars, aqueducts and irrigated gardens — evidence that urban prosperity was engineered, not accidental, resting on a planned water-supply system. He also recorded women employed as wrestlers, astrologers, accountants and palace guards, showing that elite female participation extended well beyond the domestic sphere, even if political power remained closed to them.
- Duarte Barbosa (Portuguese, c. 1516–18) catalogued weavers, metalworkers, oil-pressers and traders living street by street according to occupation. This matters because it confirms that caste operated as an occupational-residential ordering principle in the capital, not merely a ritual one, and that Brahmins retained ritual and administrative primacy.
- Abdur Razzaq (Persian envoy of Shah Rukh, 1443, reign of Devaraya II) reported the city as unequalled by anything his eyes had seen, with a huge treasury and a bazaar of jewellers where diamonds and pearls were sold openly — a marker of both security of property and the empire's command over Deccan bullion flows.

## Religious Life
- Barbosa recorded that the king allowed each man to live according to his own creed without harassment, and that Muslims held office and had mosques in the capital. This is the strongest external evidence that Vijayanagara's self-image as a defender of dharma coexisted with pragmatic religious accommodation; Devaraya II is known to have recruited Muslim cavalrymen and permitted a Quran to be placed before his throne.
- Niccolò de' Conti (Venetian, c. 1420, reign of Devaraya I) described mass festivals with chariot processions, temple lamps and large public gatherings, indicating that the temple was the central institution of civic life, absorbing royal grants and redistributing them as food, employment and festival spectacle.
- Paes described the nine-day Mahanavami festival at the Mahanavami Dibba as a royal ritual of state: military reviews, tribute from nayakas and dance performances. The festival was thus simultaneously a religious act and an annual re-enactment of the political order.

## Cultural Life
- Paes and Razzaq both dwell on monumental architecture — gopurams, pillared mandapas and the "House of Victory" — confirming that architecture was the chosen medium of royal display.
- Temple dance and music were institutionalised: Paes recorded dancing women attached to temples and palaces, receiving land and maintenance, which is corroborated by devadasi endowments in inscriptions.
- Andhra Pradesh anchor: The cultural world these travellers glimpsed survives most vividly not at Hampi but in Andhra Pradesh. The Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi (Sri Sathya Sai district), built under Achyutaraya (1529–42 CE), preserves the only substantially surviving mid-Vijayanagara mural cycle, and ASI's Amaravati Circle records mural traditions at Lepakshi and Somapalle. UNESCO placed "Sri Veerabhadra Temple and Monolithic Bull (Nandi), Lepakshi" on India's Tentative List on 17 February 2022 under criteria (i), (ii) and (vi), explicitly for the Vijayanagara sculpture and painting tradition.

## Critical Limits of Traveller Testimony
- All four saw only the capital and the coast; village society, the amara-nayankara base of the state and the peasantry are almost invisible in their accounts.
- Portuguese writers were commercial rivals and religious outsiders, prone to exoticising sati and devadasi practice; Razzaq, an envoy, wrote partly to impress his own court. Their testimony is therefore best used with inscriptions, not instead of them.
- Infographic suggestion (30 seconds, hand-drawable): Draw a simple horizontal timeline bar. Mark four notches left to right: 1420 Conti (Devaraya I) → 1443 Razzaq (Devaraya II) → 1516–18 Barbosa (Krishnadevaraya) → 1520–22 Paes (Krishnadevaraya). Below each notch write one keyword: Festivals / Splendour & Treasury / Tolerance & Crafts / City & Mahanavami. Add a fifth notch c. 1535 Nuniz marked "Markets & History". This single line shows the examiner you have the chronology under control.

## Conclusion

Taken together, the four accounts converge on a picture of a wealthy, densely urban, ritually vibrant and pragmatically plural polity, while diverging enough in emphasis to remain credible rather than formulaic. Their real significance is methodological: they supply an independent external control on inscriptional self-representation, allowing historians to distinguish royal claim from lived reality. Their continuing relevance is institutional too — the sites they described are today protected under the AMASR Act, 1958, with Hampi inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1986 and Lepakshi awaiting nomination from the Tentative List.

## Value addition
- Fernao Nuniz (c. 1535–37), a Portuguese horse-trader, wrote a dynastic chronicle of Vijayanagara and described its markets as glutted with fruit, meat and game at low prices — used by historians as evidence of agrarian surplus and market integration.
- Athanasius Nikitin, a Russian merchant (1470s), left an account of Bahmani–Vijayanagara relations, useful as a non-European, non-Persian counterpoint.
- Barbosa on housing: common people's houses were thatched but solidly built and arranged street-wise by trade — supporting evidence for occupational zoning.
- Paes on the "House of Victory": a two-tiered sculpted platform used for the Mahanavami; today identified with the Mahanavami Dibba in the Royal Centre at Hampi.
- Current data (examiner-facing): ASI conserves 3,686 centrally protected monuments including 27 World Heritage properties (Ministry of Culture, Lok Sabha reply, 23 March 2026). India's World Heritage tally rose to 45 with the inscription of the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee, Busan (July 2026). India's Tentative List stands at 69 properties, and the September 2025 additions included two Andhra Pradesh entries — Erra Matti Dibbalu and the Natural Heritage of Tirumala Hills.
- AP link for any Vijayanagara answer: Penukonda and Chandragiri served successively as later Vijayanagara capitals after 1565, making Andhra Pradesh the empire's political refuge in its final century.

## Introduction

The collapse of the Kakatiyas in 1323 and the brief Tughlaq occupation left Andhradesa without a legitimising centre. Into that vacuum stepped the Reddis (c. 1325–1448), a peasant-warrior lineage who ruled successively from Addanki, Kondavidu and Rajahmundry. Their significance lies less in territory than in a deliberate cultural project: restoring Brahmanical institutions, dignifying a non-Kshatriya dynasty through patronage, and thereby giving Telugu its first courtly self-confidence.

## Religious restoration as a political instrument
- Prolaya Vema Reddi's Vilasa grant presents him as the restorer of agraharas dispossessed during the Tughlaq disruption — the earned title of an "unequalled giver of land". This was not piety alone: rebuilding the Brahmana settlement network rebuilt the tax, record-keeping and scribal infrastructure the Kakatiyas had lost.
- Saiva and Vaishnava streams flourished together. Anavema Reddi's works at Srisailam (including the Veerasiromandapam) and Reddi attention to Ahobilam, Draksharama and Simhachalam show a court that endowed both sects rather than choosing between them — pluralism as statecraft in a frontier zone.
- Temples doubled as schools, granaries and employers, so religious endowment was simultaneously an investment in literacy and in the local economy that sustained poets.

## Social mobility and the legitimacy problem
- The Reddis rose from the cultivating Kapu/Reddi stratum, not from a Kshatriya lineage. Lacking inherited status, they purchased legitimacy through Vedic ritual, land grants and, decisively, literary patronage — which explains the unusual intensity of their support to poets.
- The same opening allowed Velamas, Kammas and Padmanayakas to consolidate as service elites, loosening varna rigidity in practice even while it was affirmed in theory.

## Fort-and-port prosperity as the material base
- Hill forts at Kondavidu (Palnadu district), Kondapalli and Vinukonda gave defensible revenue cores; the port of Motupalli (Prakasam district) kept coastal Andhra linked to Southeast Asian trade. Anavota Reddi's bilingual merchant charter there guaranteed cargo security and moderate duties — a working example of surplus being deliberately generated, not merely taxed.

4. Telugu literature: from translation to independent kavya

- Errapragada (Errana), "Prabandha Parameswara", under Prolaya Vema Reddi, completed the Aranya Parva and wrote Nrisimha Puranam and Harivamsam. His achievement was stylistic reconciliation — Nannaya's Sanskritic dignity fused with Tikkana's spoken fluency — which gave later poets a usable literary Telugu.
- Srinatha, "Kavisarvabhauma", served as Vidyadhikari under Pedakomati Vema Reddi at Kondavidu. Sringara Naishadham marks Telugu's shift from translation to independent poetic composition, while Kasikhandam, Bhimakhandam and Haravilasam extended the range.
- Crucially, the vernacular also moved downward: Srinatha's Palnati Veeracharitra in dwipada metre and Kridabhiramam (associated with Vallabharaya under Kumaragiri) capture fairs, courtesans and street life in Orugallu — evidence that Telugu was becoming a language of social observation, not only of gods and kings.
- Bilingual depth: Kataya Vema Reddi wrote Sanskrit commentaries on Kalidasa, and Kumaragiri Reddi is credited with the dance treatise Vasantarajiyam — showing patronage extended to performance theory, not just poetry.

## Conclusion

The Reddi achievement was therefore not a spontaneous "renaissance" but a calculated cultural reconstruction: a lineage without inherited rank bought permanence by restoring temples, securing trade and endowing poets. Its lasting return was linguistic — Telugu emerged from the Reddi courts confident enough to sustain original kavya, and it was this confidence that Vijayanagara inherited and Krishnadevaraya's Ashtadiggajas brought to full flower.

## Value addition
- ASI, Amaravati Circle: Kondaveedu Hill Fort is a centrally protected monument, listed in the ASI's Centrally Protected Monuments list for Andhra Pradesh — usable as living evidence of Reddi fortification.
- Ministry of Culture:Telugu received Classical Language status in 2008 (notified 31 October 2008); with the Cabinet decision of 3 October 2024 adding Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali, India now recognises 11 classical languages. The Reddi-era corpus is part of the antiquity claim that underpinned Telugu's case.
- A Centre of Excellence for Studies in Classical Telugu functions under the Central Institute of Indian Languages framework, supporting research on precisely this classical corpus.
- Gyan Bharatam Mission (Ministry of Culture, Central Sector Scheme, 2024–31, outlay Rs. 482.85 crore): the Gyan Bharatam National Manuscript Survey was launched on 16 March 2026 to build a geo-tagged national inventory of manuscript repositories — directly relevant to surviving Reddi-era palm-leaf texts held in temples and mathas of coastal Andhra.
- UNESCO Tentative List: Sri Veerabhadra Temple and the Monolithic Nandi at Lepakshi (Anantapuramu district) were submitted on 17 February 2022; India's Tentative List now stands at 69 properties after seven natural sites were added, including Erra Matti Dibbalu and the Natural Heritage of Tirumala Hills, both in Andhra Pradesh.

## Introduction

Gurajada Venkata Apparao (1862–1915) and Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (1863–1940) were friends from their Vizianagaram years who divided the same task between them. Both concluded that reform could not travel in a language the people did not speak. Gurajada attacked the content of custom through drama and verse; Gidugu attacked the medium itself, insisting that Vyavaharika — spoken Telugu — displace the Sanskritised Grandhika register in schooling and print.

## (i) Gurajada Apparao — literature as an instrument of social reform
- Kanyasulkam: written around 1890, first staged in 1892, first published in 1897 (dedicated to Maharaja Ananda Gajapati) and issued in a greatly expanded seven-act version in 1909. It is the first Telugu play written in the spoken idiom of the region.
- Method — satire rather than sermon: Girisam, Madhuravani and Ramappa Pantulu ridicule bride-price, the marriage of girls to old men, the ruin of widows and the hypocrisy of the English-educated. Because audiences laughed rather than were lectured at, the play's phrases entered daily speech and shifted opinion where a tract could not.
- Beyond the stage:Mutyala Saralu (1910) freed Telugu poetry from classical metre; Diddubatu is regarded as an early modern Telugu short story; Kanyaka and Poornamma dramatised the destruction of girls by custom. His nationalism was explicitly humanist — Desamunu Preminchumanna (1910) defines the nation as its people, not its territory.
- Institutional weight: as a member of the Madras University Board of Studies (1911) he argued the case for spoken Telugu from inside the academic establishment; titles Kavisekhara and Abhyudaya Kavita Pitamahudu record the verdict of posterity.

## (ii) Gidugu Ramamurthy — the Vyavaharika Bhasha movement
- The argument: if examination, textbook and administration all use a register no child speaks, literacy itself becomes a caste privilege. Gidugu therefore framed language reform as a question of social access, not of literary taste.
- The campaign: he founded the Vartamana Vyavaharikandhra Bhasha Parivartaka Samajam (1919) with its journal Telugu, and Veeresalingam presided over it — linking language reform to the older social-reform lineage. He also advanced the "direct method", teaching speech before script, decades before it became standard pedagogy.
- The opposition and the outcome: the Andhra Sahitya Parishat, Kakinada, led the Grandhika defence and withdrew from the contest in 1924; in 1933 the Abhinavandhra Kavi Pandita Sabha resolved that modern vyavaharika be the medium of instruction. Today cultivated spoken Telugu is the medium of schooling, journalism and even research writing — a completed victory, which is the strongest way to close this half.
- Linguistic inclusion beyond Telugu: he produced a grammar, dictionary and primers for the Savara (Sora) tribal language of the Srikakulam hills, and was honoured as Rao Sahib, with the Kaisar-i-Hind Medal and the Kalaprapoorna, explicitly for service to the Savaras and to Telugu pedagogy.

## Conclusion

The two men solved complementary halves of one problem. Gurajada proved that a play in ordinary speech could do what a reformist tract could not, and Gidugu ensured that ordinary speech would be admitted to the school, the press and the examination hall. Their joint legacy is the modern Telugu public sphere itself — and the principle, now written into national education policy, that a people cannot be reformed in a language they do not speak.

## Value addition
- Verified current hook (PIB / Budget documents): in the Union Budget speech of 1 February 2025, the Finance Minister opened with Gurajada's line "Desamante Matti Kaadoi, Desamante Manushuloi" — "a country is not just its soil, a country is its people" — from Desamunu Preminchumanna (1910), and tied it to the Viksit Bharat goals. A 110-year-old Telugu verse framing a national budget is the sharpest possible illustration of literature as public persuasion.
- Language policy (Ministry of Culture / Ministry of Education): Telugu received Classical Language status in 2008; the Cabinet decision of 3 October 2024 raised the national total to eleven classical languages. A Centre of Excellence for Classical Telugu operates under the Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysuru.
- Gidugu's argument, institutionalised: the Bharatiya Bhasha Pustak Pariyojana (Union Budget 2025–26; about ₹5,100 crore) will create 2.43 lakh digital textbooks in 22 Indian languages during 2025–28 under the Bharatiya Bhasha Samiti — the state now doing at national scale what Gidugu did with primers and pamphlets.
- Commemoration: Telugu Bhasha Dinotsavam is observed on 29 August, Gidugu's birth anniversary, with State awards for Telugu literature — a rare instance of a language reformer, rather than a poet or king, becoming a state occasion.

## Introduction

The Company's Andhra districts were shaped by three officials whose interventions fell in different domains but converged in effect. Munro reorganised the land revenue relationship, Cotton re-engineered the deltas, and Brown salvaged Telugu's classical corpus. Each acted within the logic of colonial extraction, yet each left an institution that outlived the Company.

(i) Sir Thomas Munro (1761–1827): revenue and administration

- As Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts from 1800 to 1807 — Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary, the tract ceded by the Nizam — Munro subdued some eighty poligars and used the pacified tract as his laboratory for the Ryotwari settlement, assessing each cultivator directly and eliminating the intermediary.
- The rationale was that a direct state–ryot link would protect the peasant and stabilise revenue. In practice it exposed cultivators to rigid cash demands and to moneylenders, so the intermediary returned in a private form — the standard critique to record.
- As Governor of Madras (1820–27) he enforced Ryotwari across the Presidency in 1822, ordered the first survey of indigenous schools, and pressed for Indians in higher service.
- Andhra anchor: Munro died of cholera at Pattikonda in Kurnool district on 6 July 1827 while touring the districts he had governed as Collector. A memorial stone and a four-pillared mantapa at Pattikonda commemorate him, and he is remembered locally to this day.

(ii) Sir Arthur Cotton (1803–1899): water and the delta economy

- After the famine of 1832–33 devastated the Godavari districts, Cotton built the Dowleswaram Anicut across the Godavari (1847–1852), diverting the river into a canal network that converted a famine-prone tract into the "rice bowl" of the Presidency.
- He also designed the Krishna (Bezwada) Anicut, built 1852–55 by Captain Charles Orr to serve about 5.8 lakh acres in the Krishna, Guntur, West Godavari and Prakasam tracts, and promoted the Kurnool–Cuddapah (K.C.) Canal.
- His larger argument, set out in Public Works in India, was that canal navigation would distribute prosperity inland more cheaply than railways — a view the colonial state ultimately rejected in favour of rail.
- Andhra anchor: the replacement Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage (1970–82) at Dhavaleswaram and the Sir Arthur Cotton Museum at Rajamahendravaram, which preserves the tools and drawings of the 1847–52 works.

(iii) Charles Philip Brown (1798–1884): language and recovery

- Posted to Cuddapah (Kadapa), Brown mastered Telugu and turned to rescuing manuscripts that were physically decaying. He collected palm-leaf copies of Vemana's verses, translating and publishing about 1,200 verses in 1829 — the act that carried Vemana from oral circulation into print.
- His Telugu–English and English–Telugu dictionaries (1852) remain reference works. He also edited classical texts and financed copying from his own salary, famously spending several times his monthly pay on a fair copy of the Telugu Mahabharata.
- He assembled a research collection running to 34 volumes of over 20,000 pages, donated to the India Office Library

— a rescue operation without which several works would be lost.

- Andhra anchor: the C.P. Brown Library and Language Research Centre at Kadapa, taken over by Yogi Vemana University in 2006, holds rare manuscripts and copies of the Mackenzie Kaifiyats, and remains an active research centre.

## Conclusion

These three careers illustrate the ambivalence of colonial administration in Andhra. Ryotwari was designed for revenue certainty yet reshaped rural property relations for a century; canal engineering served export agriculture yet permanently ended famine in the deltas; philological scholarship served administrative command of the vernacular yet preserved Telugu's classical inheritance. Their monuments — the Cotton Barrage, the Pattikonda mantapa, the C.P. Brown Library — survive because their effects outran their intentions.

## Value addition
- Government of Andhra Pradesh (Krishna district): the Prakasam Barrage was constructed 1954–57 at a cost of about Rs. 2.28 crore, replacing Cotton's 1852 anicut which breached in 1952; it now serves an ayacut of roughly 13 lakh acres across the Krishna, Guntur, West Godavari and Prakasam tracts.
- Godavari delta system: in operation since 1852, with the modern Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage built 1970–82; the delta remains among India's oldest continuously functioning large irrigation systems and is a recognised heritage irrigation structure.
- Government of Andhra Pradesh (Kurnool district): the stone inscription at Pattikonda records Munro's death on 6 July 1827 due to cholera, alongside a four-pillar mantapa — a rare instance of a colonial administrator commemorated in local memory.
- C.P. Brown Library, Kadapa: a unit of Yogi Vemana University since 1 November 2006, holding tens of thousands of volumes and copies of the Mackenzie Kaifiyats obtained from the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library.
- Gyan Bharatam Mission (Ministry of Culture, Rs. 482.85 crore, 2024–31) and the National Manuscript Survey of 16 March 2026 continue, with state backing and digital tools, the salvage work Brown began by hand — a strong closing link between colonial philology and current policy.

## Introduction

The Rampa or Manyam Rebellion of 1922–24 was the last major armed tribal uprising of colonial Andhra, fought across the Godavari and Visakhapatnam agency tracts of the Eastern Ghats. Its leader, Alluri Sitarama Raju — born on 4 July 1897 at Pandrangi and shot dead at Koyyuru on 7 May 1924 at the age of twenty‑seven — was not himself an Adivasi. Examining his role therefore means explaining how an outsider converted scattered agrarian grievance into a disciplined two‑year insurgency that tied down the Madras government.

1. From Gandhian reform to armed struggle: the logic of the shift

- The structural grievance was forest law, not taxation. The Madras Forest Act, 1882, tightened by the 1918 amendment, criminalised podu (shifting cultivation), restricted grazing and minor forest produce, and converted the Adivasi from proprietor to trespasser on his own hill. This is why the revolt spread through muttas rather than remaining a single village affair.
- The immediate trigger was forced labour. The colonial drive to build the Narsipatnam–Chintapalle ghat road in 1922 revived vetti or begar — unpaid coolie labour under police supervision. Raju's rebellion begins precisely where this coercion peaked, which shows his timing was tactical, not merely emotional.
- His Gandhian phase was real but instrumental. He first ran panchayat courts, pushed temperance and khadi, and used his reputation as an ascetic, astrologer and healer to acquire legitimacy among the Koya and Konda Dora. When the Non‑Cooperation Movement was withdrawn in February 1922 after Chauri Chaura, the constitutional route closed — and Raju drew the conclusion that the agency's grievances would not be redressed by petition.

2. Guerrilla method: why it worked for two years

- The opening raids were sequenced, not random. Chintapalle (22 August 1922), Krishnadevipeta (23 August) and Rajavommangi (24 August) were struck on three successive days, followed by Addateegala and Rampachodavaram. Each raid was an arms‑capture operation: he was building a magazine, since the rebels had no supply line.
- Terrain was his force multiplier. Operating in the Papikonda–Chintapalle forests with local guides, a band of a few hundred fighters — not a fixed 500 — used ambush and dispersal against a force with rifles and roads. At Damanapalli in September 1922 two British officers, Scott Coward and Heiter, were killed in ambush, forcing the government to escalate.
- Leadership was shared, and that made it durable. Gam Gantam Dora and Gam Mallu Dora, both hereditary muttadars, gave the movement indigenous authority; Aggiraju supplied the link to revolutionary networks outside the agency. The rebellion survived Gantam Dora's death in 1923 precisely because command was distributed.

## Moral authority and its limits
- He enforced a code. Raju forbade plunder and personal revenge, issued written receipts for arms seized from police stations, and even announced his raids in advance — conduct that converted banditry into recognised political insurgency and denied the British the label of dacoity.
- But the movement had a ceiling. It remained confined to the agency tracts, never fused with the plains Congress organisation, and depended on one charismatic figure — so his capture ended it. This is the honest limit an examine answer must state.

## Conclusion

Examined on evidence, Raju's role was that of a converter: he translated a forest‑law grievance into the vocabulary of Swaraj, and an unarmed hill population into a disciplined guerrilla force. The rebellion was militarily crushed, yet it forced the colonial state into martial law and punitive taxation in a region it had assumed was quiescent, and it established that Adivasis were agents rather than spectators of the freedom struggle. That is why he survives in Telugu memory as Manyam Veerudu, and why the Government of India chose his life as a national commemorative anchor a century later.

## Value addition
- British counter‑insurgency response: Malabar Special Police were deployed under Commissioner T. G. Rutherford, martial law was imposed, and punitive taxes were levied on agency villages. A bounty of Rs 10,000 was announced on Raju and Rs 1,000 each on Gam Gantam Dora and Gam Mallu Dora — note the correct names, frequently mis‑spelt in coaching material.
- Government of India commemoration (PIB / PMO): the Prime Minister launched a year‑long 125th birth anniversary celebration at Bhimavaram on 4 July 2022, unveiling a 30‑foot bronze statue. PIB explicitly recorded the confluence of Azadi ka Amrit Mahotsav, the 125th Jayanti, and 100 years of the Rampa Rebellion.
- Heritage restoration approved under the same programme: Raju's birthplace at Pandrangi (Vizianagaram district), Chintapalle Police Station — the site whose attack began the rebellion — and an Alluri Dhyana Mandir at Mogallu with mural narration of his life.
- Living administrative memorial: Alluri Sitharama Raju district, headquartered at Paderu, was notified on 3 April 2022 and came into effect on 4 April 2022 when Andhra Pradesh's districts were raised from 13 to 26. Following the State's reorganisation notification effective 31 December 2025, the number now stands at 28, with a separate Polavaram district carved out at Rampachodavaram — covering the very agency mandals of the rebellion.
- Analytical hook for the introduction: the 1922–24 rising was the second Rampa revolt; an earlier uprising of 1879–80 against muttadar and excise exactions shows the grievance was structural and recurrent, not a one‑off.

## Introduction

Telugu Dalit literature is not merely writing about Dalits but writing from Dalit experience, treating lived humiliation as a legitimate source of knowledge. Emerging from Jashuva’s early protest verse and hardening into a movement after the Karamchedu massacre of July 1985, it replaced the classical ideal of rasa (aesthetic pleasure) with anubhavam (experience) as the test of literary worth — a shift rooted in Ambedkarite and Phule’s egalitarian thought.

1. The Precursor Phase (1910s–1950s): Dignity within the Canon

- Gurram Jashuva attacked exclusion using the enemy’s own weapons. Gabbilam (1941) recasts Kalidasa’s Meghadutam with a bat, not a cloud, as messenger — because only a creature that hangs in temple eaves at night can enter a shrine an untouchable cannot. The choice of a classical khandakavya form was itself the argument: mastery denied the charge of incapacity.
- Boyi Bhimanna’sPaleru (1940) dramatised bonded farm-servitude and made education the exit route, reportedly prompting many poor families to enrol children in school — literature producing measurable behavioural change.
- Kusuma Dharmanna of Rajahmundry wrote directly against untouchability and for Adi-Andhra self-naming, linking verse to the conference movement.

2. The Radical Phase (1985–1991): Massacre as Catalyst

- The killing of Madiga agricultural labourers at Karamchedu, Prakasam district (17 July 1985) destroyed the assumption that constitutional guarantees sufficed. Kathi Padma Rao and Bojja Tharakam founded the Dalit Maha Sabha in its aftermath; Padma Rao’s Padunekkina Pata (“The Song Sharpened to an Edge”) gave the movement its idiom of armed dignity.
- Tsundur, Guntur district (6 August 1991) radicalised it further. Kalekuri Prasad responded with verse declaring the poet the reincarnation of every murdered ancestor — converting mourning into political inheritance rather than lament.
- Sivasagar (K.G. Satyamurthy), co-founder of the CPI(ML) People’s War who later founded Mala Mahanadu, embodied the movement’s central critique: that class analysis alone could not explain caste, so Dalits needed autonomous organisation.

3. The Anthology Phase (1990s): From Voices to Canon

- Chikkanavutunna Pata (1995), edited by G. Laxmi Narasaiah and Tripuraneni Srinivas, gathered scattered poets into a recognisable school and forced university syllabi and literary journals to concede a separate stream.
- Endluri Sudhakar (Mallechettu, Vargeekarana), Madduri Nagesh Babu and Satish Chandar extended the range from village humiliation to urban, professional and psychological caste.

## The Dalit-Bahujan Women’s Phase (2000s onward)
- Joopaka Subhadra and Gogu Shyamala exposed the double burden of caste and gender, writing in unstandardised Telangana and Madiga dialects — the choice of dialect asserting that the “pure” literary language was itself a caste artefact.
- Kolakaluri Enoch’s Sahitya Akademi Award for Vimarsini (2018) confirmed that Dalit writing had entered mainstream critical evaluation on its own terms.

## Conclusion

Examined across a century, Telugu Dalit poets achieved three things no reform organisation could. They shifted the site of authority from scripture to experience; they converted episodic atrocity into a durable ideology of self-respect; and they compelled Telugu literature to concede that aesthetics and politics are inseparable. Their limitation was equally real — literary assertion could not by itself deliver land or end atrocity, which is why the movement moved from verse into law, reservation politics and Madiga sub-quota mobilisation.

## Value addition

The PM-AJAY Portal and AJAY Mobile App were launched on 26 May 2026, and continuation with an enhanced outlay for 2026–31 was proposed (PIB, 28 July 2026).
- Legal architecture: Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, strengthened by the 2015 and 2018 amendments — the statutory descendant of what the poets demanded.
- AP anchor: The Statue of Social Justice, a 125-ft bronze Ambedkar on an 81-ft pedestal (206 ft total) at Dr B.R. Ambedkar Swaraj Maidan, Vijayawada, unveiled 19 January 2024 within the 18.81-acre Smriti Vanam — the tallest Ambedkar statue in the world, sculpted by Ram Vanji Sutar.

## Introduction

The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 (Act No. 6 of 2014), enacted under Article 3, bifurcated the State with effect from the appointed day, 2 June 2014. Part VIII of the Act, comprising Sections 47 to 68, governs the apportionment of assets and liabilities, and Section 47(3) expressly promises that apportionment shall be subject to such financial adjustment as is necessary to secure a "just, reasonable and equitable" division. The difficulty for the residuary State of Andhra Pradesh is not that this promise was absent, but that the sections meant to deliver it apply two mutually inconsistent yardsticks — and the yardstick that governs assets works systematically against a State that lost its capital city.

1. The core inconsistency: assets divided by location, liabilities by population

- Assets follow location. Section 48 vests land and goods in the State where they lie. Section 53 goes further: the assets and liabilities of any commercial or industrial undertaking exclusively located in a local area pass to the State containing that area, "irrespective of the location of its headquarters". Physical situs, not contribution, decides ownership.
- Liabilities follow population. Section 54 apportions the entire Public Debt and Public Account of the undivided State on the population ratio, roughly 58.32 : 41.68 in Andhra Pradesh's favour on 2011 Census figures. Section 57 (deposits) and Section 58 apply the same or a service-linked test.
- Why this is an inconsistency, not merely a hardship. Andhra Pradesh inherited about 58% of the debt because it holds about 58% of the people, but it inherited only those assets physically standing on its soil. Since Hyderabad — the administrative, industrial and institutional core built by the undivided State over fifty-eight years — fell within Telangana, the location test allocated the accumulated capital to one successor while the population test allocated the accumulated debt largely to the other. Two provisions of the same Part measure the same estate by different rulers.

2. The undefined "headquarters": a legislative gap filled by executive order

- Section 68 read with the Ninth Schedule covers 91 companies and corporations, whose assets are apportioned "in the manner provided in Section 53". But the Act nowhere defines what constitutes a headquarters, even though Section 53 turns on distinguishing headquarters from operational units.
- The Ministry of Home Affairs had to supply the meaning by clarification in May 2017 — that the location of the principal office building determines the headquarters. A statutory silence being cured seventeen years' worth of disputes later, by executive gloss rather than amendment, is itself evidence of drafting inconsistency.
- Consequence: the definition became the object of litigation rather than the solution to it. The A.P. State Financial

Corporation dispute, including the contest over 238 acres in Rangareddy district under a High Court status quo order since November 2015, turns precisely on whether disputed land forms part of "headquarters" assets.

## Revenue provisions that reward the place of assessment
- Sections 50, 51 and 56 — arrears of taxes, the right to recover loans and advances, and refund of taxes collected in excess — allocate by reference to the place of assessment or the situs of the transaction.
- Because most large corporate assessees of the undivided State were registered in Hyderabad, arrears realised after bifurcation accrue overwhelmingly to Telangana, while the corresponding refund liability can fall on the residuary State. Andhra Pradesh has pressed for amendment of exactly these sections.
- Section 46 attempted a corrective by providing for a revenue-deficit grant and a Presidential reference to the Fourteenth Finance Commission — but this was a transitional palliative, not a structural repair of the split yardstick.

## A promise of equity with no timeline and no arbiter
- Section 47(4) says disputes over financial assets and liabilities shall be settled by mutual agreement, failing which by order of the Central Government on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor-General. There is no outer time limit and no consequence for delay.
- The contrast within the Act is instructive: Section 85 gave the River Management Boards a statutory existence and Section 84 gave water disputes an Apex Council, but assets got no equivalent standing machinery. Water was institutionalised; property was left to negotiation.
- Result: the Sheela Bhide Expert Committee recommended division for 89 of the 91 Ninth Schedule institutions; Telangana accepted the recommendations selectively while Andhra Pradesh sought their acceptance in full, and the deadlock has held. Andhra Pradesh ultimately moved the Supreme Court seeking a "just, reasonable and equitable" apportionment — invoking Section 47(3) against the very Act that contains it.

## Capital-building cost treated as the successor's burden, not a bifurcation liability
- Section 5 made Hyderabad the common capital for up to ten years and required Andhra Pradesh to build a new one, yet the Act nowhere treats the cost of creating an entire capital, Secretariat, High Court and Raj Bhavan as a liability of the division to be shared.
- The asymmetry is stark: Telangana inherited a functioning capital as a located asset; Andhra Pradesh inherited the obligation to build one, financed from its own borrowing, which then counted against its debt ceiling. Statutory finality came only with the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2026, which substituted Section 5(2) to declare Amaravati the sole capital — twelve years after the appointed day.

## Conclusion

The Act's failure was not of intention but of internal coherence. Section 47(3) held out equity as the governing standard, yet Sections 48, 53 and 54 were left to operate on incompatible tests, the pivotal term "headquarters" was never defined, and no forum was armed with a deadline. The residuary State therefore carried a population-sized debt against a territory-sized asset base, and negotiation without a clock produced twelve years of stalemate rather than settlement. The remedy suggested by this experience is generic to Article 3 reorganisations: any future division statute should fix a single, stated principle for both assets and liabilities, define its operative terms, and vest a time-bound adjudicatory authority — on the model of the Section 85 Boards — so that equity is enforced rather than merely promised.

## Value addition
- Statutory anatomy: Part VIII = Sections 47–68. Section 47(3) — "just, reasonable and equitable"; Section 47(4) — CAG-advised Central order; Section 53 — location over headquarters; Section 54 — public debt on population ratio.
- The numbers to quote: Ninth Schedule — 91 companies and corporations, assets of about ₹1.42 lakh crore. Tenth Schedule — 142 institutions, about ₹24,018.53 crore. A further 12 institutions not listed in the Act at all, about ₹1,759 crore.
- Population ratio: 58.32 : 41.68 (AP : Telangana), from the 2011 Census — residuary Andhra Pradesh is the larger share. A very common error is to reverse this.
- MHA machinery: May 2017 clarification defining headquarters as the principal office building; dispute-resolution sub-committee's three-phase formula — 53 uncontested PSUs, 15 acceptable to Telangana alone, 22 not acceptable to Telangana.
- Current anchor (2026): Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2026 — passed by Lok Sabha 1 April and Rajya Sabha 2 April 2026, Presidential assent 6 April 2026; amends Section 5(2) to make Amaravati the sole and permanent capital, with retrospective effect from 2 June 2024 (Source: newsonair.gov.in).
- Fiscal anchor (2026): Sixteenth Finance Commission (Dr. Arvind Panagariya) report submitted 17 November 2025 and tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2026 for 2026–31; vertical devolution retained at 41%, with a new 10% weight for a State's contribution to GDP (Source: PIB).
