## Introduction

The Eleventh Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, read with Section 85(7)(e), lays down ten principles governing the functioning of the River Management Boards. Its architecture is three-tiered: Section 84 creates an Apex Council chaired by the Union Minister for Water Resources with the two Chief Ministers as members; Section 85 constitutes the Krishna River Management Board (KRMB) and the Godavari River Management Board (GRMB), both established on the appointed day; and the Eleventh Schedule supplies the substantive rules by which the Boards must decide. The Schedule's ambition is to convert a political quarrel over water into an administered allocation. Its record shows how far substantive rules can travel without enforcement power behind them.

## Family one — supremacy of adjudication (Principles 1, 4 and 5)
- Principle 1 makes the operation protocol notified by the Ministry of Water Resources, arrived at on appropriate dependability criteria after adjudication by the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal, binding on both successor States.
- Principle 4 preserves tribunal allocations already made for projects on the Godavari and Krishna, and Principle 5 makes any future tribunal allocation of excess flows binding on both.
- Significance: together these subordinate bargaining power to adjudicated hydrology. Neither State may re-open a settled share by pleading need, drought or political urgency — the tribunal award, not the assembly resolution, is the currency of entitlement.

## Family two — a hierarchy of use (Principles 2 and 3)
- Principle 2: where irrigation and power compete, irrigation prevails. Principle 3: where irrigation and drinking water compete, drinking water prevails. The resulting order of precedence is drinking water → irrigation → power.
- Why it matters: the two successor States sit at different points on both rivers, and hydel generation at an upstream reservoir physically competes with downstream releases. Without a stated hierarchy, every low-flow year would become a fresh negotiation.
- Illustration: the Srisailam and Nagarjuna Sagar complexes on the Krishna serve hydel generation, Rayalaseema and coastal delta irrigation, and municipal supply for large populations in both States simultaneously. Principle 3 is what allows a drinking-water indent to be honoured ahead of a power indent in a deficit rabi season.

## Family three — regulatory gatekeeping over new projects (Principle 7)
- Principle 7 bars either State from taking up any new project on the Krishna or Godavari without sanction of the Apex Council, and requires that every such proposal be first appraised and technically cleared by the respective Board. It is reinforced by Section 85(8)(d), which makes appraisal of new-project proposals a statutory function of the Boards.
- This is the most litigated principle in the Schedule, because it is the only one that constrains a State's freedom of action on its own territory.
- Live illustration: Andhra Pradesh's proposed diversion of about 200 TMC of Godavari flood water towards the Krishna and Penna basins — the Polavaram–Banakacherla link, now advanced as the Polavaram–Nallamala Sagar Link Project under the National River Linking Policy. Telangana objected that the proposal proceeded without GRMB, KRMB and Apex Council clearance and announced in June 2025 that it would move the Supreme Court.

4. Family four — execution, penalty and protection (Principles 6, 8, 9 and 10)

- Principle 8 places execution of ongoing and future projects on the State in whose territory the project lies — responsibility follows territory even where the water is shared.
- Principle 9 provides that a State which does not implement a decision shall bear the responsibility and face financial and other penalties imposed by the Central Government. This is the Schedule's only sanction, and it has never been invoked.
- Principle 6 makes the Boards advisers on disaster, drought and flood management while leaving actual calamity management with the States; Principle 10 protects irrigation projects already under construction, which must be completed as per plan.

5. The functioning record: principles ahead of practice

- Delayed empowerment. Both Boards were constituted on the appointed day in 2014, but their jurisdiction was notified only on 15 July 2021, following the Apex Council meeting of 6 October 2020. For seven years the Boards existed without defined project-wise authority — the clearest evidence that the Schedule's principles lacked an enforcement engine.
- Allocation still ad hoc. Krishna water between the two States has been shared on a working ratio of 512 : 299 out of the undivided State's 811 TMC entitlement under the Bachawat award, renewed year to year rather than adjudicated. The Union Cabinet issued further Terms of Reference to KWDT-II on 4 October 2023, under Section 5(1) of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, to make project-wise allocations between Telangana and Andhra Pradesh — twelve years of interim arrangement preceding the reference.
- Godavari has no post-bifurcation tribunal at all. The Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal award dates from 1980 and predates the division. In February 2026 the Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister formally sought constitution of a new Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal along with gazette notification of the Vamsadhara Tribunal report — a gap the Eleventh Schedule assumes away by presupposing tribunal awards it does not have.
- Executive substitution for statutory process. At the meeting chaired by the Union Jal Shakti Minister with both Chief Ministers on 16 July 2025, it was decided to constitute a high-level technical committee on the Polavaram– Banakacherla issue, to install telemetry devices at reservoir off-take points, to set up a separate KRMB office at Amaravati with GRMB at Hyderabad, and to address Srisailam dam maintenance. That a ministerial committee, not the Boards, brokered these outcomes shows where real authority sits.
- Structural weakness — the Boards are funded by the parties they regulate. Under Section 86(2) the successor States must provide the funds for the Boards' expenses, apportioned as the Central Government specifies. A regulator financed by its regulatees has limited leverage over either.

## Conclusion

The Eleventh Schedule is substantively sound: it makes adjudication supreme, fixes a defensible hierarchy of use, and requires prior appraisal of every new project. Its weakness is remedial rather than normative. The Boards can appraise but cannot restrain; the only penalty lies with the Centre and has never been used; the Boards are financed by the States they oversee; and on the Godavari the Schedule presumes an adjudicated framework that bifurcation never produced. The Banakacherla episode and the twelve-year interim on Krishna sharing both point the same way — towards a binding project-wise award from KWDT-II, a fresh Godavari tribunal, and real-time telemetry as the factual foundation on which any of these principles can actually bite. Until then, the Schedule remains a well-drafted charter awaiting an enforcer.

## Value addition
- Exact citation to quote: The Eleventh Schedule is expressly headed "[See section 85(7)(e)]" and is titled "Principles governing the functioning of the River Management Boards". It contains ten numbered principles.
- Order of precedence (the single most quotable point): drinking water over irrigation (Principle 3); irrigation over power (Principle 2).
- Institutional dates: Boards constituted 2 June 2014; Apex Council meeting 6 October 2020; jurisdiction notified 15 July 2021; further ToR to KWDT-II approved by Union Cabinet 4 October 2023 under Section 5(1), ISRWD Act, 1956 (Source: pmindia.gov.in).
- Krishna figures: KWDT-I (Bachawat, 1976) allotted 811 TMC to undivided Andhra Pradesh at 75% dependability; post-2014 working share 512 TMC (AP) : 299 TMC (Telangana). Do not attribute 811 TMC to residuary AP.
- Current anchors (2025–26): 16 July 2025 — Union Jal Shakti Minister's meeting with both CMs: high-level technical committee on Polavaram–Banakacherla, telemetry at off-take points, KRMB office at Amaravati and GRMB at Hyderabad, Srisailam dam maintenance. 10 February 2026 — AP CM sought permanent withdrawal of the

Polavaram stop-work order, support for Polavaram Phase-II (about ₹32,000 crore), approvals for the Polavaram– Nallamala Sagar Link under the National River Linking Policy, and constitution of a Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal (Source: newsonair.gov.in).

- Polavaram fiscal data: Phase-I revised cost estimate ₹30,436.95 crore at 41.15 m; balance central grant limited to ₹12,157.53 crore; central releases of about ₹12,620.53 crore over the last five years (Ministry of Jal Shakti reply, Rajya Sabha).
- Constitutional linkage: Article 262 and Entry 56 of the Union List — the Boards operate in the space where the Union may regulate inter-State rivers, which is why Principle 9 vests the penalty in the Central Government rather than in the Boards.

## Introduction

Climatic controls are the permanent physical factors that govern the temperature, pressure, wind and precipitation regime of a place. Six are conventionally recognised: latitude, altitude, pressure and wind systems, distance from the sea, ocean and atmospheric circulation, and relief. India's climate is classified as tropical monsoon, but that single label conceals extremes ranging from the near-perpetual snow of the Karakoram to the rain shadow aridity of Anantapuram — a range explained entirely by how these six controls combine over a very large landmass.

## Latitude — the primary control
- India extends from about 8°N to 37°N, with the Tropic of Cancer bisecting it. The south therefore receives near-vertical insolation year round and has a small annual temperature range, while the north lies in the sub-tropics and experiences a marked seasonal swing.
- Consequence: Kerala's annual range is a few degrees; Punjab swings from near freezing to above 45 °C. Andhra Pradesh lies wholly within the tropics, which is why the state has no true winter and why its coastal districts show an annual range of only about 18 °C to 32 °C.

## Altitude — the modifier that overrides latitude
- Temperature falls with height at roughly 6.5 °C per kilometre, so elevation can invert what latitude dictates.
- Consequence: Shimla is cooler than Delhi though further south. Within a wholly tropical state, Lambasingi in Alluri Sitarama Raju district records near 0 °C and occasional frost, earning it the name "Andhra Kashmir" — the cleanest possible illustration that altitude, not latitude, is decisive locally.

## Pressure and wind systems — the control that creates the monsoon
- Differential heating of land and sea shifts the pressure field seasonally; the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone migrates north in summer and south in winter, reversing the wind direction. The upper-air jets, as discussed in the previous answer, fix the timing.
- Consequence: the entire four-season Indian calendar — cold weather, hot weather, advancing monsoon and retreating monsoon — is a product of this single control.

## Distance from the sea — continentality
- Water heats and cools more slowly than land, so maritime locations have moderated ranges and interior locations extreme ones.
- Consequence: Mumbai and Chennai are equable; Nagpur and Delhi are extreme. Within Andhra Pradesh the same contrast is visible at short range — the coastal districts are moderated by land and sea breezes, while Rayalaseema, cut off from maritime influence, shows a much larger annual and diurnal range, and Rentachintala in Palnadu records the state's highest temperatures at around 47–48 °C.

## Ocean and atmospheric circulation
- Correction — distinguish two different things here. The relevant current is the seasonally reversing monsoon current of the North Indian Ocean, with the Somali upwelling that cools the western Arabian Sea in summer. The El Niño–Southern Oscillation and the Indian Ocean Dipole are not currents; they are coupled ocean–atmosphere oscillations that alter the pressure field.
- Consequence: an El Niño year shifts convection eastward into the Pacific and typically suppresses Indian rainfall, while a positive Indian Ocean Dipole warms the western Indian Ocean and can offset it. India is largely spared the strong thermal currents that shape Western European or Japanese climate, so these oscillations, not currents, are the main source of interannual variability.

## Relief — the control that creates local extremes
- Mountains block, lift and shelter. The Himalayas exclude cold Central Asian air; the Western Ghats intercept the Arabian Sea branch, giving a windward-leeward contrast of an order of magnitude.
- Consequence: Mawsynram receives world-record rainfall from orographic lifting in the Khasi hills, while barely 100 km from the drenched Ghat crest lies the Deccan rain shadow. That same shadow reaches Andhra Pradesh: Anantapuram, receiving under 600 mm, is among the driest districts in India, while the Eastern Ghats force lifting of

the Bay branch and make the Sabari–Sileru valley the wettest tract of the state.

A simple radial diagram: write "India's Climate" in a small circle at the centre and run six spokes outward, one per control. On each spoke write the mechanism in three words and one named example — "Latitude → insolation → Kerala v. Punjab", "Relief → rain shadow → Anantapuram". Six spokes reproduce in under a minute and demonstrate the "how" half of the question visually.

## Conclusion

Climatic controls do not operate in isolation; they compound. Latitude makes India tropical, the Himalayan relief keeps it so, continentality and altitude create the internal extremes, and the seasonal reversal of the pressure and wind field welds the whole into a single monsoon regime. Andhra Pradesh is a useful microcosm — within one tropical state, relief produces a near-frost station at Lambasingi, continentality produces 48 °C at Rentachintala, and rain shadow produces chronic drought at Anantapuram. Understanding the controls is therefore not academic: it is the basis for agro-climatic zoning, cropping advisories and climate resilience planning.

## Value addition
- The four-season framework to name explicitly: cold weather (December–February), hot weather (March–May), advancing south-west monsoon (June–September) and retreating north-east monsoon (October–November). Seasonal contrast is sharpest in the interior and muted along the coast, where rainfall rather than temperature varies.
- Andhra Pradesh climatic superlatives worth carrying into any climate answer: coldest place Lambasingi, Alluri Sitarama Raju; hottest place Rentachintala, Palnadu; driest district Anantapuram; wettest tract the Sabari–Sileru valley; normal annual rainfall about 912 mm; pre-monsoon showers known locally as mamidi tuparlu or mango showers.
- Observed change, useful in the conclusion of any climate question: the number of very heavy rainfall days is rising while moderate rain days fall, so the same annual total now arrives in fewer and more damaging events; the state has warmed roughly 0.5–0.8 °C over the past century; and severe cyclonic storms in the Bay of Bengal are becoming more frequent.
- Policy hooks: the State Action Plan on Climate Change, the Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming programme — among the largest agro-ecological programmes anywhere — and mangrove restoration at Coringa as coastal adaptation.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh shows marked edaphic diversity because parent rock, rainfall and drainage all change sharply from west to east. Red soils dominate at about 65 per cent of the area, followed by black soils at about 25 per cent, alluvial at about 5 per cent, laterite about 3 per cent and coastal sandy about 2 per cent. Black and alluvial soils together carry the state's two principal farming systems — dryland cotton and chilli in the interior, and irrigated paddy and sugarcane in the deltas — which is why they are singled out for examination.

## Black soils (regur, locally nalla regadi)

## Origin and parent material
- Formed under low rainfall of roughly 500–1,000 mm and high temperature, conditions that favour clay accumulation over leaching.
- Correction — in Andhra Pradesh these soils are derived largely from lime-rich Cuddapah shales and

limestone and from weathered gneiss, not from Deccan Trap basalt. Trap basalt is confined to a small north-western fringe of the state. Writing "weathered from Deccan lava" is the standard mistake in this answer and the examiner notices it, because it is a Maharashtra explanation transplanted to Andhra.

## Physical characteristics
- Deep black to dark brown, from iron and titanium compounds combined with humus, not from high organic content.
- Very high clay fraction of the swelling montmorillonite type, giving high shrink–swell capacity. The soil swells and seals when wet and cracks widely when dry.
- Those cracks are agriculturally decisive: they carry the surface layer downward and turn the profile over, which is why regur is called self-ploughing and why it sustains rain-fed crops through long dry spells on stored moisture alone.

## Chemical characteristics
- Rich in lime, iron, magnesia, alumina and potash; deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter.
- High cation exchange capacity, and a neutral to slightly alkaline reaction, which is why nutrient response is good but drainage-induced alkalinity is a standing risk.

## Distribution and crops
- Kurnool, Nandyal, Guntur, Palnadu, Prakasam and parts of Anantapuram.
- Cotton, chilli, turmeric, tobacco, jowar and gram. The Guntur–Palnadu black soil tract underlies India's largest chilli market at Guntur; Kurnool's irrigated black soils under the Tungabhadra system carry cotton and sunflower.

## Alluvial soils

## Origin and parent material
- Transported soils, deposited by the Krishna, Godavari and Penna. Because deposition is continuous, the profile is geologically young and constantly renewed — the source of their fertility.

## Physical characteristics
- Light grey to ash brown; loamy to sandy loam, with clay loams in the older delta interiors.
- Stratified rather than horizoned, because each flood lays a fresh layer; profiles are deep, easily worked and moderately drained — ideal for intensive multiple cropping.

## Chemical characteristics
- Rich in potash and lime, moderately supplied with phosphate, deficient in nitrogen and organic carbon.
- Reaction near neutral. Micronutrient deficiency, particularly zinc, is widespread — a general feature of Andhra soils rather than of the deltas alone.

## Distribution and crops
- The Krishna, Godavari and Penna basins and deltas — Konaseema, East and West Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Bapatla and Nellore.
- Paddy, sugarcane, banana, coconut, oil palm and vegetables, supported by the Dowleswaram anicut on the Godavari and the Prakasam barrage on the Krishna, which together made this one of India's most productive agro-ecosystems.

## Degradation — the point that converts description into evaluation
- Black soils: waterlogging where canal irrigation has been introduced without drainage; salinity and alkalinity build-up; sheet and gully erosion on the Rayalaseema slopes and ravines along the Penna.
- Alluvial soils: salinity and sodicity along the delta margins, worsened by aquaculture effluent in Krishna, Guntur and Nellore; declining organic carbon under continuous paddy; and loss of fertile deltaic land to urban and industrial conversion.

## Conclusion

The two soils are the physical basis of the state's dual agrarian economy. Black soils allow a rain-fed system in a semi-arid interior, because their moisture retention substitutes for irrigation; alluvial soils allow an intensive irrigated system in the deltas, because continuous deposition substitutes for fertility management. Both are now under stress from the same source — water applied or withheld in the wrong quantity, producing alkalinity in one and salinity in the other. Soil health card based nutrient management, drainage alongside irrigation, zinc and organic carbon correction, and the state's natural farming programme are therefore not soil-conservation extras but the condition for sustaining output.

## Value addition
- The correct shares, worth memorising in order: red about 65 per cent, black about 25, alluvial about 5, laterite about 3, coastal sandy about 2. Mnemonic: Red > Black > Alluvial > Laterite > Sandy. Reject the 30 per cent alluvial figure that circulates in coaching material — alluvium is confined to two delta tracts and cannot approach a third of the state.
- The general deficiency across Andhra Pradesh is zinc, with nitrogen and organic carbon widely low. Naming zinc specifically signals familiarity with state soil survey findings rather than generic textbook content.
- Laterite and sandy soils, in one line each for a fuller answer if time allows: laterite forms by intense leaching in the high-rainfall Eastern Ghats of North Andhra and at Sullurpeta and Kavali, hardens on exposure and is quarried as brick, and carries cashew and plantation crops; coastal sandy soils are saline and highly permeable and support casuarina and cashew shelter belts.
- Conservation measures to close on: contour bunding and contour ploughing on plateau slopes, terracing in the agency areas, check dams and percolation tanks, casuarina shelter belts along the coast, green manuring and crop rotation, and the state's community managed natural farming programme.

## Introduction

About 95 per cent of India’s trade by volume and 70 per cent by value moves by sea, yet logistics costs have long run well above comparable economies, and a coastline of roughly 11,099 km with 14,500 km of navigable waterways was carrying a fraction of domestic freight. The Sagarmala Programme, launched in March 2015 by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, addresses this by shifting the development model from building ports to organising economic activity around them — port-led development.

## Objectives
- Reduce logistics cost for domestic and EXIM cargo by correcting the modal mix. Coastal shipping and inland waterways move bulk far more cheaply per tonne-kilometre than road, so shifting even a fraction of bulk freight lowers the cost of the entire traded economy rather than of any single sector.
- Improve export competitiveness by locating manufacturing adjacent to ports, so that the exporter pays inland freight once rather than twice.
- Modernise capacity — de-bottleneck existing ports and build deep-draft greenfield ports for larger vessels, since vessel size determines unit freight cost — and integrate hinterland connectivity through rail, road, waterway and freight corridors, because a modern port with a congested approach is no improvement at all.
- Develop coastal communities through skilling, fisheries infrastructure and tourism, so that the coastal population shares in port-led growth instead of being displaced by it.

## Five Pillars and Twenty-Four Categories
- Port modernisation and new port development — mechanisation, digitisation and greenfield ports such as Vadhavan in Maharashtra and Galathea Bay as a transshipment hub.
- Port connectivity enhancement — multimodal links under the Comprehensive Port Connectivity Plan, dedicated freight corridors, Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax services.
- Port-led industrialisation — Coastal Economic Zones and port-proximate industrial clusters.
- Coastal community development — livelihoods, fishing harbours, skilling and coastal tourism.
- Coastal shipping and inland waterways transport — the lowest-carbon freight mode, relieving road and rail congestion simultaneously.
- Institutional backbone: the National Sagarmala Apex Committee (May 2015), the Maritime States Development Council for Centre–State coordination, State Sagarmala Committees, and the Sagarmala Finance Corporation Limited (SMFCL) — SDCL restructured in June 2025 into India’s first maritime-sector NBFC, which sanctioned about Rs.4,300 crore in loans by December 2025.

## Why It Matters — Outcome Evidence
- Scale.845 projects worth Rs.6.06 lakh crore have been taken up; as of 24 March 2026, 315 projects worth Rs.1.57 lakh crore are complete, 210 under implementation and 320 in planning.
- Throughput and efficiency. Major ports handled a record 915.17 million tonnes in FY 2025–26, above the 904 MT target and 7.06 per cent higher year on year, while average vessel turnaround time fell from 96 hours in 2014 to 49.5 hours in 2025 — turnaround being the single metric that most directly converts into freight cost.
- Modal shift. Inland waterway cargo rose from 18.10 MTPA in 2013–14 to 145.50 MTPA in 2024–25, roughly 700 per cent, and coastal shipping grew 118 per cent over the decade.

- Livelihoods. Eleven fishing harbour projects worth Rs.1,057 crore are complete, benefiting over 30,000 fishermen; 17 Ro-Pax and ferry projects have served more than 35 lakh passengers; cumulative employment potential is about one crore jobs.
- Strategic value. Deep-draft capacity and a domestic transshipment hub reduce dependence on Colombo and Singapore, keeping cargo and value addition within Indian jurisdiction — a supply-chain resilience argument as much as an economic one.

## Conclusion

Sagarmala’s contribution has been to reframe ports from transit points into organising centres for industry, employment and freight choice. The measurable gains — halved turnaround, a sevenfold rise in waterway cargo, record throughput — establish that the model works. The unfinished agenda is shipbuilding capacity and last-mile hinterland connectivity, which Sagarmala 2.0 and the Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 now target directly.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh has a coastline of 1,053.07 km — the third longest in India — carrying one major port at Visakhapatnam under the Government of India and 17 notified ports under the state government, of which three are captive. Its strategic value lies less in length than in bathymetry: tranquil, deep water close to shore at many points, with NH-16 and the Howrah–Chennai trunk railway running parallel to the coast. The state projects a US$20 billion Blue Economy by 2035 on this base.

## The Port System as It Actually Stands
- Visakhapatnam — the only major port, a natural deep-water harbour, India’s largest east-coast port by cargo and among the world’s top 20 for container traffic; it handles iron ore, coal, petroleum and containers.
- Operational non-major ports and their 2025–26 performance to November 2025: Krishnapatnam (11 berths, 98 MMT capacity) handled 41.09 million tonnes yielding Rs.2,561.94 crore of gross revenue; Gangavaram (64 MMT capacity) handled 24.39 million tonnes; Kakinada Deep Water Port (7 berths, 26 MMT) handled 12.93 million tonnes with a government share of Rs.117.48 crore; Kakinada Anchorage handled 2.01 million tonnes; and Ravva, a single-buoy-mooring crude terminal, 0.398 million tonnes.

- Stalled: Vodarevu in Bapatla and Nizampatnam in Guntur, proposed on BOOT terms, have not progressed as the matter is under CBI investigation — a useful and honest illustration that port-led growth is contingent on governance, not only on geography.

## How Ports Transmit Into Economic Development
- Trade and freight cost. A deep-draft port close to the producer converts a landlocked cost structure into a coastal one. Krishnapatnam serves not only Nellore but the Rayalaseema and Telangana hinterland — which is the economic case for a network of non-major ports rather than a single national port.
- Industrial clustering. Ports anchor the corridors: Kakinada SEZ for petroleum and fertiliser, the Krishnapatnam node under CBIC, and the Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor — India’s first coastal economic corridor under ADB assistance — linking port capacity to hinterland manufacturing. Heavy industry at Visakhapatnam exists because of the harbour, not merely beside it.
- Employment. The four upcoming ports carry investment of about Rs.16,000 crore and are projected to add 145 MTPA of capacity by 2030 with direct and indirect employment above 75,000; the APMB’s Phase-II proposal of roughly Rs.18,000 crore targets a further 300 MTPA and over 1,00,000 jobs by 2047.
- Multimodal integration. The Obulavaripalli–Krishnapatnam rail link improved evacuation, NH-16 runs the length of the coast, the Raipur–Visakhapatnam Expressway will connect Chhattisgarh’s mineral hinterland, and NW-4 offers a low-cost inland option. Evacuation capacity, not berth capacity, is usually the binding constraint.
- Fisheries and the Blue Economy. The state is building four Phase-I fishing harbours at Juvvaladinne, Nizampatnam, Machilipatnam and Uppada (Rs.1,522.80 crore, at 97.98, 81.61, 71.45 and 84.29 per cent progress), five more in Phase-II (Rs.1,977.77 crore) and six fish landing centres (Rs.126.91 crore) — converting an artisanal fishery into an export supply chain, given that Andhra Pradesh leads India in fish and shrimp production.

- Utilisation lags capacity. Against 2025–26 targets, Krishnapatnam achieved 41.09 MT of a 61.25 MT target and Kakinada Deep Water 12.93 MT of 20 MT by November 2025 — adding berths does not by itself add cargo.
- Inter-port competition. A dense cluster of ports chasing the same hinterland risks stranding assets at the smaller facilities.
- Environmental and social cost. Capital dredging, shoreline alteration, effluent discharge and displacement of fishing communities remain unresolved where greenfield ports occupy active fishing shoreline — and governance risk is real, as the Vodarevu–Nizampatnam stalling shows.

Andhra Pradesh’s ports have already decentralised industrial growth away from inland cities and given the Rayalaseema and Telangana hinterland a competitive sea outlet. The next phase, however, turns on utilisation rather than construction — hinterland evacuation, cargo aggregation and resolution of the governance and environmental questions that currently hold four projects short of completion. Managed well, the 1,053 km coastline is the state’s answer to the fiscal constraint that bifurcation imposed on it.

## Introduction

The demographic dividend is the accelerated economic growth that becomes available when falling fertility shrinks the child cohort faster than the elderly cohort expands, so that the working-age population (15–64) grows as a share of the total and the dependency ratio falls. India entered this phase around 2005–06 and is now near its peak, with roughly two-thirds of its population in the working ages and a median age of about 28. Crucially, the dividend is conditional, not automatic: age structure only creates the possibility of growth, and converts into growth solely when the additional workers are healthy, skilled and actually employed.

1. How age structure becomes growth: the transmission channels

- Labour supply: a larger working-age share directly raises output per head of total population, even before productivity improves. This is the arithmetic component and the easiest to realise.
- Savings and capital deepening: households in their prime earning years save more than those supporting many children, so the national savings rate rises, lowering the cost of capital and financing investment. This is the channel East Asia exploited most successfully.
- Human capital: with fewer children per household, spending per child on schooling and nutrition rises. The dividend thus compounds into a "second dividend" through a better-educated succeeding generation.
- Female participation: lower fertility releases women into the labour force. India's recent gains here — female LFPR rising from 23.3 per cent in 2017–18 to about 40 per cent now — represent the single largest untapped source of growth, though much of the increase is in unpaid family work in agriculture rather than in paid employment, which tempers the claim.

## The binding constraints
- Employability rather than enrolment is the deficit. India has near-universal primary enrolment, but only a small single-digit share of the workforce has received formal vocational training, and industry repeatedly reports that a large proportion of graduates are not job-ready. The gap is between certification and capability.
- Youth unemployment remains concentrated among the educated and the urban: at 9.9 per cent overall in 2025, but 13.6 per cent for urban youth. Unemployment in India is not a shortage of work but a shortage of work that matches aspirations — which is why the problem worsens with education level.
- Informality caps the quality of the dividend. A workforce overwhelmingly without written contracts or social security cannot accumulate the savings or skills that the dividend theory assumes.
- Asynchronous transition across states is a structural complication: Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh are already ageing, while Bihar and Uttar Pradesh remain in the high-fertility phase. National averages therefore mislead,

and the policy response must be state-specific — skilling and job creation in the north, care economy and productivity in the south.

3. The Andhra Pradesh case: a window closing early

- Andhra Pradesh's dividend window is narrower than India's and will shut sooner. Decadal growth in 2001–11 was 9.21 per cent against 17.72 per cent nationally, total fertility has been below replacement for years, and the share of persons above 60 is among the higher figures for Indian states.
- The policy consequence is asymmetric urgency. For Bihar the task is to create jobs for a still-expanding youth cohort; for Andhra Pradesh it is to raise productivity and build a care and silver economy before the elderly share climbs further. Sustained out-migration of working-age men to Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai and the Gulf accelerates this ageing at home.

## Conclusion

India's demographic dividend is a one-time, time-bound endowment that will not recur. Its realisation depends less on the number of young people than on whether they are trained, healthy, mobile and absorbed into productive work — failing which a youth bulge becomes a source of social strain rather than growth. The decisive test over the next decade is whether formal job creation and female participation can rise together, and whether ageing southern states such as Andhra Pradesh can pivot from a quantity-of-labour to a productivity-of-labour strategy before their window closes.

- PM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (PM-VBRY), the renamed Employment Linked Incentive Scheme effective 1 August 2025: outlay Rs. 99,446 crore, targeting over 3.5 crore jobs in two years, of which 1.92 crore are first-time entrants; Part A pays first-timers one month's EPF wage up to Rs. 15,000, Part B incentivises employers, with extended benefits for manufacturing.

## Introduction

A rural settlement is a habitation whose inhabitants are engaged primarily in agriculture and allied primary activities, and whose form is the most direct expression of human adaptation to the physical environment available. India, with over six lakh villages, displays the full range of settlement forms. Their classification rests on a single organising variable — the degree of nucleation, that is, how closely dwellings cluster — which itself is decided chiefly by the security of water supply and the safety of the locality.

## Types of rural settlements

## (a) Compact or clustered (nucleated)
- Dwellings are built closely together around a nucleus — typically a temple, tank or market — with agricultural land lying outside the built-up core. The determining condition is fertile land plus assured water, which makes land too valuable to scatter houses across and allows a large population to be supported from a small radius.
- Found across the Indo-Gangetic plains and, in Andhra Pradesh, throughout the Krishna and Godavari deltas and the canal-irrigated tracts. Compactness also arises defensively in arid Rajasthan and Bundelkhand, where scarce water points force clustering.

## (b) Semi-clustered or fragmented
- A dominant central cluster with one or more detached hamlets at a distance. The cause is usually social rather than physical: dominant landowning groups occupy the core while subordinate caste or occupational groups settle at the margins — segregation written into the village plan itself.
- Common in Gujarat and parts of Rajasthan, and in Andhra Pradesh across the Rayalaseema and interior uplands.

## (c) Hamleted
- The village is physically split into several distinct units, known locally as panna, para, palli or dhani, although they share a single revenue identity. Found in the middle and lower Ganga plains, Chhattisgarh and the lower Himalayan valleys, driven by caste or ethnic segmentation.

## (d) Dispersed or isolated
- Isolated homesteads or tiny hamlets separated by fields or forest. The cause is fragmented terrain: where cultivable patches are small and scattered, farmers must live beside their plots rather than commute to them.
- Typical of Kerala, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and the Meghalaya hills. In Andhra Pradesh, the agency tracts of the Eastern Ghats — Alluri Sitharama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam, the Nallamala — are the classic dispersed zone, where podu cultivation and forest-produce collection require a wide catchment per household.

## Factors affecting rural settlements
- Physical factors are primary: water availability above all, then relief, soil fertility and drainage. Settlements avoid flood-prone hollows and locate on levees, terrace edges and tank bunds — which is why the deltaic villages of coastal Andhra sit on slightly raised ground.
- Socio-cultural factors: caste organisation, kinship and religious institutions determine internal layout. The persistence of separate hamlets for particular communities is a settlement-geography fact with direct welfare-delivery consequences.
- Security considerations historically produced compactness in conflict-prone tracts, fortified villages in Bundelkhand and stockaded settlements in the Naga hills being the standard examples.
- Economic and infrastructural factors: proximity to roads, markets, irrigation works and building materials. Modern additions reshape settlements actively — PMGSY all-weather roads pull habitations toward road alignments, Jal Jeevan Mission piped supply weakens the old constraint of siting near a water source, and PMAY-Gramin has replaced thatch with pucca construction at scale.
- Policy and land-tenure factors: land reform, resettlement colonies, irrigation-project displacement and rurban clustering all create new settlements outright. In Andhra Pradesh, the Polavaram project's rehabilitation colonies are a live instance of state-created settlement.

## A note on rural settlement patterns in India
- Pattern refers to the geometric arrangement of dwellings, determined by the alignment of the controlling feature — a road, river, canal or tank.
- Linear: houses strung along a road, canal bund, river levee or coast — seen along the delta canal bunds and the Andhra fishing coast.
- Rectangular or grid: the commonest form in flat plains with intersecting roads, typical of the Sutlej–Ganga plains and the planned delta villages.
- Circular or ring: houses arranged around a tank or open space — characteristic of the tank-irrigated tracts of Rayalaseema.
- Star, T-shaped, Y-shaped and cruciform: arising at road junctions, where growth extends outward along each radiating route.

## Conclusion

Rural settlement form is the visible record of a long negotiation between terrain, water, social organisation and, increasingly, public policy. Recognising whether a region is compact or dispersed is not an academic exercise: it determines the unit cost of delivering piped water, roads, electricity and schooling, since dispersed habitations cost several times more per household to serve. As Andhra Pradesh extends saturation programmes into its agency tracts, settlement geography is precisely what decides whether those programmes reach the last habitation or stop at the last cluster.

## Value addition
- Census definition of a village rests on the revenue village, while the census town requires all three of: population 5,000 or more, density 400 per sq km or more, and at least 75 per cent of male workers in non-agricultural activity. The growth of census towns is "in-situ urbanisation" — villages becoming urban without anyone migrating.
- Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission sought to develop rural clusters with urban amenities while preserving rural character — the operative successor to the discontinued PURA idea.
- Census 2027 Phase I — the Houselisting and Housing Census, under way from April to September 2026 — is collecting exactly the data this question rests on: housing condition, amenities and assets, with three categories for the sex of the head of household (male, female, transgender).
- Andhra Pradesh house types worth a line: palmyra and coconut thatch in the deltas, mud walls with terraced roofs in the dry interior, bamboo and thatch in the agency — each an adaptation to locally available material and climate.

## Introduction

The National Forest Policy, 1988 set India a target of 33% of geographical area under forest and tree cover, and two-thirds in hill and mountain regions, on the reasoning that forests are not a land-use category but a life-support system regulating hydrology, soil and climate. Thirty-eight years on, ISFR 2023 places India at 25.17% — 7,15,343 sq km of forest cover (21.76%) plus 1,12,014 sq km of tree cover (3.41%). Closing that eight-point gap under pressure from mining, infrastructure and agriculture has produced a layered conservation strategy that runs from constitutional policy down to village institutions.

## Policy and Mission Architecture
- National Forest Policy, 1988 shifted the governing objective from revenue extraction to ecological security and made local community involvement a stated principle — the intellectual parent of Joint Forest Management.
- National Mission for a Green India (GIM), one of the missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change, had its revised plan for 2021–2030 released on 17 June 2025, the

World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought. The National Afforestation Programme has been merged into GIM for unified implementation — a rationalisation that ends duplicate reporting between two afforestation streams.

- Nagar Van Yojana (2020) extends the effort to cities, targeting Nagar Vans and Nagar Vatikas in urban and peri-urban land where tree cover is otherwise falling.

## Legal and Regulatory Instruments
- Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 (formerly the Forest Conservation Act) bars diversion of forest land for non-forest use without Central approval. Its 2023 amendment defines permitted activities — zoos, eco-tourism, silviculture — and exempts certain strategic and border-area projects.
- Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and Eco-Sensitive Zones regulate the immediate periphery of protected areas. In Andhra Pradesh, for instance, a 500-metre eco-sensitive zone around Rajiv Gandhi National Park was notified in May 2017 to restrain quarrying on the Penna sands.
- The 2025 flashpoint. On 31 August 2025 the Ministry amended the Forest (Conservation and Augmentation) Rules, 2023 to simplify approvals for mining 24 critical and strategic minerals in forest areas under the National Critical Mineral Mission, 2025. This is the sharpest live tension in Indian forest governance — energy-transition self-reliance pulling directly against the precautionary principle — and citing it lifts an answer above the ordinary.

## Financing and Market Mechanisms
- Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 (CAMPA) institutionalised the levies collected against diverted forest land, with 90% devolved to States and 10% retained centrally. Its persistent weakness is absorption capacity: money accumulates faster than States can deploy it on survivable plantations.
- Green Credit Programme. Launched October 2023, its revised methodology was notified on 29 August 2025, followed by Guidelines for Eco-Restoration of Degraded Forest Land on 1 September 2025. The revision allows direct private participation and sets minimum restoration commitments — an attempt to fix the criticism that early green credits rewarded sapling counts rather than surviving ecosystems.
- Environment Audit Rules, 2025 (notified 29 August 2025) create a two-tier auditor system with a dedicated oversight agency, supplementing rather than replacing existing inspection.

## Community Participation and Trees Outside Forests
- Joint Forest Management (1990) gave village-level institutions a share in usufruct in exchange for protection duty. Andhra Pradesh is one of the pioneer States in JFM, with roughly one-third of its forest area under the arrangement (FSI) — the AP-specific example this question rewards.
- Forest Rights Act, 2006 converted forest dwellers from encroachers into rights-holders, with individual rights up to four hectares and community forest resource rights; AP extends PM-KISAN and Annadata Sukhibhava benefits to tribal farmers holding recognised titles, making the right economically real.
- Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam had recorded 262.4 crore saplings planted till 31 December 2025 — the largest people-centred plantation drive undertaken anywhere.
- Agroforestry now accounts for about 1,27,590 sq km of tree cover, and MISHTI restored 4,536 hectares of mangrove in 2025 across 13 States and UTs.

## Technology-Enabled Protection
- The Forest Survey of India runs a satellite-based real-time forest fire alert system with SMS and email dissemination and a 24×7 national control room. This matters acutely for Andhra Pradesh, where FSI classes 4.26% of forest as extremely fire-prone and 13.04% as very highly fire-prone.
- The National Forest Inventory and biennial remote-sensing assessment provide the evidence base without which none of the above could be audited.

## Critical Appraisal — Where Is the Gain Coming From?
- Of the 1,445 sq km increase since 2021, only 156 sq km is forest cover; 1,289 sq km is tree cover outside recorded forests. Growth is being driven by plantations and agroforestry, not by recovery of natural forest.
- ISFR 2023 recorded a loss of 58.22 sq km of forest in the Western Ghats Eco-Sensitive Area over a decade, and a decline of 327.30 sq km in the North-East — both biodiversity-rich zones where plantation gains elsewhere cannot substitute.

## Conclusion

India's forest conservation strategy has matured from prohibition to a mix of regulation, market incentive and rights recognition, and the aggregate numbers are moving in the right direction — India now ranks 9th globally in total forest area and 3rd in annual net gain (FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025). But the composition of that gain is the real test. So long as expansion comes chiefly from plantations and trees outside forests while dense natural forest in the Western Ghats and North-East continues to thin, the 33% target risks being met on paper without being met ecologically. The task ahead is to make survival rate, canopy density and species composition — not sapling counts — the measure of success, and to ensure that critical-mineral urgency does not quietly reopen what the 1980 Act closed.

## Introduction

In situ conservation protects species inside their natural habitat, so that the ecological relationships and evolutionary pressures that produced them continue to operate. Its superiority over ex situ methods is functional: a Red Sanders tree in a botanical garden is a specimen, whereas a Red Sanders stand in the Seshachalam hills is a self-regenerating population with its own pollinators, soil biota and genetic variation intact. Andhra Pradesh, sitting in the Deccan Bio-Geographic Zone with a genuinely endemic flora and fauna, pursues in situ conservation through a network of 3 National Parks and 13 Wildlife Sanctuaries covering 7,311.08 sq km — about 4.49% of the State — supported by biosphere, wetland and community instruments.

## The Strictly Protected Core
- National Parks are the highest protection category under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, where grazing and rights are extinguished. AP's three — Papikonda (1,012.86 sq km), Sri Venkateswara (353.62 sq km) and Rajiv Gandhi, Kadapa (about 2.4 sq km) — were chosen for habitat complementarity: Godavari moist deciduous, Seshachalam dry evergreen, and Penna dune-scrub respectively.
- Critical Tiger Habitat. The core of the Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam Tiger Reserve in the Nallamala is managed as an inviolate space under the core-buffer model, with Gundla Brahmeswaram Wildlife Sanctuary functioning as extended core. The reserve doubles as the catchment protection for the Srisailam and Nagarjunasagar reservoirs — conservation here is simultaneously water-security policy.

## The Buffer and Regulated Periphery
- Wildlife Sanctuaries (13) permit regulated human use and therefore carry the ecosystems that lie outside park boundaries — Coringa in the Godavari estuary for mangroves, Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary for deltaic wetland, Rollapadu for grassland, Koundinya for the Asiatic elephant, Sri Lankamalleswara for the Jerdon's Courser scrub and Kambalakonda for peri-urban Visakhapatnam forest.
- Eco-Sensitive Zones extend regulation beyond the notified boundary; the 500-metre ESZ around Rajiv Gandhi National Park (notified May 2017) is the AP illustration. ESZs matter because most conflict and encroachment occurs at the edge, not the core.
- Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve (2010), AP's first, applies the graded core–buffer– transition model over the Chittoor–Kadapa hills, protecting the only natural Red Sanders belt on earth.

## Habitat- and Species-Anchored In Situ Programmes
- Red Sanders in situ protection runs across the Seshachalam, Veligonda, Lankamala, Nallamala and Talakona ranges over roughly 5,300 sq km. It received ₹39.84 crore from the National Biodiversity Authority in November 2025 for frontline staff, protection infrastructure and scientific management — funds generated from access and benefit-sharing, which is in situ conservation financed by the resource itself.
- Olive Ridley turtle protection at Coringa and Hope Island keeps nesting on the natal beach rather than relocating the population — essential, since the species returns to its own hatching beach.
- Mangrove restoration in the Krishna and Godavari deltas under MISHTI and the National Coastal Mission (extended 2025–31, ₹767 crore) delivered AP the largest mangrove gain in India in ISFR 2023, +13.01 sq km.
- Kolleru Lake, AP's only Ramsar site (90,100 ha, designated 2002), conserves a functioning flood-balancing wetland between the two deltas, not merely a bird habitat.

## Community-Governed In Situ Conservation
- Biodiversity Management Committees and People's Biodiversity Registers. The AP State Biodiversity Board's PBR project and web portal record village-level biological resources, giving legal standing to the Access and Benefit Sharing claims of the communities that conserve them.
- Sacred groves and traditional protection in the Nallamala and Eastern Ghats represent in situ conservation that predates statute, and are now recognised as candidates for community reserve status.
- Eco-development around protected areas. Tribal households in ITDA Paderu and Rampachodavaram participate in forest management, while the Girijan Cooperative Corporation added value worth ₹211.97 crore to forest produce — the economic case for leaving the forest standing.

## What the Network Still Misses
- At 4.49% of geographical area, AP's protected estate is modest; grassland and dry evergreen systems remain under-represented, and only one wetland has Ramsar status despite 974 km of coast.
- Connectivity is the binding constraint: Papikonda faces partial submergence from Polavaram, Sri Venkateswara faces quarrying and pilgrim pressure, and highways cut the Eastern Ghats corridor.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh's in situ strategy is architecturally complete — it has core, buffer, landscape and community tiers, and a financing route through access and benefit-sharing that few States have operationalised as well. What it lacks is scale and connectivity. A 4.49% protected estate, cut by reservoirs, highways and quarries, cannot by itself hold an endemism-rich Eastern Ghats together. Strengthening in situ conservation now means less about new notifications inside parks and more about corridor protection between them, community reserve status for sacred groves, and additional coastal wetland designations — that is, extending legal protection to the landscape in which the parks are embedded.

## Value addition
- AP endemics to name: Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus, CITES Appendix II), Jerdon's Courser, Indian Golden Gecko and the Grey Slender Loris — all Eastern Ghats endemics whose survival depends entirely on in situ protection.
- Key sites and figures: NSTR, India's largest tiger reserve, shared with Telangana; Coringa (235.70 sq km) in the Godavari estuary; Rollapadu for the Great Indian Bustard; Koundinya, AP's only Asiatic elephant habitat under Project Elephant; Kolleru (90,100 ha), AP's only Ramsar site.
- FSI biodiversity assessment for AP: 242 tree, 64 shrub and 58 herb species recorded; the Champion & Seth "Dry Red Sanders-Bearing Forest" type covers 2.63% of AP's forest cover; Southern Dry Mixed Deciduous Forest dominates at 42.97%.
- Current hooks: NBA released ₹39.84 crore to AP for Red Sanders (November 2025); India's NBSAP 2024–2030 launched at CBD COP16, Cali; National Coastal Mission extended for 2025–31 with ₹767 crore.
- Legal basis: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 (National Parks, Sanctuaries, Conservation and Community Reserves) and Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (BMCs, People's Biodiversity Registers, Access and Benefit Sharing).

## Introduction

Environmental Impact Assessment is the process of predicting, evaluating and mitigating the environmental, social and health consequences of a proposed project before a decision on it is taken. Its defining feature is anticipation: it converts the precautionary principle from a judicial maxim into an administrative procedure. In India, EIA was first made mandatory by a 1994 Notification, but the operative instrument today is the EIA Notification, 2006, issued under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, as amended.

## The Statutory Architecture
- Category A projects — large or ecologically sensitive, such as major ports, refineries and river valley projects — are appraised centrally by an Expert Appraisal Committee and cleared by the MoEFCC. Category B projects go to the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority and State Expert Appraisal Committee; B1 requires a full EIA, B2 is exempt from it.
- The clearance process has four stages: Screening (does the project need a full EIA?), Scoping (Terms of Reference fixing what must be studied), Public Consultation (public hearing in the affected area plus written responses) and Appraisal (EAC recommendation, on which the Ministry grants clearance with conditions or rejects).

## Evaluation — Where EIA Works
- It internalises costs that markets ignore. By requiring baseline studies and a mitigation plan before sanction, EIA forces the proponent to price effects — submergence, displacement, effluent load — that would otherwise be borne by the public. For a project such as Polavaram, it is the mechanism through which forest submergence, tribal displacement and catchment treatment enter the project cost rather than remaining externalities.
- It creates a participation channel. The public hearing is often the only formal opportunity for affected communities to place objections on record — significant in Fifth Schedule areas of the Andhra agency, where it interacts with the Forest Rights Act, 2006 and PESA.
- It generates an enforceable record. Clearance conditions become legally binding, giving the NGT and the pollution control boards a documentary standard against which to measure compliance.

## Evaluation — Where EIA Fails
- Proponent-funded consultants. The developer commissions and pays for its own impact assessment, a structural conflict of interest that produces optimistic baselines, copied chapters and understated impacts.
- Public consultation reduced to formality. Hearings are held far from affected hamlets, technical reports are not translated, and objections are recorded without being answered — a particular problem for tribal communities in the agency tracts.
- The regularisation problem — the central failure. Projects begun without prior clearance were being regularised afterwards. In Vanashakti v. Union of India (16 May 2025) the Supreme Court struck down the MoEFCC's 2017 Notification and 2021 Office Memorandum, holding ex post facto clearance alien to environmental jurisprudence. That judgment was recalled on review in November 2025, and the matter was finally settled by a three-judge Bench on 29 July 2026 (2026 INSC 761), which held that prior environmental clearance under the 2006 Notification is mandatory, upheld the 2017 Notification as a closed, time-bound amnesty, and struck down the 2021 Office Memorandum prospectively as an administrative instrument that could not amend delegated legislation. Clearances already granted were saved; future regularisation is permissible only through a statutory notification satisfying a narrow public interest test.
- Weak post-clearance monitoring and diluted deterrence. Compliance is largely self-reported and rarely verified. The Court itself noted public projects worth about ₹20,000 crore operating in violation, and observed that decriminalisation of contraventions under the Environment (Protection) Act by the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 has further reduced deterrence. The LG Polymers plant at Visakhapatnam, which operated for years without valid clearance before the 2020 styrene leak, is the local illustration of what this permits.

## Suggestions to Make EIA Effective
- Break the consultant conflict: route EIA commissioning and payment through a regulator-managed pool, with accreditation withdrawn for demonstrably falsified baselines — reforming the incentive rather than merely auditing the output.
- Make consultation substantive: hearings in the affected habitation and in Telugu and the relevant tribal language, with a mandatory written, reasoned response to each objection in the appraisal record.
- Fund and publish compliance monitoring: third-party verification of clearance conditions at fixed intervals, with results on a public dashboard; the Supreme Court has, in effect, made prior clearance non-negotiable, so enforcement must now shift to the post-clearance stage.
- Strengthen the science: mandatory cumulative and carrying-capacity assessment for clustered projects — indispensable on the Andhra coast, where ports, thermal units and

aquaculture interact — plus GIS and remote-sensing verification of baselines, and integration of climate risk and sea-level rise into coastal appraisals.

- Institutional capacity: full-time, adequately staffed SEIAAs and SEACs, since appraisal delay is what generates the political pressure for shortcuts in the first place.

## Conclusion

EIA remains India's principal instrument for making the precautionary principle operational, and the 2026 settlement has strengthened it decisively by restoring prior clearance as a mandatory, non-negotiable requirement. Its weakness has never been the design of the process but the political economy around it — a proponent-funded assessment, a consultative stage without consequence, and a compliance stage without resources. Correcting those three, rather than adding further procedural stages, is what would turn EIA from a clearance formality into the genuine gatekeeper of sustainable development that the 2006 Notification intended.

## Value addition
- Litigation timeline to quote precisely: MoEFCC Notification of 14 March 2017 (one-time, six-month window for regularisation) and Office Memorandum of 7 July 2021 (standard operating procedure for post-facto clearance) → Vanashakti v. Union of India, 16 May 2025, both struck down, ex post facto clearance held alien to environmental jurisprudence and violative of Article 21 → review allowed in CREDAI v. Vanashakti, 18 November 2025, judgment recalled and petitions restored → final three-judge decision, 29 July 2026, 2026 INSC 761: prior EC mandatory; 2017 Notification upheld as a bounded amnesty; 2021 OM quashed prospectively; existing clearances saved; future schemes only by statutory notification under Section 3 of the EP Act, subject to a public interest test.
- Supporting precedents: Common Cause v. Union of India (2017), Alembic Pharmaceuticals v. Rohit Prajapati (2020) and Electrosteel v. Union of India (2023), all cited in the Vanashakti line.
- Institutional vocabulary: Expert Appraisal Committee; State Environment Impact Assessment Authority; Terms of Reference; Environment Management Plan; Environmental Clearance; Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019 — the last being indispensable for any Andhra Pradesh coastal project.
- AP anchors: Polavaram Irrigation Project (national project; submergence, R&R and catchment treatment conditions); LG Polymers, Visakhapatnam (operation without valid clearance, ₹50 crore NGT interim deposit, 2020); port and industrial corridor expansion

along the 1,053.07 km coast, where cumulative rather than project-by-project assessment is the live regulatory gap.

## Introduction

Drought is a prolonged deficiency of moisture relative to the long-term normal of a place, sufficient to cause hydrological imbalance and adversely affect agriculture, water supply and livelihoods. Two features distinguish it from other hazards. First, it is relative — 600 mm is normal in Anantapuramu but a severe drought in Srikakulam — so no absolute rainfall figure defines it. Second, it is a creeping disaster with no clear onset, peak or end, which is why its declaration is contested and its relief delayed. The India Meteorological Department defines meteorological drought as seasonal rainfall below 75% of the long period average.

## Types of Drought — a Sequence, Not a List
- Meteorological drought is the trigger stage: rainfall deficiency against the long period average. The IMD grades it as moderate at a 26–50% deficiency and severe above 50%. It is the only type that can be declared from rainfall data alone, which is why it is the first indicator in the Manual for Drought Management.
- Agricultural drought follows when soil moisture falls below the requirement of the standing crop. Crucially, it can occur without meteorological drought — a normal seasonal total delivered around a three-week dry spell at flowering will still destroy the crop. This is the commonest form in Rayalaseema and the reason rainfall-only declaration under-reports distress.
- Hydrological drought appears next, as reservoir storage, streamflow and groundwater levels fall below normal. It lags the rainfall deficit by months and persists after the rains return, because aquifers recharge slowly. Its signature is the failure of drinking-water sources and of irrigation releases in the following season.
- Socio-economic drought is the terminal stage, where the supply of water-dependent goods — food, fodder, drinking water, employment — falls short of demand, producing price rise, indebtedness and distress migration. NDMA guidance additionally recognises

ecological drought, where reduced water availability stresses ecosystems, triggering forest fire, wetland shrinkage and wildlife mortality.

## Drought-Prone Areas in India — Extent
- About 68% of India's cropped area is vulnerable to drought, per the Manual for Drought Management. Of this, 33% is "chronically drought-prone", receiving under 750 mm of mean annual rainfall, and a further 35% is "drought-prone", receiving 750–1,125 mm. Roughly half of India's net sown area remains rain-fed, which is the underlying reason the exposure is this large.

## Drought-Prone Areas — Spatial Distribution
- Arid western belt: western Rajasthan, especially the Marusthali, and the Kutch– Saurashtra tract of Gujarat. Rainfall below 500 mm with extreme variability; drought here is a permanent aridity problem rather than a periodic failure.
- Central peninsular belt: Marathwada and Vidarbha in Maharashtra, western Madhya Pradesh, and Bundelkhand across Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. The Deccan lava plateau's shallow soils and low groundwater potential in hard rock make recharge difficult even in good years.
- Southern rain-shadow belt: north-interior Karnataka, Rayalaseema in Andhra Pradesh and the Telangana plateau — all lying leeward of the Western Ghats and dependent on an unreliable north-east monsoon.
- Eastern pocket: the Kalahandi–Bolangir–Koraput tract of Odisha and parts of the Jharkhand plateau, where the problem is not low rainfall but poor retention on lateritic and undulating terrain, illustrating that drought proneness is as much edaphic as climatic.

## Andhra Pradesh Anchor
- Anantapuramu, at roughly 550 mm, is the driest district of the State and among the driest in peninsular India after Jaisalmer. ANGRAU data for 2002–2024 records drought in 17 of 22 kharif seasons in Anantapuramu, Chittoor and Kadapa — demonstrating that the "once in three years" formulation commonly quoted in textbooks now understates the frequency in the worst-affected districts.

## Conclusion

Drought is best understood as a process that propagates from atmosphere to soil to aquifer to society, each stage lagging and outlasting the last. Its management must therefore mirror that sequence: indicator-based early declaration under the Manual for Drought Management, soil-moisture conservation and crop contingency at the agricultural stage, aquifer recharge and conjunctive use at the hydrological stage, and employment guarantee with insurance at the socio-economic stage. The decisive shift now under way — from post-facto relief to anticipatory risk management — is what will determine whether a rainfall deficit still becomes a human disaster.

## Value addition
- Declaration framework: the Manual for Drought Management prescribes five categories of indices — rainfall, agriculture, soil moisture, hydrology and remote sensing (crop health) — across six climatic zones, replacing eye-estimation methods such as annewari, paisewari and girdawari. Drought is declared by the State Government; central assistance flows through the State Disaster Response Fund and, for severe cases, the National Disaster Response Fund.
- Consequences to list: crop failure and food grain scarcity (akal) with fodder scarcity (trinkal); large-scale livestock mortality; human and cattle migration; waterborne disease from consumption of contaminated water — gastroenteritis, cholera, hepatitis; and long-term land degradation and desertification.
- Programmes worth naming: Drought Prone Areas Programme (1973); Desert Development Programme (1977–78); Integrated Watershed Management Programme, now under PMKSY 2.0 (Watershed Development Component); Per Drop More Crop; MGNREGA for drought-proofing assets; and the National Disaster Management Authority's Guidelines on Drought Management.
- Comparative pointer: India recorded major droughts in 2002, 2004, 2009, 2014–15 and 2015–16; the 2002 drought reduced sown area from about 124 to 112 million hectares. The Drought in Numbers 2022 report of the UNCCD records a global rise in both drought frequency and duration.

## Introduction

Article 19(1) confers six freedoms on citizens alone — not on foreigners or corporations — and each is paired with a limitation clause in Articles 19(2) to 19(6). The framers deliberately enumerated the permissible grounds rather than leaving a general public-interest override, and the First Amendment (1951) inserted the word “reasonable” itself. Reasonableness is therefore not a judicial invention but a textual command, and the Supreme Court has spent seven decades giving it content through an evolving standard of review.

## Scope of the restriction power — the correct clause mapping
- **Freedom (Art. 19(1))** — Limitation clause · Permissible grounds
- **(a) Speech and expression** — 19(2) · Sovereignty & integrity of India; security of the State; friendly relations with foreign States; public order; decency; morality; contempt of court; defamation; incitement to an offence
- **(b) Assembly, peaceably and without arms** — 19(3) · Sovereignty & integrity; public order

- **Freedom (Art. 19(1))** — Limitation clause · Permissible grounds
- **(c) Associations, unions, co-operative societies** — 19(4) · Sovereignty & integrity; public order; morality
- **(d) & (e) Movement and residence** — 19(5) · Interests of the general public; protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe
- **(g) Profession, occupation, trade, business** — 19(6) · General public; plus professional/technical qualifications and State monopoly, expressly saved

- Three conditions are cumulative. First, the restriction must be imposed by a law — executive instruction will not do. Second, it must be reasonable. Third, it must fall within an enumerated ground. Kaushal Kishor v. State of UP (3 January 2023, Constitution Bench) settled that the Article 19(2) grounds are exhaustive: a court cannot manufacture a new ground by invoking Article 21 dignity as a competing right.
- The grounds are a closed but amendable list. The First Amendment (1951) added public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement to an offence; the Sixteenth Amendment (1963) added sovereignty and integrity of India — evidence that the framework contemplates change by amendment, not by interpretation.

## The test of reasonableness — how the standard hardened
- Chintaman Rao v. State of MP (1951): a total ban on manufacturing bidis during the agricultural season was struck down as excessive. The Court held a restriction must not go “in excess of the requirement” — the earliest statement of what would become proportionality.
- State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952): the classic multi-factor test. The Court must weigh the nature of the right, the purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil sought to be remedied, the disproportion of the imposition, and prevailing conditions — with no abstract standard of universal application.
- Narendra Kumar v. Union of India (1960): ‘restriction’ can extend to total prohibition, but only where nothing less will achieve the object — a necessity requirement in embryo.
- Modern Dental College v. State of MP (2016), consolidated in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017): the four-prong proportionality test — legitimate goal, rational nexus, necessity (least restrictive alternative), and balancing of the competing interests. This is now the governing standard and should be named in any full-marks script.
- Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015): vagueness and over-breadth are independent vices. Section 66A, IT Act fell because undefined ‘grossly offensive’ speech chills lawful expression, and because incitement must be distinguished from mere advocacy or discussion.
- Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020): proportionality applied to executive action. Indefinite internet suspension in Jammu & Kashmir was held disproportionate as it burdened Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); such orders must be published, reasoned, and periodically reviewed.

## Andhra Pradesh anchor — Article 19(6) in practice
- Article 19(6)(ii) expressly saves State monopoly in any trade. Andhra Pradesh’s excise regime, run through the AP State Beverages Corporation with State-operated retail outlets, rests on exactly this saving clause; and Cooverjee B. Bharucha v. Excise Commissioner (1954) held there is no fundamental right to trade in intoxicants at all. The AP case shows that the reasonableness enquiry varies with the subject-matter of the trade.

## EXAM-HALL DIAGRAM

reproduce the freedom-to-clause table above; it is compact, examiner-friendly and instantly signals accuracy. Pair it with a vertical funnel for the test: Legitimate Goal → Rational Nexus → Necessity (least restrictive means) → Balancing → valid restriction.

## Conclusion

The scheme of Article 19 is a balance struck in the text itself: enumerated freedoms matched by enumerated grounds, with reasonableness as the judicially administered valve between them. The trajectory of the case law runs from a loose ‘not excessive’ enquiry in 1951 to a structured four-prong proportionality standard today, which shifts the burden onto the State to prove that no less restrictive alternative existed. Reasonableness is thus not a deferential formula but the principal safeguard against the erosion of liberty by ordinary legislation.

## Value addition
- CORRECTION (booklet): The source states that Article 19(3) restricts assembly and Article 19(4) also deals with ‘the right to assemble peaceably’. Article 19(4) governs associations and unions, not assembly. The source also places Anuradha Bhasin (2020) under Article 19(3); the case arises under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g).
- Article 19 originally contained seven freedoms; the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property was deleted by the 44th Amendment (1978) and relocated as a constitutional right in Article 300A.
- Availability: Article 19 rights vest in citizens only. A company cannot claim them, though shareholder-editors may — Bennett Coleman v. Union of India (1973).
- Suspension: after the 44th Amendment, Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically only during an Emergency declared on grounds of war or external aggression, not armed rebellion.
- Reasonableness is examined on both substantive and procedural counts, and the burden of justifying a restriction lies on the State — Saghir Ahmad v. State of UP (1954).
- Kaushal Kishor (2023 INSC 4) also held Articles 19 and 21 horizontally enforceable against non-State actors (4:1, Nagarathna J. dissenting) — quotable on both halves of this question.

## Introduction

Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council whenever it appears that the public interest would be served by inquiring into and advising upon inter-State disputes, investigating subjects of common interest, and recommending better policy coordination. Though available since 1950, the power lay unused for forty years — the ISC was finally constituted by Presidential Order on 28 May 1990 (Inter-State Council Secretariat, MHA).

## Genesis
- Constitutional basis: Article 263(a) inquiry into disputes, 263(b) investigation of common-interest subjects, 263(c) recommendations for policy coordination. Notably, disputes under 263(a) are advisory — unlike Article 131 adjudication or Article 262 water tribunals.
- Sarkaria Commission (1983–88): Recommended a permanent Council under Article 263, preferably named 'Inter-Governmental Council,' charged with clauses (b) and (c) — the immediate trigger for its creation.
- Establishment: Constituted in May 1990 by the V.P. Singh government under the Ministry of Home Affairs, with a dedicated Inter-State Council Secretariat.
- Composition: Prime Minister (Chair); Chief Ministers of all States and of UTs with legislatures; Administrators of other UTs; and six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the PM. A Standing Committee, chaired by the Union Home Minister, does preparatory work.

## Relevance in Centre-State and inter-State coordination
- Deliberative forum on shared problems: The 11th meeting (16 July 2016) considered the Punchhi Commission's recommendations on Centre-State relations, Aadhaar-based delivery of subsidies, and improving learning outcomes in education.
- Executive federalism: Unlike the Rajya Sabha, where States are represented by indirectly elected members, the ISC brings State executives face-to-face with the Union executive — the only such constitutional forum.
- Complementary to NITI Aayog: NITI Aayog handles developmental planning and competitive rankings; the ISC is designed for political, legislative and administrative coordination — the two are not substitutes.
- Zonal Councils as the working arm: Statutory bodies under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, they have carried much of the actual coordination: only 25 zonal council meetings were held between 2004 and 2014, against 63 between 2014 and 2025, with the issue-resolution rate rising from 43% to 64% (Ministry of Home Affairs / PIB, 2025).

The central limitation, and an AP instance The ISC has not met in full session since 16 July 2016, despite being reconstituted in November 2024 with the Prime Minister as Chairman, nine Union Ministers as members and thirteen as permanent invitees, and a Standing Committee under the Union Home Minister that includes the Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh (MHA notification, 2024). In its absence, Andhra Pradesh has pursued unresolved bifurcation issues through the Southern Zonal Council: at its 30th meeting (Thiruvananthapuram, September 2022) 26 issues were taken up and 9 resolved, with 9 of the 17 pending items relating specifically to AP reorganisation (PIB, 2022); the Council next met at Chennai on 31 January 2025.

## Conclusion

The Inter-State Council remains the Constitution's only dedicated forum for executive federalism, and its design — a Prime Minister sitting with every Chief Minister — is precisely what contested issues like delimitation, GST compensation and river-water sharing require. Its potential, however, is undercut by disuse. Mandating a minimum number of sittings a year, publishing action-taken reports, and empowering its Secretariat would convert a dormant provision into a living federal institution.

## Value addition
- The Punchhi Commission (2010) made 273 recommendations on Centre-State relations, routed largely through the ISC Standing Committee for processing.
- There are five Zonal Councils under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; Andhra Pradesh belongs to the Southern Zonal Council along with Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry.
- North-Eastern States are covered not by a Zonal Council but by the North Eastern Council under the NEC Act, 1972, with Sikkim added in 2002.
- Zonal Councils are statutory and advisory; the ISC is constitutional and equally advisory — neither can bind a State, which is why political will determines their effectiveness.
