## Introduction

Since the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS), 1992 and full unification in March 1993, the rupee has been market-determined under a managed float, with current-account convertibility accepted under IMF Article VIII (August 1994). The rate is set in the interbank market by demand and supply; the RBI intervenes not to fix a level but to curb disorderly movement. With the rupee at a record low of ₹96.84 (20 May 2026) and trading around ₹96.5 in July 2026, the question of how “free” this float truly is has real policy salience.

## Is it fully market-determined? — A qualified “No”
- **Dimension** — Position
- **De jure (official)** — Floating — no target, no band, no peg; the RBI publishes the reference rate daily
- **De facto (IMF Article IV)** — Reclassified from floating → “stabilized arrangement” (2023) → “crawl-like arrangement” (2025) — both classified as soft pegs, citing frequent intervention
- **RBI’s position** — Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta: virtually all emerging markets operate managed floats; the RBI’s objective is to curb undue volatility on either side, not to target a level — the IMF’s six-month window is too short a lens
- **Verdict** — The rupee is market-determined in direction but managed in speed — a managed float with intervention, not a free float

## Effects of rupee depreciation — a two-sided balance sheet Gains
- Export competitiveness: a cheaper rupee offsets tariff disadvantage. ES 2025–26 (Box IV.5, ARDL model) quantifies this: a 1% appreciation of the rupee worsens net total trade by 1.26% and net merchandise trade by 1.45% — meaning depreciation materially improves the trade balance.
- Services are inelastic: elasticity of only −0.38, reflecting India’s market power in IT / GCC services — quality, not price, drives demand.
- Import substitution & remittances: higher rupee value of the USD 135.4 bn annual remittance inflow; encourages domestic sourcing.
- Net verdict of ES 2025–26: for India the trade-channel gains outweigh the financial-channel costs — a weaker currency is, on balance, positive for the BoP. Costs
- Imported inflation: with ~88–90% crude import dependence, depreciation feeds straight into CPI — visible in transport inflation of 4.31% in June 2026 as the energy shock passed through with a lag.
- Fiscal strain: higher fertiliser, LPG and edible-oil subsidy bills.
- Financial channel: ES 2025–26 finds that a 1% appreciation of the debt-weighted exchange rate raises net capital inflows by 0.87% — that is, depreciation

discourages capital inflows and raises unhedged corporate repayment costs.

- Household impact: costlier education abroad, travel and electronics; erosion of real incomes if inflation follows.
- Confidence risk: rapid, disorderly depreciation can become self-fulfilling through speculative dollar front-loading.

## Role of the RBI in defending the rupee
- **Tool** — Application
- **Spot & forward intervention** — Net dollar sales of USD 8.9 bn (April 2026) and USD 6.1 bn (May 2026); state-run banks selling dollars on the RBI’s behalf in July 2026 to prevent a breach of record lows
- **Reserve management** — Reserves at USD 676.2 bn (17 July 2026); peak USD 728.5 bn (Feb 2026) — about 11 months import cover, ~94% external-debt cover; gold diversification to USD 117.5 bn cushions dollar risk
- **Monetary policy** — Repo held at 5.25% with a neutral stance (June 2026), balancing currency defence against growth support
- **Capital-flow management** — Fully Accessible Route expanded to all new 15 / 30 / 40-year G-secs; FPI investment and concentration limits removed under the General Route; NRI / OCI equity caps raised; Government removed capital-gains and withholding tax on certain foreign investment in G-secs — a coordinated fiscal–monetary strategy to attract stable long-tenor inflows
- **Structural de-dollarisation** — Rupee internationalisation via Special Rupee Vostro Accounts and rupee invoicing of trade
- **Liquidity tools** — FX swaps, tactical liquidity facilities, participation in the NDF market

Critical note: intervention is symmetric — the RBI also bought dollars (net USD 1.7 bn in May 2025) when the rupee appreciated, confirming that its objective is volatility management, not a one-way defence. Excessive defence, however, burns reserves and imports global monetary conditions; hence

the recent shift towards greater two-way flexibility under Governor Sanjay Malhotra.

ConclusionThe rupee is market-determined in principle and managed in practice — a pragmatic middle path suited to an economy that is deeply trade-exposed yet not fully capital-account convertible. Moderate depreciation improves competitiveness; disorderly depreciation destabilises prices and confidence. The RBI’s role is therefore that of a shock absorber, not a price-setter — smoothing the path while reserves, sound fundamentals and a credible inflation framework do the heavier lifting. Durable currency stability will ultimately come not from intervention but from export diversification, reduced oil dependence and stable long-term capital inflows.

20. What is human development? Discuss the importance and measurement of the Gross National Happiness Index. (APPSC, 2020)

Human development, as defined by Mahbub ul Haq in the first Human Development Report (UNDP, 1990), is "the process of enlarging people's choices" — grounded in Amartya Sen's capability approach. Gross National Happiness (GNH), pioneered by Bhutan, extends this further by treating well-being, not output, as the goal of governance — famously: "Gross National

Happiness is more important than Gross National Product."

## Human Development and its Measurement (HDI)
- **Dimension** — Indicator
- **Long and healthy life** — Life expectancy at birth
- **Knowledge** — Mean + Expected years of schooling
- **Decent standard of living** — GNI per capita (PPP $)

- India (HDR 2025): rank 130/193, HDI 0.685, life expectancy 72 years; still in the "medium human development" category.
- Companion indices: IHDI (inequality-adjusted — India loses 30.7%), GDI, GII, MPI and PHDI.

## Gross National Happiness Index — Concept & Measurement
- Origin: Coined by King Jigme Singye Wangchuck of Bhutan (1972); embedded in Article 9 of Bhutan's Constitution (2008).
- Four Pillars: (i) Sustainable and equitable socio-economic development, (ii) Environmental conservation, (iii) Preservation and promotion of culture, (iv) Good governance.

## Measurement — Alkire–Foster (Oxford OPHI) methodology

9 Domains → 33 Indicators → 124 Variables↓Sufficiency thresholds applied↓"Happy" = sufficiency in at least 6 of the 9 domains

- Nine Domains: Psychological well-being • Health • Education • Time use • Cultural diversity and resilience • Good governance • Community vitality • Ecological diversity and resilience • Living standards.
- Policy use: Bhutan's GNH Policy Screening Tool — every new policy or project must clear a GNH score before approval.

## Importance of GNH
- Beyond-GDP measure: GDP counts output, not well-being; GNH counts what people value.
- Holistic: Integrates mental health, culture, community and ecology — invisible in national accounts.
- Sustainability: Bhutan is carbon-negative with about 70% forest cover, a direct GNH outcome.
- Global influence: Bhutan sponsored UNGA Resolution 65/309 (2011); 20 March was declared the International Day of Happiness; it inspired the Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Commission (2009), the OECD Better Life Index and the World Happiness Report.

## Limitations (Critical Balance)
- Subjectivity — happiness is self-reported and culture-specific.
- Comparability — indicators are Bhutan-specific and hard to scale to large, diverse economies.
- Data intensity — long household surveys, costly for populous nations.
- Risk of misuse — can mask material deprivation (the "happy but poor" fallacy).

## Indian Relevance
- World Happiness Report 2026: India 116/147 (score 4.536), improved from 118 (2025) and 126 (2024); Finland first for the ninth consecutive year.
- Domestic adaptations: Madhya Pradesh's Happiness Department (2016); Ease of Living Index (MoHUA); Andhra Pradesh's Swarnandhra @2047 vision of a "Wealthy, Healthy and Happy Andhra."

## Conclusion

Human development and GNH are complementary, not competing. HDI measures capabilities; GNH measures contentment and balance. India's path — combining rising HDI, falling multidimensional poverty and well-being-sensitive governance — must ensure that growth translates into dignity, equity and sustainability, the true test of Viksit Bharat @2047.

- HDI: Introduced in 1990 by Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen; geometric mean of three normalised indices.
- World Happiness Report 2026: Published by the Wellbeing Research Centre, University of Oxford, with Gallup and UN-SDSN; six variables — GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom of choice, generosity, perception of corruption. Top five: Finland, Iceland, Denmark, Costa Rica, Sweden. India 116; Afghanistan last (147).
- Bhutan GNH: 9 domains, 33 indicators; Alkire–Foster method; "happy" = sufficiency in at least 6 domains.
- Related frameworks: Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Commission (2009); Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI); Green GDP.
- One-liner: "Not everything that counts can be counted, and not everything that can be counted counts."

22. What are the factors responsible for the narrow tax base in India? Explain in brief. (APPSC, 2020)

The tax base is the aggregate of income, wealth and transactions legally liable to tax. Despite being the world's fourth-largest economy, India's base remains shallow: a record 7.3 crore ITRs were filed for AY 2025-26, yet barely 2% of the population pays income tax, and gross tax revenue averages only about 11.5% of GDP (Economic Survey 2025-26) against 15–18% for emerging economies and roughly 34% for the OECD. This constrains fiscal capacity precisely when capital expenditure needs are

rising.

## Structural Factors
- Dominance of informality: Roughly 85% of the workforce is informal (PLFS); cash-intensive, unrecorded transactions escape both PAN and GST trails.
- Low income levels: A large majority earn below the exemption threshold. Budget 2025-26 made income up to ₹12 lakh (₹12.75 lakh for salaried taxpayers) tax-free — welcome relief, but it further narrows the paying base; income tax RE 2025-26 fell to ₹13.12 lakh crore against a BE of ₹14.38 lakh crore.
- Agricultural exemption: Agricultural income is exempt under Section 10(1); the Union cannot tax it (Entry 82, Union List vs

Entry 46, State List), and no State meaningfully does. Wealthy agri-businesses route income through this shelter.

## Policy and Design Factors
- Exemptions and revenue foregone: Deductions, area-based exemptions and concessional regimes erode the effective base.
- Threshold-driven GST exclusion: Registration thresholds (₹40 lakh for goods / ₹20 lakh for services) and composition schemes keep lakhs of traders outside the net; registrants have grown from 60 lakh (2017) to over 1.5 crore (Economic Survey 2025-26) but remain small relative to enterprise count.
- Narrow corporate coverage: Many registered companies file nil or minimal taxable income; high compliance costs deter MSME formalisation.

## Administrative and Institutional Factors
- Evasion, avoidance and shell entities; the "tax gap" is estimated at 3–4% of GDP.
- Litigation and dispute backlog locks up revenue and deters voluntary compliance — GST disputes rose from about 10,000 cases (₹22,000 crore) in 2021-22 to about 22,000 cases (₹1.14 lakh crore) in 2023-24.
- Data fragmentation across agencies weakens third-party matching and tax intelligence.

## Recent Base-Widening Efforts
- **NUDGE initiative (ES 2025-26)** — 8,500 deductors revised TDS returns; 1.08 crore deductees and ₹4,825 crore added; detected ₹2,038 crore of non-genuine agricultural income
- **Digital compliance** — e-invoicing, e-way bills (+21% YoY, Apr–Dec 2025), AIS/TIS, PAN–Aadhaar linkage, faceless assessment
- **Income Tax Act, 2025** — Enacted 21 August 2025, effective 1 April 2026; simplification without rate disruption
- **GST 2.0 (56th Council)** — Two slabs (5% / 18%) plus a 40% de-merit rate; automated registration for small, low-risk businesses (from 1 Nov 2025); GSTAT operational
- **15th Finance Commission** — Minimise exemptions, merge slabs, target a GST-to-GDP ratio of 7%, strengthen State capacity

## Conclusion

India's narrow base is less a failure of rates than of coverage — informality, constitutional exemptions and compliance friction. The direction of reform is sound: lower rates, a wider net, digital trails and voluntary compliance. Broadening the base is not merely an accounting goal — it is the fiscal foundation for welfare, capital expenditure and consolidation to a 4.3% fiscal deficit without punishing existing taxpayers.

- Tax-to-GDP ratio: Total tax collections as a share of GDP; an indicator of fiscal capacity. India's gross tax revenue rose from

10.8% of GDP (FY16–FY20 average) to about 11.5% (FY22–FY25) — Economic Survey 2025-26.

- Buoyancy: Non-corporate (personal) tax buoyancy 1.8 during FY23–FY25; corporate tax buoyancy close to 1; customs buoyancy only 0.4.
- Constitutional anchor: Article 265 — no tax without authority of law; Article 246 + Seventh Schedule; 101st Amendment (2016) for GST.
- Committees: Chelliah Committee (1991–93), Kelkar Task Force (2002), Vijay Kelkar Committee on fiscal consolidation (2012), 15th Finance Commission (2020).
- **AP link:** As a State heavily reliant on central devolution and its own indirect taxes, AP's GSDP of ₹19.75 lakh crore (2026-27, growth 12%) must be matched by improved own-tax effort — stamps and registration and State GST are its key levers.

23. What are the changes effected in tax policy in India after the implementation of the recommendations of the Tax Reforms Committee in 1994? (TGPSC, 2016)

The Tax Reforms Committee (TRC) was constituted in August 1991 under Prof. Raja J. Chelliah, submitting its reports between 1991 and 1993, with implementation beginning from Budget 1994-95. Its guiding philosophy was a break from the earlier confiscatory regime: "moderate rates, a broad base, few exemptions, and simple administration."

## Direct Tax Reforms
- Rate rationalisation: The peak personal income tax rate was cut from 56% (1990-91) to 40%, then compressed into three slabs — 10%, 20% and 30% in the 1997-98 "Dream Budget."
- Corporate tax: Reduced from over 50% (1990-91) to 35% (1997-98) and progressively to 30%; the distinction between closely-held and widely-held companies was removed.
- Base broadening: Pruning of exemptions and deductions; rationalisation of capital gains (indexation introduced) and wealth tax (restricted to unproductive assets, 1993).
- Anti-avoidance: Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) introduced in 1996-97 to bring "zero-tax companies" into the net.

## Indirect Tax Reforms
- Service Tax introduced in 1994 — through Chapter V, Finance Act 1994, on three services at 5% (telephone, general insurance, stock broking), levied under the residuary Entry 97, Union List. It expanded to a negative-list regime by 2012 and became a major revenue source before merging into GST.
- Excise simplification: MODVAT was widened and converted into a single-rate CENVAT of 16% (2000-01), reducing cascading.
- Customs liberalisation: The peak rate was slashed from 150% (1991-92) to 40% (1997-98) and then to 10% (2007-08), aligning India with WTO commitments and improving competitiveness.

## Administrative and Procedural Reforms
- PAN made mandatory (Section 139A, 1995) — the foundation of India's taxpayer identification system; later TAN, TIN and computerised processing.
- Presumptive taxation (Sections 44AD / 44AE) to ease compliance for small traders and transporters.
- Strengthening of TDS and modernisation of assessment and appeal machinery.

## The Long Arc: TRC to Today

TRC (1991–93) → Service Tax 1994 → MAT 1996 → CENVAT 2000→ Kelkar Task Force 2002 → State VAT 2005 (Asim Dasgupta EC)→ GST 2017 (101st Amendment) → Faceless Assessment 2019→ Corporate rate cut to 22% / 15% (2019) → GST 2.0 (2025)→ Income Tax Act, 2025 (effective 1 April 2026)

## Impact Assessment
- **Indicator** — Pre-Reform · Present
- **Peak personal income tax rate** — 56% (1990-91) · 30% (nil up to ₹12 lakh)
- **Share of direct taxes in total taxes** — about 19–23% · 58.8% in FY25 (PA) — ES 2025-26
- **Peak customs duty** — 150% · about 10%
- **Gross tax revenue / GDP** — about 10% · about 11.5%

Limitations: agricultural income remains untaxed; revenue foregone through exemptions persists; the litigation backlog and the informal sector still cap the base.

## Conclusion

The post-1994 reforms, rooted in the Chelliah vision, converted India's tax system from a high-rate, narrow-base, evasion-

prone structure into a moderate-rate, broad-base, technology-driven one. They created the intellectual foundation for VAT and GST, restored revenue buoyancy, and aligned taxation with liberalisation. The Income Tax Act, 2025 completes this arc by prioritising simplicity and certainty over frequent policy churn.

- Chelliah Committee (TRC), 1991: Recommended fewer rates, moderate levels, minimal exemptions, taxation of services, drastic customs reduction and a modernised administration.
- Income-tax Act, 2025: Enacted 21 August 2025, effective from tax year 2026-27. Guided by three principles — (i) textual and structural simplification, (ii) no major policy change, (iii) no change in tax rates — to preserve continuity and predictability. Budget 2026-27 also reduced MAT from 15% to 14%.
- Milestone dates: Service tax 1994 · MAT 1996-97 · PAN 1995 · CENVAT 2000 · State VAT 2005 · GST 1 July 2017 · Faceless assessment 2019 · GST 2.0 from 22 September 2025.
- Quote: Raja Chelliah is often called the "Father of Indian tax reforms."

24. Examine the relative shares of direct and indirect tax revenues of the Indian Government in the post-reforms period. (APPSC, 2012)

The most significant structural change in India's post-1991 fiscal architecture is the inversion of the direct–indirect tax ratio. A regime once dependent on customs and excise has become direct-tax led: the share of direct taxes rose from about 19–23% in the early 1990s to 58.8% in FY25 (Provisional Actuals) — a marker of a formalising, income-responsive economy (Economic Survey 2025-26).

## Phase-wise Shift in Composition
- **Period** — Direct : Indirect · Defining Feature
- **1990-91 / 1991-92** — about 19–23 : 77–81 · Customs and excise dominance; high rates, narrow base
- **2007-09** — about 55 : 45 · Historic crossover after the Chelliah and Kelkar reforms
- **FY16–FY20 (avg)** — 51.9 : 48.1 · Corporate tax cut (2019); GST transition
- **FY22–FY25 (avg)** — 55.5 : 44.5 · Post-pandemic formalisation, digital compliance
- **FY25 (PA)** — 58.8 : 41.2 · Highest direct share in decades
- **Budget 2026-27 (per rupee)** — 39 paise direct : 25 paise indirect · Income tax 21p + corporation tax 18p; GST 15p + excise 6p + customs 4p

Of total tax receipts in BE 2026-27, direct taxes account for roughly 61% and indirect taxes 39%.

## Key Drivers of the Shift
- Policy reform: Chelliah Committee (1991) and Kelkar Task Force (2002); rate moderation with base broadening.
- Administrative modernisation: PAN–Aadhaar linkage, AIS / TIS, faceless assessment, TDS expansion and the NUDGE

behavioural-compliance initiative.

- Growth and formalisation: Corporate profits of listed companies rose from ₹2.5 trillion (FY21) to ₹7.1 trillion (FY25) — RBI; personal income tax buoyancy averaged 1.8 during FY23–FY25.
- Indirect tax rationalisation: GST subsumed multiple levies; excise fell from 1.7% to 0.9% of GDP after the 2021–22 petroleum duty cuts; customs buoyancy is only 0.4 owing to deliberate duty reduction on inputs.

## Current Performance (Latest Data)
- **Net direct taxes, FY26** — ₹23.40 lakh crore (up 5.12% YoY) — CBDT
- **Gross GST, FY25** — ₹22.08 lakh crore (record)
- **Gross GST, Apr–Dec FY26** — ₹17.4 lakh crore (up 6.7% YoY), multiple all-time monthly highs
- **GST registrants** — 60 lakh (2017) to over 1.5 crore
- **e-way bill volumes** — up 21% YoY (Apr–Dec 2025)
- **Gross tax revenue / GDP** — about 11.5% (post-pandemic average)

## Examination of Implications

Positive:

- Progressivity and equity: Direct taxes follow ability to pay; a rising share reduces the regressive incidence borne by the poor.
- Growth-friendly financing: Buoyant direct revenue funds record capital expenditure — ₹12.22 lakh crore in BE 2026-27 — while the fiscal deficit consolidates to 4.3% of GDP.
- Credibility: Three sovereign rating upgrades in 2025 reflect this revenue quality.

Concerns:

- Narrow shoulders: A rising share resting on a small taxpayer base concentrates risk; the FY26 income-tax shortfall (RE ₹13.12

lakh crore against BE ₹14.38 lakh crore) illustrates this.

- Cyclical sensitivity: Direct taxes fall faster in downturns than consumption-based GST.
- Federal dimension: States rely heavily on indirect taxes (SGST, excise, stamps); GST 2.0's estimated ₹48,000 crore revenue foregone and the end of the compensation cess sharpen vertical and horizontal fiscal concerns.

## Conclusion

India's post-reform trajectory shows a decisive move from indirect-tax dominance to a direct-tax-led, income-responsive fiscal structure — evidence of economic maturity and formalisation. Yet the optimum is not maximum directness but balance: direct taxes for equity, indirect taxes for stability and reach. Sustaining this mix while widening the base is the central design

challenge of India's next-generation tax policy.

- GST 2.0 (56th GST Council): Two-slab structure — Merit 5% and Standard 18%, with a 40% de-merit rate on sin and luxury goods (subsuming the compensation cess, so no net increase in burden). Effective 22 September 2025. The median rate moved from 12% to 5%.

Essentials (soaps, toothpaste, Indian breads) to 5% or Nil; 36 lifesaving drugs to Nil; individual life and health insurance policies exempt; two-wheelers, small cars, TVs, ACs and cement from 28% to 18%; farm machinery and irrigation equipment from 12% to 5%.

Estimated boost to nominal GDP growth: 20–30 basis points; estimated revenue foregone about ₹48,000 crore.

GSTAT operational; automated registration for small, low-risk businesses from 1 November 2025.

Rupee goes to: States' share of taxes 22p, interest 20p, central sector schemes 17p, defence 11p.
- "Tripod of tax reforms" (ES 2025-26): Corporate tax cuts (2019) → personal income tax relief (April 2025) → GST rationalisation (September 2025).

P4-Q2a:
## Introduction

Monetary policy transmission is the process by which a change in the RBI’s policy repo rate travels through money markets, bank balance sheets and asset prices to finally influence spending, output and inflation. The weighted average call rate (WACR) is the operating target; the LAF corridor (SDF–repo–MSF) is the steering mechanism.

## Channels of transmission
- **Interest rate** — Repo → WACR/G-sec yields → EBLR/MCLR → EMIs, investment
- **Credit** — Bank balance-sheet strength and borrower net worth → volume and pricing of credit
- **Asset price** — Yields, equity and property valuations → wealth effect
- **Exchange rate** — Rate differentials → capital flows → rupee → import prices
- **Expectations** — Policy signalling and MPC minutes → anchoring of inflation expectations

## Where transmission falters
- Long and variable lags: rate changes take two to four quarters to reach demand.
- Loan-pricing mix: although about 61% of floating-rate loans were EBLR-linked (December 2024), a substantial MCLR stock re-prices sluggishly; pass-through is faster in private banks than in PSBs.
- Sticky deposits: banks fund over 80% of their books from deposits; deposit rates fall slower than lending rates, squeezing net interest margins and slowing further cuts.
- Administered rates: small savings rates held above the formula-implied level (historically 65–100 bps) set a floor under bank deposit rates.
- Liquidity swings: government cash balances, forex operations and GST/festival flows push the system between surplus and deficit.
- Risk premia and segmentation: MSMEs and lower-rated borrowers face spreads that blunt rate sensitivity.

## Evidence of marked improvement in FY26

The FY26 easing cycle was the best transmission episode in a decade. Against a cumulative 100 bps repo cut, the WALR on fresh rupee loans fell 64 bps to 8.71% and on outstanding loans 56 bps to 9.21% (November 2025) — the lowest since September 2022. This was made possible by an average net LAF surplus of ₹1.89 lakh crore (against just

₹1,605 crore in FY25), which kept the WACR on average 8 bps below the repo rate. Steps to strengthen transmission

- Complete the EBLR migration and mandate cohort-wise disclosure of pass-through to spur competition.
- Keep liquidity in mild, predictable surplus — VRR/VRRR across tenors, published liquidity calendars, and a shift to shorter (7-day) main operations.
- Align small savings rates strictly to the 2016 formula with smoothing caps.
- Deepen bond and term-money markets — India’s corporate bond market is only 15–16% of GDP against Korea’s 79% — to compress spreads.
- Sustain bank health: PSB gross NPAs at 1.93% and CRAR at 16.6% (March 2026) already make balance sheets far more rate-responsive than a decade ago.

## Conclusion

India’s repo-centred corridor with WACR as the operating target has made transmission faster and more complete, as FY26 demonstrated. Residual frictions are structural — loan-pricing legacy, deposit stickiness and administered rates — and can be addressed only through market deepening and rule-based coordination between the RBI and the Ministry of Finance.

## Value addition
- MSF rate: penal rate at which banks borrow overnight by dipping into the SLR portfolio (up to 2%); 25 bps above repo.
- LAF corridor: MSF as ceiling, SDF as floor, repo in the middle — currently 5.50 / 5.25 / 5.00 with CRR at 3% and SLR at 18%.
- FY26 liquidity operations: ₹2.39 lakh crore of durable liquidity via nine OMO purchases (April-May 2025); a further

₹1 lakh crore OMO plus a US$5 billion three-year buy/sell swap in December 2025; CRR cut releasing ₹2.5 lakh crore.

- One-line revision point: Transmission is not a rate cut — it is the journey of that cut from Mint Street to the borrower’s EMI.

## Introduction

Fiscal policy operates through taxation, expenditure and borrowing to influence growth, distribution and stability. After GST subsumed most indirect levies, customs and Union excise (largely on petroleum) became the government’s principal discretionary indirect-tax levers, since GST rates require GST Council consensus.

## Fiscal policy tools in India (Union Budget 2026-27)
- **Taxation** — Direct (income, corporate); indirect (GST, customs, excise) · Gross tax receipts ₹44.04 lakh crore
- **Expenditure** — Revenue and capital spending · Total ₹53.47 lakh crore; capex ₹12.22 lakh crore; effective capex ₹17.15 lakh crore
- **Borrowing** — Market borrowings, small savings · Fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP
- **Subsidies & transfers** — Food, fertiliser, DBT · Rationalised through DBT and Just-in-Time releases
- **Public debt management** — Bond switches, maturity profile · Debt anchor 50±1% of GDP by FY31

## Can customs and excise be flexible tools? — Yes, with three qualifications As revenue instruments — moderately effective
- They are executive-notified, requiring no Council consensus, so they can be changed overnight.
- But the base is narrow: excise collections fell from about 1.7% of GDP (FY22) to 0.9% (FY25) after petroleum duty cuts, showing how quickly this lever erodes when used for price relief.

## As inflation-control instruments — demonstrably effective for supply shocks
- Duty cuts transmit to retail prices within days: excise cuts on petrol and diesel (2021, 2022), and the customs duty reduction on crude edible oils from 20% to 10% (June 2025), directly softened food and fuel inflation.
- Duty increases on non-essential imports curb consumption and protect the current account.
- This is precisely the domain where monetary policy is weak: as the June 2026 MPC noted while raising the FY27 inflation forecast to 5.1% on the back of West Asian conflict and fuel price increases, supply shocks require fiscal, not monetary, instruments.

## As trade and industrial policy instruments
- Customs rationalisation (fewer tariff slabs, inverted duty correction) supports Make in India and PLI; exemptions on cancer drugs and critical inputs serve welfare and competitiveness goals.

## Limits on their flexibility
- Revenue–inflation trade-off: every duty cut that lowers prices also widens the deficit.
- Asymmetric pass-through: cuts may be absorbed by intermediaries rather than reaching consumers, given the absence of a standing anti-profiteering authority.
- WTO and treaty ceilings on bound tariff rates.
- Regressive incidence: indirect taxes fall harder on low-income households.
- Petroleum’s exclusion from GST perpetuates cascading, even as it preserves this flexibility.

## Conclusion

Customs and excise remain India’s most nimble fiscal instruments — the only ones the executive can adjust between budgets — and they are best used surgically and temporarily against supply shocks, not as a standing revenue crutch. Durable revenue must come from a broader direct-tax base and GST buoyancy, leaving duties free to do the stabilisation work for which they are uniquely suited.

## Value addition
- GST 2.0 (September 2025): two-slab structure (5% and 18%) with a 40% demerit rate; estimated revenue foregone about ₹48,000 crore.
- Constitutional basis: Art. 265 (no tax without authority of law); Art. 246A and 279A (GST Council); Art. 112 (Annual Financial Statement).
- Structural gap: petroleum, electricity and alcohol remain outside GST — a source of both cascading and fiscal flexibility.
- FRBM Act, 2003 and the shift (Budget 2025-26 onward) from a deficit target to a debt-to-GDP anchor.
- Quality of fiscal policy: revenue expenditure fell from 13.6% of GDP (FY22) to 10.9% (FY25), and effective capex (₹17.15 lakh crore) now exceeds the fiscal deficit (about ₹16.9 lakh crore).

## Introduction

Note on the acronym: the correct expansion is APIIATP — Andhra Pradesh Integrated Irrigation and Agriculture Transformation Project (World Bank Project ID P160463).

Externally Aided Projects (EAPs) are development projects financed by multilateral institutions (World Bank, ADB, AIIB, NDB) or bilateral agencies (JICA, KfW, DFID, USAID) through loans, credits or grants. Because Article 293(1) confines State borrowing to within India, a State cannot borrow abroad directly: the Union Government contracts the loan and passes it on to the State as a back-to-back loan or grant, through the Department of Economic Affairs.

- What externally aided projects are — and why States use them
- **Sources** — Multilateral — World Bank (IBRD/IDA), ADB, AIIB, NDB; bilateral — JICA, KfW, AFD
- **Routing** — Contracted by the Union under Art. 293(1); passed to the State as back-to-back loan or grant
- **Terms** — Long maturity with a grace period; concessional or near-market interest depending on the window
- **Why States seek them** — Long-tenure finance for capital projects; technical expertise and international best practice; results-based disbursement discipline; and — importantly — funds additional to the State’s normal borrowing ceiling
- **The cost** — It is debt, not aid. It carries currency risk, procurement and safeguard conditionalities, and reporting obligations

- APIIATP — objectives

The Project Development Objective is “to enhance agricultural productivity, profitability and climate resilience of smallholder farmers in selected tank systems of Andhra Pradesh.”

The specific objectives are to: 1. Rehabilitate and modernise minor irrigation tanks and small-scale community-based irrigation systems. 2. Improve water-use efficiency and water security at the level of the individual farm. 3. Promote climate-resilient agriculture — drought-tolerant varieties, diversified cropping, soil health. 4. Strengthen market linkages for small and marginal farmers through producer organisations and post-harvest technology. 5. Build the capacity of Water Users Associations (WUAs) to manage irrigation delivery themselves. 6. Promote inclusive rural growth, with explicit attention to women, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

- Principles underlying the project
- **Integration, not sectoral silos** — Irrigation, agriculture, horticulture, fisheries, livestock and marketing are addressed together within a single tank command, rather than by separate departments
- **Community management** — Water Users Associations and Cascade Coordination and Management Committees plan and operate the systems — the project restores the community management that the tank system historically had and lost
- **The cascade approach** — Tanks are treated as chains, since the overflow of one feeds the next; rehabilitating a single tank in isolation achieves little
- **Climate resilience** — An integrated weather forecasting system delivering crop advisories scaled down to individual irrigation cluster areas
- **Cost-effectiveness over new construction** — The project’s explicit rationale is that conventional canal irrigation cannot be extended to all arable land because of water scarcity, environmental impact and cost — so rehabilitating existing tanks is the most cost-effective route to climate-resilient agriculture in rain-fed areas
- **Inclusion and safeguards** — A Tribal People’s Planning Framework for ITDA mandals and an Environment and Social Management Framework
- **Sustainability** — Reduced greenhouse gas emissions and improved natural resource management as project outcomes

- Funding
- **Lender** — World Bank (IBRD)
- **Credit** — US$172.20 million, approved 23 October 2018
- **Terms** — Maturity 24 years, grace period 6 years
- **Project ID** — P160463
- **Counterpart funding** — State share, with the Union contracting and on-lending the credit
- **Implementing agency** — Government of Andhra Pradesh, through the Water Resources and Agriculture departments, with a dedicated project unit

- Components
- Improving irrigated agriculture efficiency — tank rehabilitation, distribution system modernisation, micro-irrigation, and water security at farm level.
- Enhancing agricultural productivity and profitability — climate-resilient varieties, crop diversification, soil health, horticulture, livestock and inland fisheries within tank commands.
- Market linkage and value addition — producer organisations, post-harvest handling, storage and market access.
- Project management, monitoring and capacity building — including WUA strengthening and the weather advisory system.
- Scope of beneficiaries
- **Number of families** — Over 200,000 families of poor and marginalised farmers, agro-entrepreneurs, women and other vulnerable groups
- **Irrigation systems** — 1,000 Small-Scale Community-Based Irrigation (SSCBI) systems — minor irrigation tanks and cascades
- **Area** — About 90,000 hectares of command area
- **Villages** — Over 1,000 villages
- **Districts** — 12 of the State’s most climate-vulnerable districts — Anantapuramu, Chittoor, YSR Kadapa, Kurnool, Nellore, Prakasam (Rayalaseema and southern AP); Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam (North Coastal Andhra); East Godavari, West Godavari and Krishna
- **Priority groups** — Small and marginal farmers, tenant cultivators, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (with a dedicated Tribal People’s Planning Framework for ITDA mandals), and women, organised through SHG and WUA structures

Note the district selection: the project deliberately targets the rain-fed and climate-vulnerable districts of Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra — precisely the regions bypassed by canal irrigation and the Green Revolution. APIIATP is therefore as much a regional disparity instrument as an agricultural one.

- Significance and assessment

Significance - It addresses the neglected middle tier of irrigation: Andhra Pradesh has about 40,000 minor irrigation sources, between major canals and private borewells, which received little investment for decades. - Tank rehabilitation restores groundwater recharge, addressing depletion at source rather than by drilling deeper. - The integrated design tackles the standard failure of irrigation projects — that water alone does not raise income without seed, advisory and market access. - It builds on predecessors — the AP Community Based Tank Management Project (APCBTMP) and the AP Water Sector Improvement Project (APWSIP) — giving a two-decade institutional continuity.

Limitations to note - Debt, not aid — the credit must be repaid, with currency risk borne ultimately by the exchequer. - WUA sustainability beyond the project period is the classic weakness of participatory irrigation management. - Coverage is limited to 1,000 tanks of about 40,000 minor sources, so State-wide replication depends on domestic financing. - Procurement and safeguard conditionalities slow implementation.

## Conclusion

APIIATP illustrates the modern form of externally aided project: modest in size (US$172.20 million) but integrated in design, using World Bank finance and technical practice to rehabilitate 1,000 tank systems across 90,000 hectares in 12 climate-vulnerable districts, benefiting over 200,000 families. Its real contribution is conceptual — it treats tank rehabilitation as the cost-effective route to climate resilience in rain-fed Andhra Pradesh, restores community management through Water Users Associations, and links water to seed, soil, advisory and market in a single package. Whether it endures depends on whether the WUAs outlive the credit.

## Value addition
- Constitutional routing: Article 293(1) confines State borrowing to within India — external loans are contracted by the Union and passed on, which is why all State EAPs appear as central assistance.
- AP’s wider EAP portfolio: World Bank US$800 million and ADB US$788.8 million for the Amaravati capital region (approved December 2024); AIIB-assisted AMRUT 2.0; KfW’s €90 million agroecology grant supporting APCNF; historically the AP Economic Restructuring Project and the AP Power Sector Restructuring Project (1999-2004).
- Predecessor projects: APCBTMP (community-based tank management) and APWSIP (water sector improvement) — APIIATP’s institutional lineage.
- The comparison worth drawing: Mission Kakatiya in Telangana pursued the same tank-restoration logic with State rather than external finance.

## Introduction

The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 created Telangana on 2 June 2014 and left the residuary State without Hyderabad — its capital, its services engine and its single largest revenue centre. The bifurcation was therefore not a division of a homogeneous economy but the removal of its most productive node.

## Sectoral changes after bifurcation
- **Services** — Sharpest loss — Hyderabad’s IT, pharma, real estate and financial services all went to Telangana · New clusters built at Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Tirupati; IT & GCC Policy 4.0; Fintech Valley Vizag
- **Industry** — Weak base; most large units and headquarters were in and around Hyderabad · Visakhapatnam–Chennai and Chennai–Bengaluru Industrial Corridors; nodes at Krishnapatnam, Orvakal, Kopparthy
- **Agriculture** — Remained the backbone with an unusually high GVA share; water-sharing disputes over Krishna and Godavari (Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam) created uncertainty · Micro-irrigation, diversification into aquaculture, horticulture and oil palm; Polavaram as the anchor project
- **Infrastructure** — Need to build an entire capital and administrative apparatus from scratch · Amaravati under the CRDA Act, 2014 using land pooling of about 33,000 acres

## The resource gap
- Hyderabad contributed the dominant share of the undivided State’s own revenue; the residuary State lost roughly a third of its revenue base overnight while retaining most of its population and welfare obligations.
- A revenue deficit of ₹24,194 crore in 2014-15 (CAG) and a structural deficit thereafter; the debt–GSDP ratio rose from 22.3% (2014-15) to 32.4% (2019-20).

## Disputes over the apportionment of assets, liabilities, power dues and institutions under Schedules IX and X

of the Reorganisation Act prolonged the uncertainty.

- Central commitments — resource-gap funding, Special Category Status, Polavaram, backward-district packages and the Kadapa steel plant — were only partly fulfilled.

## Steps taken to mobilise resources
- Own revenue effort: widening the GST base, a revamped Excise Policy that plugged leakages, and modernisation of stamps and registration.
- External and institutional finance: World Bank (US$800 million) and ADB (US$788.8 million) for Amaravati Phase-I; AIIB-assisted AMRUT 2.0 projects; an additional ₹4,000 crore under UIDF over two years.
- Central capex support: ₹6,544 crore availed under SASCI in 2025-26 — nearly double the ₹4,090 crore of 2023-24.
- Debt management: renegotiation of ₹43,298 crore of high-cost loans from as high as 12.3% down to 9% or below, saving ₹327 crore a year, with ₹1.2 lakh crore more under review.
- Investment-led revenue building: the Global Partnership Summit 2025 yielded commitments exceeding ₹13.25 lakh crore across 610 MoUs, and Google’s US$15 billion AI data centre at Visakhapatnam — the largest single FDI commitment in the country.
- Institutional innovation: proposed AP Wealth Fund, the AP Logistics Corporation, and the “Reimagining Public Finance” Summit (Visakhapatnam, November 2025).

## Conclusion

Bifurcation inflicted a severe and asymmetric shock, and the recovery has been slow and uneven. But the fiscal indicators now point in the right direction — the revenue deficit has narrowed from 3.79% of GSDP (FY25) to 1.11% (BE 2026-27) and the fiscal deficit from 5.11% to 3.84%, with capital expenditure rising to ₹53,915 crore. The task ahead is to convert investment commitments into operating capacity, complete Polavaram and Amaravati, and secure the remaining Reorganisation Act entitlements.

## Value addition
- AP Reorganisation Act, 2014: Section 46(2) (special financial assistance), Section 90 (Polavaram declared a national project), Section 93 and the Thirteenth Schedule (institutions and infrastructure), Schedules IX and X (asset apportionment); Special Category Status was a Rajya Sabha assurance, not a statutory provision — a distinction worth stating precisely.
- 16th FC (2026-31): AP’s share raised to 4.22%; but revenue-deficit and state-specific grants discontinued.
- Marquee projects: Integrated Steel Plant (Anakapalli), Bulk Drug Park (Nakkapalli), semiconductor facility (Orvakal), Green Aluminium (Kakinada), Amaravati Quantum Valley, Ratan Tata Innovation Hub; ports at Ramayapatnam (75%), Mulapeta (65%), Machilipatnam (50%); Alluri Sitaramaraju International Airport, Bhogapuram — 97% complete.

## Introduction

The Goods and Services Tax is a destination-based, multi-stage, value-added indirect tax with seamless input tax credit, subsuming most central and state indirect levies into one structure — “one nation, one tax, one market.” Introduced through the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 and effective from 1 July 2017, it rests on Article 246A (concurrent power to levy), Article 269A (inter-state supply) and Article 279A (GST Council).

## The structure
- CGST + SGST on intra-state supplies; IGST on inter-state supplies and imports, apportioned between Centre and destination State; UTGST for Union Territories; a compensation cess (now largely transitioned out).
- GST 2.0, effective 22 September 2025, merged the four slabs (5, 12, 18, 28) into two — 5% and 18% — with a 40% demerit rate on tobacco, pan masala, aerated drinks and luxury goods. Rates were cut on about 375 items.

## Steps to facilitate trade and ease of doing business

Structural simplification

- Two-slab structure ends most classification disputes; essentials, life-saving drugs, farm machinery and irrigation equipment moved to nil or 5%; two-wheelers, small cars, TVs, ACs and cement moved from 28% to 18%.
- Correction of inverted duty structures, improving working capital for manufacturers.

Technological integration

- GSTN as the digital backbone; e-invoicing (progressively extended down the turnover threshold), e-way bills, auto-population of returns (GSTR-2B, GSTR-3B), dynamic QR codes, and pre-filled annual returns — sharply reducing manual data entry.

Procedural relief

- Composition scheme and higher registration thresholds (₹40 lakh for goods, ₹20 lakh for services) exempting most small businesses.
- QRMP scheme — quarterly returns with monthly payment — for taxpayers below ₹5 crore turnover.
- Faster, risk-based electronic refunds, critical for exporter liquidity: refunds in April 2026 rose 19.3% to ₹31,793 crore as backlogs were cleared.
- Amnesty schemes and waiver of late fees for legacy non-filers.

Institutional and dispute resolution

- GST Council (Art. 279A) — Union Finance Minister as chair, Union MoS Finance, and one minister from each State; Centre holds one-third of the weighted vote, States two-thirds, with a 75% majority required — a genuine federal bargain.
- GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) operationalised to clear the appellate backlog that had been clogging High Courts.
- Sector-specific guidance notes in regional languages for textiles, MSMEs and e-commerce.

## Outcomes
- Gross GST collections reached ₹22.27 lakh crore in FY 2025-26 (+8.3%), with net collections of ₹19.34 lakh crore; April 2026 set an all-time monthly record of ₹2,42,702 crore.
- Post-GST 2.0, a steady 7-8% monthly growth has become the norm despite lower rates — evidence that volume and compliance effects are offsetting the rate cut.
- Logistics improved with the abolition of check-posts; India ranks 38th on the World Bank’s Logistics Performance Index (2023), up from 44th in 2018.

## Remaining challenges

Petroleum, electricity, alcohol and real estate remain outside GST, perpetuating cascading; the absence of a standing anti-profiteering authority weakens pass-through of rate cuts; and revenue foregone from GST 2.0 is estimated at about

₹48,000 crore.

## Conclusion

GST has evolved from a complex five-slab compromise into a genuinely simplified two-rate structure backed by one of the world’s largest tax IT systems. Its trade-facilitation record — digital compliance, faster refunds, unified markets

— is substantial. Completing the reform requires bringing residual sectors into the net and institutionalising benefit pass-

through to consumers.

## Value addition
- Constitutional journey: the 122nd Amendment Bill was passed by the Rajya Sabha on 3 August 2016 and the Lok Sabha on 8 August 2016, ratified by more than 15 States, and received Presidential assent on 8 September 2016 as the 101st Amendment.
- GST Council composition: Union Finance Minister (Chair), Union MoS (Revenue/Finance), and the Finance/Taxation Minister of each State; decisions by a three-fourths weighted majority.
- Judicial position: in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022), the Supreme Court held that GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding, since both Parliament and State legislatures have simultaneous power under Art. 246A — a significant affirmation of fiscal federalism.
- GST 2.0 relief examples: household essentials (soaps, toothpaste, Indian breads) to 5% or nil; life-saving drugs from 12% to nil or 5%; farm machinery and irrigation equipment from 12% to 5%.

## Introduction

Fiscal consolidation means a credible, gradual reduction in deficits and debt without choking public investment. The Fifteenth Finance Commission set out explicit glide paths for both the Union and the States, and India’s record since has been one of the more successful consolidations among major economies.

## 15th FC recommendations on fiscal consolidation
- **Centre’s glide path** — Reduce the fiscal deficit to 4.0% of GDP by 2025-26
- **State ceilings** — 4.0% of GSDP (2021-22), 3.5% (2022-23), 3.0% (2023-26), with flexibility to carry forward unutilised borrowing within the award period
- **Debt targets** — General government debt to be brought to about 56% of GDP by 2025-26 — Centre 49.1%, States 32.5%
- **Extra borrowing space** — An additional 0.5% of GSDP for States, linked to power sector reforms
- **Quality of spending** — Revenue-deficit grants alongside tied capital grants, to protect growth-enhancing investment
- **Institutions** — Debt management cells in States, better public investment management, stricter FRBM compliance, and a high-powered inter-governmental group to review the fiscal responsibility architecture

## Progress — where consolidation has succeeded
- **Centre’s fiscal deficit** — 9.2% (FY21) → 6.4% (FY23) → 5.6% (FY24) → 4.8% (FY25 PA) → 4.4% (FY26) → 4.3% (BE 2026-27)
- **Revenue deficit** — 1.5% of GDP in FY27 — the lowest since FY09
- **Debt-to-GDP** — Centre’s liabilities 55.6% of GDP (BE 2026-27); general government debt down about 7.1 percentage points since 2020
- **Quality of adjustment** — Effective capex ₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP) now exceeds the fiscal deficit (≈₹16.9 lakh crore) — consolidation achieved without cutting investment
- **Revenue effort** — Revenue receipts up from 8.5% of GDP (FY16-20) to about 9.1% (FY22-25); direct-tax-to-GDP at 6.64%, a 24-year high
- **External validation** — Three sovereign rating upgrades in FY26, including S&P raising India from BBB- to BBB; the 10-year sovereign yield spread over US Treasuries more than halved

The most important structural change: from Budget 2025-26, the Centre replaced annual deficit targets with a debt-to-GDP anchor of 50±1% by 31 March 2031 — recognising that a debt path is a better medium-term discipline than a single-year number.

## Present situation — the risks
- Sub-national stress is the weak link. States’ combined fiscal deficit stood at 3.2% of GDP (FY25 PA) — 2.8% excluding SASCI loans — with the revenue deficit rising from 0.1% (FY19) to 0.7% of GDP. Guarantees reached 3.9% of GDP by March 2024.
- Unconditional cash transfers across States totalled about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26; the number of States running such schemes rose more than fivefold between FY23 and FY26, nearly half of them already in revenue deficit.
- Off-budget borrowings understate true liabilities — Andhra Pradesh alone carried ₹1.28 lakh crore (9.7% of GSDP) as of March 2023.
- Committed expenditure absorbed 51.76% of States’ revenue expenditure in FY24, leaving little flexibility.
- External shocks — the 2026 West Asia conflict, higher fuel prices and a rupee at about ₹95-96 per dollar — could force temporary loosening.

## Conclusion

The Fifteenth Finance Commission provided a credible roadmap, and the Union has broadly delivered on it — reducing the deficit by nearly five percentage points of GDP in five years while raising capital spending, an unusually high-quality

consolidation. The unfinished task is at the State level, which the 16th FC (2026-31) now addresses directly: a 3% GSDP cap for States, the Centre to reach 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31, combined debt projected to fall from 77.3% to 73.1% of GDP, and — most significantly — all off-budget borrowings to be discontinued and brought within the definition of debt.

## Value addition
- Legal architecture: FRBM Act, 2003; the N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee (2017) — recommended debt as the primary anchor (60% general government, 40% Centre) and an independent Fiscal Council, still unimplemented.
- AP as a consolidation case: fiscal deficit 5.11% (FY25) → 4.57% (FY26 RE) → 3.84% of GSDP (BE 2026-27); revenue deficit 3.79% → 2.33% → 1.11%; a debt swap of ₹43,298 crore of high-cost loans saving ₹327 crore a year.
- The enabling instrument: SASCI 50-year interest-free capex loans to States rose from ₹12,000 crore (FY21) to about

₹1.5 lakh crore (FY26), with ₹1.85 lakh crore in Budget 2026-27 — allowing States to consolidate and invest.

## Introduction

Budgetary policy performs three classical functions — allocation, distribution and stabilisation (Musgrave). The allocation function matters most in a mixed economy: private enterprise, driven by profit, systematically under-provides public goods and merit goods. The budget is the instrument through which the State corrects this market failure and directs resources towards socially desirable ends.

## Why reallocation is necessary
- Public goods (defence, street lighting, flood control) are non-rival and non-excludable — no private producer can charge for them.
- Merit goods (education, healthcare, nutrition) generate positive externalities that individuals under-value when deciding privately.
- Demerit goods (alcohol, tobacco) generate negative externalities that individuals under-count.
- Regional and social disparities persist because capital flows to where returns are highest, not where need is greatest.

## Instruments of reallocation
- **Taxation** — Heavy duties discourage socially harmful production and consumption · State excise on liquor; the 40% GST demerit rate on tobacco and pan masala
- **Subsidies and concessions** — Lower the effective cost of desirable activity · AP’s ₹11,000 crore agricultural power subsidy benefiting 22.5 lakh farmers; ₹890 crore aqua tariff subsidy
- **Direct public provision** — The State produces where private supply fails · Government schools, primary health centres, irrigation
- **Transfers** — Redistribute purchasing power directly · NTR Bharosa pensions of ₹4,000- ₹15,000 through DBT — over ₹58,000 crore disbursed in 19 months
- **Capital expenditure** — Creates assets that shift the economy’s productive frontier · AP capex of ₹53,915 crore in 2026-27

## Social sector allocation in the AP Budget 2026-27
- **School Education** — ₹32,308 crore
- **Health, Medical & Family Welfare** — ₹19,306 crore
- **BC component** — ₹51,021 crore
- **SC component** — ₹20,644 crore
- **ST component** — ₹9,190 crore
- **Minorities Welfare** — ₹6,090 crore
- **Women, Children, Differently Abled and Senior Citizens** — ₹4,582 crore
- **Housing** — ₹6,357 crore
- **Panchayati Raj & Rural Development** — ₹22,942 crore
- **Higher Education / Skill Development** — ₹2,567 crore / ₹1,232 crore

## Programmatic expression
- Health: Project Sanjeevani shifts the emphasis from curative reimbursement to preventive, outcome-based care

— the Kuppam pilot screened 63,867 individuals across 41 diagnostic tests and identified over 6,300 high-risk cases.

- Women and children: 33% reservation for women in jobs and education; One Family–One Entrepreneur targeting one lakh women entrepreneurs a year; 9,958 Anganwadi Centres upgraded.
- Inclusion: Indradanussu, a comprehensive programme for persons with disabilities; Deepam 2.0 delivering three free LPG cylinders a year to 1.08 crore women, with ₹2,897 crore credited directly.

## Critical assessment
- Strength: allocations are large, DBT-based and increasingly outcome-oriented; the shift to preventive healthcare is a genuine quality improvement.
- Weakness: the bulk remains revenue expenditure, with capital outlay at about 16% of total spending. Per capita public health spending stays modest relative to Kerala and Tamil Nadu, and learning outcomes have not kept pace with infrastructure spending.
- Systemic caution: the Economic Survey 2025-26 warns that expanding unconditional transfers across States — about

₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26 — creates expenditure rigidity that crowds out capital and human-capital investment.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s budget uses fiscal policy deliberately to reallocate resources towards equity — education, health, and the welfare of SCs, STs, BCs, minorities and women. The next stage is to convert allocation into outcomes: outcome-linked financing, teacher and clinical quality, and a rising share of capital spending, so that welfare expenditure builds capability rather than only providing relief. The State’s improving fiscal position — revenue deficit down to 1.11% of GSDP — creates exactly the space in which that shift becomes possible.

## Value addition
- Musgrave’s three functions of public finance: allocation (correcting market failure), distribution (equity), stabilisation (managing demand, employment and prices).
- AP economy for context: GSDP of about ₹19.8 lakh crore (2026-27); sectoral shares in 2023-24 — agriculture 37%, manufacturing 23%, services 40%; per capita GSDP ₹2,70,295 against India’s ₹2,15,935.
- Union benchmark: Gender Budget outlay rose from ₹0.98 lakh crore (2014-15) to ₹4.49 lakh crore (2025-26) — 8.86% of the Budget, up from 5.46% in 2014-15.
- SDG linkage: AP’s social sector allocations map directly onto SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 3 (Health), SDG 4 (Education), SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

(APPSC, 2023)Q.91 — What is meant by ‘Gender Budgeting’ and ‘Child Budgeting’? Does Andhra Pradesh follow gender budgeting and child budgeting? Evaluate. (APPSC, 2023)SECTION XI — Gender Budgeting and Andhra Pradesh Budgets (Q. 91–93)

Gender Budgeting is not a separate budget for women. It is the application of a gender lens across the entire budget cycle — formulation, allocation, execution and audit — to assess how public spending affects men and women differently. Child Budgeting applies the same logic to persons under 18, tracking what share of public expenditure actually reaches children’s health, education, nutrition and protection.

## The two concepts compared
- **Purpose** — Correct gender-blind allocation; make outcomes for women visible · Ensure children — who cannot vote or lobby — are not fiscally invisible
- **Method** — Gender Budget Statement classifying schemes by benefit incidence · Child Budget Statement tracking child-specific allocations
- **Illustrations** — Maternal health, SHG credit, skill training, safe transport · Mid-day meals/PM POSHAN, immunisation, ICDS, scholarships
- **Underlying principle** — Substantive equality (Art. 15(3) permits special provision for women and children) · The child’s right to development (Art. 39(f), Art. 21A, UNCRC)

## Does Andhra Pradesh follow them? Gender Budgeting — yes, institutionally
- AP formally adopted Gender Responsive Budgeting from FY 2021-22, with an initial outlay above ₹47,000 crore, expanded to about ₹55,015 crore in 2022-23.
- A five-year State Action Plan on GRB (2021-25) was launched, and Gender Budget Cells were established across departments for monitoring.
- The Gender Budget Statement follows the Union template: Part A — schemes with 100% allocation to women and girls (about ₹27,697 crore in 2022-23); Part B — composite schemes with 30-99% benefit to women (about ₹27,317 crore).
- Current programmatic expression (Budget 2026-27): ₹4,582 crore for the Women, Children, Differently Abled and Senior Citizens Welfare Department; 33% reservation for women in jobs and educational institutions; Adabidda Nidhi (₹1,500 a month to women aged 19-59 via DBT); Deepam 2.0 — three free LPG cylinders a year to 1.08 crore women, with ₹2,897 crore already credited; Stree Shakti free bus travel for women, girls and transgender persons; the One Family–One Entrepreneur drive targeting one lakh women entrepreneurs a year; and gratuity for Anganwadi workers, helpers and ASHAs.

## Child Budgeting — partially, and informally
- AP funds child-focused programmes generously — School Education ₹32,308 crore and Talliki Vandanam (₹15,000 a year to the mother or guardian for every child from Class 1 to Intermediate) — and upgraded 9,958 Anganwadi Centres, converting 4,687 mini-Anganwadis into main centres, with 192 new centres sanctioned in PVTG areas under PM JANMAN.
- But there is no formalised Child Budget Statement of the kind the Gender Budget Statement provides. Child-

related spending is dispersed across education, health, nutrition and welfare heads without a consolidated, auditable tracking framework.

## Evaluation
- **Strengths** — Gaps
- **GRB institutionalised with cells, a State Action Plan and a two-part statement** — Child budgeting remains unformalised — the principal structural gap
- **DBT delivery ensures transparency and reaches women directly** — Statements track allocations, not outcomes — no systematic gender or child impact audit
- **Life-cycle convergence: education (Talliki Vandanam) → livelihood (One Family–One Entrepreneur) → old-age security (NTR Bharosa)** — Frequent scheme redesign across governments disrupts longitudinal tracking
- **Recognition in national indices — AP performed strongly on SDG-5 (Gender Equality)** — Persistent low female LFPR (about 35.8%) shows cash transfers alone do not translate into economic participation

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh has made real institutional progress on gender budgeting and has substantial, well-targeted child-focused spending — but it practises child budgeting without a child budget. The next step is to formalise a Child Budget Statement, shift from allocation-tracking to outcome-auditing, and link women’s schemes to labour-force participation rather than only to income support — so that budgeting becomes genuinely transformative rather than compensatory.

- India’s Gender Budget: outlay rose from ₹0.98 lakh crore (2014-15) to ₹4.49 lakh crore (2025-26) — 8.86% of the Union Budget, up from 5.46% in 2014-15. The Gender Budget Statement (Statement 13) was introduced in 2005-06 following the Ministry of Finance’s Charter for Gender Budget Cells (2007).
- Constitutional anchor: Art. 15(3) (special provision for women and children), Art. 39(a) and (f), Art. 42 (maternity relief), Art. 21A (right to education), and the 73rd/74th Amendments reserving one-third of local body seats for women.
- Andhra Pradesh’s “Super Six”: Adabidda Nidhi (₹1,500/month for women aged 19-59), Talliki Vandanam (₹15,000/year per child), Deepam (three free LPG cylinders), Annadata Sukhibhava (₹20,000/year for small, marginal and tenant farmers), free bus travel for women, and 20 lakh jobs or a ₹3,000 monthly unemployment allowance.
- Safety architecture: the Shakti App with a seven-minute response target, 164 Shakti teams, and One Stop (Sakhi) Centres providing police, medical, legal and shelter support under one roof.

## Introduction

The Differentiated Banking Policy, flowing from the Nachiket Mor Committee (2013), abandoned the “one-size

universal bank” model in favour of licensed specialists — Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks — designed to serve segments that universal banks found unprofitable. It marked a shift from mandating inclusion to building institutions for inclusion.

## Scope of the Differentiated Banking Policy
- **Mandate** — Small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro enterprises, unorganised sector · Deposits, remittances and payments at the last mile
- **Lending** — 75% of ANBC to priority sector; 50% of loans up to ₹25 lakh · Cannot lend; deposits capped per customer
- **Reach requirement** — 25% of branches in unbanked rural centres · Access-focused, technology-led model
- **Growth path** — May seek conversion to universal bank on meeting RBI criteria (net worth, track record, asset quality) · No lending upgrade path

The policy’s logic is calibrated licensing: lighter capital and operating requirements in exchange for a binding inclusion mandate, all within the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. SFBs now hold about 16% of the microfinance market, evidence that the model reaches the intended segment.

## Potential of digital banking — analysis
- Cost collapse: India Stack — Aadhaar e-KYC, UPI, Account Aggregator — has cut the cost of opening and servicing an account to a fraction of branch-based delivery. UPI processed about 241.6 billion transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, and India accounts for roughly 49% of global real-time payment volume.
- From payments to credit — the crucial leap. The Economic Survey 2025-26 cites evidence that UPI’s verifiable transaction trail lets banks and fintechs lend to new-to-credit borrowers who lacked collateral or credit history — and default rates did not rise. Digital public infrastructure therefore deepens finance rather than merely digitising it.
- Institutional synergy: DBP institutions are the natural users of this rail — SFBs use digital underwriting for small-ticket loans; Payments Banks convert remittance relationships into savings behaviour.
- Last-mile bridges: Digital Banking Units, Business Correspondents/Bank Mitras, UPI Lite, UPI 123Pay for feature phones, and the Aadhaar-enabled Payment System for cash-in/cash-out.

## Critical analysis — access is not usage
- The access gap is largely closed — account ownership has reached roughly 89% (Global Findex 2025) and the RBI’s Financial Inclusion Index rose to 67.0 (March 2025) from 53.9 (March 2021). The usage and quality gap remains open — dormant accounts, low insurance and pension penetration, and limited formal credit for the informal sector.
- Cash has not disappeared: the Survey records that over 90% of UPI users still use cash regularly — India has a

hybrid, not a cashless, payments economy.

- New risks: UPI fraud reached about 10.64 lakh cases worth ₹805 crore in FY26 (to November), prompting NPCI to cap limits, remove collect requests and deploy AI-based mule-account detection.
- Viability question: zero-MDR on UPI leaves the rails unmonetised, straining the business case for last-mile agents.

## Conclusion

Differentiated banking supplies the institutions; digital banking supplies the infrastructure. Together they have made India a global reference point for inclusion at scale. The next phase must move from access to usage and from usage to welfare — deepening credit, insurance and pension penetration, protecting consumers from fraud and over-indebtedness, and building digital and financial literacy so the gains are evenly distributed.

## Value addition
- The 2030 Agenda identifies financial inclusion as an enabler for 7 of the 17 SDGs; the World Bank tracks it through the Global Findex Database.
- RBI Financial Inclusion Index (composite of Access, Usage, Quality): 67.0 in March 2025 against 53.9 in March 2021. RBI Digital Payments Index: 493.22 (March 2025) from 153.47 (March 2019).
- PMJDY: over 55 crore accounts, roughly 55% held by women — the foundation on which the digital layer was built.
- Andhra Pradesh: SHG-based delivery through SERP and Stree Nidhi, with repayment above 97%, shows how community institutions plus digital rails can rebuild trust after the 2010 microfinance crisis.
- One-line revision point: An account is access; a repeat transaction is inclusion; affordable credit is empowerment.

## Introduction

women entrepreneurship in India. (APPSC, 2023)

Women’s entrepreneurship in India is numerous but tiny. The Sixth Economic Census recorded 8.05 million women-owned establishments — 13.76% of all establishments, employing 13.45 million persons; but 83.19% of them operated without a single hired worker. The challenge is therefore not the number of women entrepreneurs but the scale and survival of their enterprises.

Challenges faced by women entrepreneurs

- Access to finance — the primary constraint - Collateral requirements: land and property are typically registered in male names, so women lack the security banks demand. - Credit history gap: first-time women borrowers have no formal record, so lenders price risk conservatively. - Small ticket sizes: most women’s enterprises need working capital of a few lakh rupees — a segment banks find administratively unattractive. - Dependence on informal sources, at high rates.
- Market access and scale - Weak linkages to buyers, e-commerce and government procurement. - Enterprises clustered in low-margin, traditional sectors — tailoring, food processing, beauty, handicrafts — with intense competition and thin margins. - Limited bargaining power in supply chains.
- Social and cultural - The care burden: unpaid domestic and care work, valued at ₹22.7 lakh crore or about 7.5% of GDP (Economic Survey 2022-23), leaves little time for enterprise. - Restricted mobility and safety concerns limit market visits, supplier negotiation and travel. - Family and social resistance to women running businesses, especially outside the home. - Confidence and risk-aversion shaped by socialisation rather than ability.
- Skill and information gaps - Limited exposure to financial literacy, digital tools, GST compliance and business planning. - Weak access to mentors and business networks, which are the informal infrastructure of entrepreneurship.
- Institutional and regulatory - Complex registration, licensing and compliance procedures. - Low awareness of available schemes — the commonest reason for under-utilisation. - Limited representation in industry associations and chambers.

Schemes and initiatives

- **Dedicated credit** — Stand-Up India · Bank loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore to at least one SC/ST and one woman borrower per bank branch for greenfield enterprise
- **Micro-credit** — PMMY (MUDRA) · Collateral-free loans in Shishu, Kishore and Tarun categories; women form the majority of beneficiaries
- **Micro-enterprise** — PMEGP · 35% margin money subsidy in rural areas for women (against 25% for general category), with own contribution of only 5%
- **SHG-based livelihood** — DAY-NRLM, Lakhpati Didi, Namo Drone Didi · Federated SHGs, credit linkage, and drones supplied to women’s SHGs for agri-services
- **Traditional artisans** — PM Vishwakarma, Mahila Coir Yojana · Toolkits, skill training and credit for craft-based livelihoods
- **Market access** — Mahila e-Haat, GeM’s Womaniya initiative · Online platforms connecting women producers to buyers and government procurement
- **Skilling** — PMKVY, DDU-GKY, Skill India · Vocational and entrepreneurship training
- **Support ecosystem** — Trade Related Entrepreneurship Assistance and Development (TREAD); women’s cells in DICs; Startup India’s women-focused facilitation · Handholding, incubation and fee concessions
- **Financial inclusion base** — PMJDY · Over 28 crore women with Jan Dhan accounts — the foundation for all credit-linked schemes

Assessment — what works and what does not

Works: microfinance reaches the intended population at scale — 627 lakh active borrowers with a gross loan portfolio of ₹2.38 lakh crore, of whom 95% are women and 80% rural. Financial inclusion has removed the account barrier entirely.

Does not work well: - Credit without markets: loans often fund consumption or debt-swapping rather than enterprise growth. - Survival, not scale: the vast majority of women’s units remain own-account, with no path from self-employment to employer. - Awareness and access gaps at the branch level, where scheme delivery ultimately rests. - Over-indebtedness risk: the FY25 microfinance stress, when MFI loans outstanding fell 14% on over-lending, prompted the RBI to cut NBFC-MFI qualifying assets from 75% to 60% (June 2025).

## Conclusion

India has built an impressive credit and inclusion architecture for women entrepreneurs — the account, the loan and the subsidy are all available. What is missing is the growth infrastructure: market linkage, mentoring, childcare that frees time, and asset ownership that provides collateral. Moving women from own-account survival to employer-scale enterprise is the next frontier — and it will be decided less by additional credit than by whether the surrounding constraints on time, mobility and markets are removed.

- Revised MSME classification (from 1 April 2025): Micro — investment up to ₹2.5 crore, turnover up to ₹10 crore; Small — ₹25 crore / ₹100 crore; Medium — ₹125 crore / ₹500 crore.
- Priority Sector Lending: a 7.5% sub-target for micro enterprises within the 40% PSL requirement; weaker-section lending includes women beneficiaries up to specified limits.
- Andhra Pradesh initiative: One Family–One Entrepreneur, targeting one lakh women entrepreneurs a year, supported by the SERP and Stree Nidhi network of about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, with repayment above 97%.

## Introduction

Agricultural credit is classified along two axes — the period for which it is needed and the source from which it comes. Both matter: the period determines whether credit funds an input or an asset, and the source determines its cost, which is the difference between a viable farm and a debt trap.

- Types of agricultural credit — by period and purpose
- **Short-term (crop loan)** — Up to 15 months · Seeds, fertiliser, pesticides, labour, irrigation charges, and consumption during the crop cycle
- **Medium-term** — 15 months to 5 years · Livestock purchase, small implements, minor irrigation, land improvement
- **Long-term (investment credit)** — Above 5 years · Tractors and machinery, tube wells, orchards and plantations, land development, storage and processing units, farmhouses

A further functional distinction: - Production credit — finances the current crop cycle. - Investment credit — creates a durable productive asset. India’s structural weakness is that short-term credit dominates, so credit sustains existing yields rather than raising them.

- Sources of agricultural credit Institutional sources
- **Commercial banks** — The largest suppliers today; bound by Priority Sector Lending — 18% of ANBC to agriculture, within which 10% for small and marginal farmers
- **Regional Rural Banks** — 28 RRBs with about 22,158 branches; consolidated CRAR at an all-time high of 14.4% (FY25); credit-deposit ratio 73.8% (March 2025) — the highest in 35 years
- **Cooperatives** — Three-tier structure — PACS at village level, District Central Cooperative Banks, State Cooperative Banks; historically the largest source, now weakened by poor governance and capital erosion
- **NABARD** — Apex refinancing institution; operates the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) since 1995-96, funded from shortfalls in banks’ PSL obligations
- **Small Finance Banks and NBFC-MFIs** — Reach segments banks find costly; SFBs must lend 75% of ANBC to the priority sector
- **SHG-Bank Linkage** — NABARD’s programme since 1992; in Andhra Pradesh, SERP’s 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, with repayment above 97%

Non-institutional sources

Moneylenders, traders and commission agents, landlords, relatives and friends. Their share has fallen substantially but they remain significant — particularly for tenant farmers, who cannot access institutional credit because it follows land records, and for consumption needs that formal lenders will not fund.

- Government initiatives to improve access
- The Kisan Credit Card (1998) Designed on a NABARD model scheme; a single revolving credit line replacing repeated loan applications. Limit raised to ₹5 lakh; interest 7% with a 3% prompt repayment incentive giving 4% effective; collateral-free up to ₹2 lakh; extended to allied activities (2004) and to animal husbandry and fisheries (2018-19); delivered through the RuPay KCC card; validity five years with annual review.
- Interest Subvention — the Modified Interest Subvention Scheme (MISS) Interest subsidy rose from ₹6,000 crore (2014-15) to ₹14,252 crore (2023-24), totalling about ₹1.44 lakh crore over a decade.
- Priority Sector Lending 18% of ANBC to agriculture, with sub-targets of 14% for non-corporate farmers and 10% for small and marginal farmers; shortfalls flow into RIDF.
- Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (2020) ₹1 lakh crore for post-harvest infrastructure — warehouses, cold storage, grading and logistics; ₹52,738 crore sanctioned as of December 2024.
- PM-KISAN and its credit linkage ₹6,000 a year in three instalments by DBT, now integrated with the KCC so that every PM-KISAN beneficiary can be brought into formal credit — the KCC saturation drive.
- Digital infrastructure - The Kisan Rin Portal (KRP) — developed jointly by MoA&FW, the Department of Financial Services, DAH&D, the Department of Fisheries, RBI and NABARD — provides an integrated view of farmer data, loan disbursement, interest subvention claims and scheme utilisation. - DILRMP land records digitisation and e-KYC of KCC accounts, which are the route to bringing tenant farmers and smallholders into formal credit. - Agristack and unified farmer registries.
- Institutional strengthening Computerisation of PACS, their conversion into multi-service centres, and the World’s Largest Grain Storage Plan in the Cooperative Sector building storage at PACS level.
- Risk mitigation as a credit enabler PMFBY crop insurance reduces lender risk and therefore improves credit

supply; e-NAM improves price realisation and hence repayment capacity.

Outcomes

- Institutional credit rose from ₹8.5 lakh crore (2014-15) to ₹25.48 lakh crore (2023-24).
- Small and marginal farmers’ access rose from 57% to 76% — the most significant equity outcome.
- KCCs issued rose from 1,285.37 lakh (2012-13) to 1,895.81 lakh (March 2019) and have expanded further under saturation drives.

Remaining gaps

- Tenant farmers excluded, since credit follows title — the single largest gap.
- Term credit scarce relative to crop loans.
- Cooperative weakness, particularly at PACS level.
- Regional imbalance — credit flows to irrigated, prosperous districts.
- Asset quality: agriculture’s GNPA at 6.0% is the highest of any sector, which makes lenders cautious precisely where credit is most needed.

## Conclusion

India’s agricultural credit system has expanded dramatically in scale and, importantly, in equity — with small and marginal farmers’ access rising from 57% to 76%. The unfinished agenda is one of composition and coverage: shifting the balance from short-term crop loans toward term credit for assets, reviving the cooperative tier, and — most importantly — making credit follow the cultivator rather than the title deed, through recorded tenancy and instruments such as Andhra Pradesh’s Crop Cultivator Rights Cards.

## Value addition
- Budgetary commitment: the Department of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare budget rose from ₹11,915 crore (2008-09) to ₹21,933 crore (2013-14) and ₹1,22,528 crore (2024-25).
- Committee lineage: the All-India Rural Credit Survey (1954) — “the cooperative has failed, but it must succeed”; the Khusro Committee (1989); the R.V. Gupta Committee (1998) on agricultural credit delivery, which recommended the KCC.
- Institutional history: NABARD established in 1982 on the recommendation of the CRAFICARD (Sivaraman) Committee, taking over the agricultural credit functions of the RBI.
- AP context: SERP and Stree Nidhi for SHG credit; Rythu Bharosa Kendras as village-level input, advisory and procurement points with digital farmer registration.
