253. What is Covid-19 and how is it spread? How are immuno-diagnostic methods used in the context of the Covid-19 pandemic? (APPSC, 2020)

COVID-19 is an acute respiratory illness caused by SARS-CoV-2, a single-stranded RNA betacoronavirus whose spike (S) glycoprotein binds the human ACE2 receptor to enter respiratory epithelium. Declared a pandemic in March 2020, WHO ended its Public Health Emergency of International Concern status in May 2023, though the virus now circulates endemically. Immuno-diagnostics - tests built on antigen-antibody recognition - became the workhorse of mass screening and population-level exposure estimation, distinct from genome-based molecular testing.

1. Modes of spread (in descending epidemiological weight) - Droplet and short-range aerosol: exhaled respiratory particles during coughing, singing or speech; the dominant route, which is why masking and ventilation mattered more than surface disinfection. - Long-range airborne aerosol: fine particles persisting in poorly ventilated indoor spaces, explaining super-spreader events in closed halls and public transport. - Fomite (surface) contact: possible but epidemiologically minor. - Pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic transmission: the defining challenge -infectiousness peaks around symptom onset, so contact tracing alone could not contain spread.

## Reproducible infographic - “Two Ladders of Detection”
- **Test type** — Principle · What it detects · Turnaround · Programmatic use
- **RT-PCR (molecular, not immuno)** — Reverse transcription + amplification · Viral RNA · 4-24 hrs · Gold standard confirmation
- **Rapid Antigen Test (RAT)** — Lateral-flow monoclonal antibody sandwich · Viral N-protein · 15-30 min · Mass screening, airports, containment zones
- **IgM/IgG ELISA & CLIA** — Enzyme/chemiluminescence- linked antigen-antibody binding · Host antibodies · 2-4 hrs · Sero-surveys, past- infection estimation
- **Neutralising antibody assay** — Functional blocking of virus- ACE2 binding · Protective antibody titre · 1-2 days · Vaccine efficacy and correlate-of-protection studies

2. How immuno-diagnostics were actually used - Antigen tests decentralised testing. Because lateral-flow RATs need no cold chain or trained microbiologist, they pushed testing from district labs to PHCs and railway stations, cutting isolation delay - the single biggest determinant of transmission chains broken. - Serology mapped the invisible epidemic. ICMR’s fourth National Sero-Survey (June-July 2021) found roughly two-thirds of Indians above six years already carried SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, revealing that confirmed cases were a small fraction of true infections and directly informing the decision not to re-impose national lockdowns. - Antibody assays underpinned vaccine science. Neutralising-antibody titres served as the immunological correlate for licensing Covaxin and Covishield and for fixing booster intervals. - Limitation to state honestly: antibody tests cannot diagnose current infection (antibodies appear 7-14 days late) and RATs have lower sensitivity, so a negative RAT in a symptomatic person required RT-PCR confirmation -a caveat ICMR built into its testing advisory.

3. Indian and Andhra Pradesh institutional response - Genomic layer: INSACOG, a 54-laboratory consortium coordinated by DBT with NCDC, ICMR and CSIR, tracked variants - showing that immuno-diagnostics work best when paired with genomic surveillance. - AP anchor: the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam - India’s first integrated medical device park - mass-produced RT-PCR kits, ventilators and oxygen concentrators during the pandemic, and hosts the DBT-supported Kalam Institute of Health Technology (KIHT) and the Bio Valley Incubation Council, making coastal AP a national node for diagnostic self-reliance.

## Conclusion

COVID-19 demonstrated that pandemic control rests on a layered diagnostic architecture: molecular tests for confirmation, antigen tests for speed and scale, and serology for population-level intelligence. India’s contribution was less in inventing these platforms than in manufacturing them at scale and at low cost - an advantage AMTZ institutionalises for Andhra Pradesh. Sustaining ICMR-DBT diagnostic R&D and INSACOG-style genomic surveillance is the practical form that pandemic preparedness must now take under the “One Health” framework.

254. What is Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC)? Describe the role of MHC classes. (APPSC, 2017)

The Major Histocompatibility Complex is a densely packed cluster of genes on the short arm of chromosome 6 in humans, where it is called the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) system. Its products are cell-surface glycoproteins that display fragments of protein antigens to T-lymphocytes. Because MHC is the most polymorphic gene family known in humans, it functions as a molecular identity card - the basis on which the immune system distinguishes “self” from “non-self.”

## Reproducible infographic - comparison table
- **Feature** — MHC Class I · MHC Class II · MHC Class III
- **Genes (HLA)** — A, B, C · DP, DQ, DR · C2, C4, Bf, TNF
- **Expressed on** — All nucleated cells + platelets · Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B- cells) · Secreted, not membrane-bound
- **Antigen presented** — Endogenous (intracellular) · Exogenous (phagocytosed) · -
- **Partner T-cell** — CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell · CD4+ helper T-cell · -
- **Immune outcome** — Killing of infected/tumour cell · Cytokine release, B-cell help, antibody production · Complement cascade, inflammation

1. MHC Class I - surveillance of the cell interior Every nucleated cell continuously exports samples of its own protein content on MHC-I. In a virus-infected cell - as in SARS-CoV-2 or hepatitis-B infection - viral peptides appear on MHC-I and CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells destroy the cell before it releases progeny virions. Tumour cells that down-regulate MHC-I escape this surveillance, which is precisely the mechanism modern checkpoint-inhibitor cancer immunotherapy attempts to reverse.

2. MHC Class II - recruiting help from outside Dendritic cells and macrophages engulf extracellular pathogens and present their peptides on MHC-II to CD4+ helper T-cells. In tuberculosis, alveolar macrophages present Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens this way; the resulting cytokine release drives granuloma formation and B-cell antibody production. Every vaccine that produces durable antibody depends on this MHC-II pathway - which is why adjuvants are designed to maximise antigen uptake by dendritic cells.

3. Why polymorphism matters - three consequences - Transplantation: graft rejection is essentially T-cell recognition of foreign HLA. HLA typing and cross-matching determine donor-recipient compatibility; the closer the match, the lower the immunosuppression burden. - Disease association: specific alleles predispose to autoimmunity - HLA-B27 with ankylosing spondylitis, HLA-DR3/DR4 with Type-1 diabetes, HLA-B*57:01 with abacavir hypersensitivity (now a mandatory pre-treatment test). - Population immunity: HLA diversity explains why a pathogen never wipes out an entire population, and why vaccine responses vary across populations - the rationale for DBT’s GenomeIndia Project, which completed whole-genome sequencing of 10,000 Indians (DBT, 2025) to map such diversity.

4. Governance context in India and Andhra Pradesh Transplantation is governed by the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994, implemented through the three-tier NOTTO-ROTTO-SOTTO network under MoHFW, with the “One Nation, One Organ Allocation” reform removing domicile restrictions. Andhra Pradesh, which additionally has its own AP Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1995, operates a State Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation and recorded 41 deceased donors in 2023 (NOTTO) - modest against Telangana’s 252, indicating scope for expanding brain-death certification and HLA-typing laboratory capacity in AP’s teaching hospitals such as Andhra Medical College, Visakhapatnam and SVIMS, Tirupati.

## Conclusion

The MHC is the hinge on which adaptive immunity turns: without antigen presentation there is no T-cell response, and hence no cell-mediated immunity, no antibody class switching and no immunological memory. Its extreme polymorphism is simultaneously humanity’s evolutionary insurance against pandemics and the principal obstacle to organ transplantation. Advances in HLA typing, national organ-allocation reform and population genomics are therefore not separate stories but a single continuum from molecular immunology to public health policy.

255. (a) What is immunisation? Briefly write the history of the development of vaccines? (b) Write short notes on (i) Edible vaccines (ii) ELISA test (iii) Autoimmune diseases. (APPSC, 2016)

Immunisation is the deliberate induction of protective immunity against a specific pathogen, exploiting the immune system’s property of memory. It is either active (a vaccine presents antigen, and the body manufactures its own antibodies and memory cells) or passive (preformed antibodies are transferred, giving immediate but short-lived protection). It remains the most cost-effective public health intervention available: India’s Universal Immunisation Programme reaches about 2.9 crore pregnant women and 2.54 crore newborns annually, with full immunisation coverage rising from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026 (PIB, March 2026).

## (a) Immunisation and the evolution of vaccines

## Reproducible infographic - four-phase timeline
- **Phase** — Period · Breakthrough · Technology principle
- **Empirical** — 1796-1885 · Jenner’s cowpox smallpox vaccine (1796); Pasteur’s anthrax (1881) and rabies (1885) vaccines · Cross-protection; live attenuation
- **Classical** — 1921-1961 · BCG (Calmette-Gurin, 1921); Salk inactivated polio (1955); Sabin oral polio (1961) · Killed and attenuated whole organisms
- **Recombinant** — 1986 onwards · Hepatitis-B vaccine from yeast; HPV virus-like particles · rDNA-expressed subunit antigens
- **Nucleic acid & vector** — 2020 onwards · mRNA (Pfizer, Moderna); viral- vector (Covishield); India’s ZyCoV-D, the world’s first DNA vaccine · Delivering genetic instructions, not antigen

- Why the sequence matters: each phase reduced the amount of pathogen needed, and therefore the risk. Whole-organism vaccines carried reversion risk; subunit and nucleic-acid vaccines carry none, and can be redesigned in weeks rather than years - the reason COVID vaccines arrived within a year.
- India’s current frontier: an indigenously manufactured Tetanus-adult Diphtheria (Td) vaccine from the Central Research Institute, Kasauli was launched on 21 February 2026, and a nationwide HPV vaccination campaign was launched on 28 February 2026 (PIB, 2026). India supplies roughly 60% of the world’s vaccines.

## (b) Short notes

(i) Edible vaccines - transgenic plants engineered to express a pathogen’s antigenic protein in an edible tissue (banana, tomato, potato, rice), inducing mucosal (IgA) immunity when eaten. Their appeal is structural: no needles, no cold chain, no trained vaccinator - precisely the three cost drivers that limit rural coverage. Transgenic potato expressing hepatitis-B surface antigen is the classic proof of concept; ICAR-IARI and DBT-supported groups have explored candidates for cholera and diarrhoeal disease. Constraints are real - inconsistent antigen dose per fruit, degradation in the stomach, and unresolved biosafety and GEAC regulatory clearance - so none is yet licensed.

(ii) ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) - a plate-based assay in which antigen-antibody binding is revealed by an enzyme-linked secondary antibody producing a measurable colour change. Its virtues are quantification, high throughput and low cost per test, which is why it remains the screening backbone for HIV under NACO, hepatitis-B, dengue and Japanese encephalitis. In 2025 ICMR licensed IgM-capture ELISA kits for dengue, chikungunya and Japanese encephalitis to Indian manufacturers at the India MedTech Expo (PIB, 2025), deepening diagnostic self-reliance.

(iii) Autoimmune diseases - conditions in which the loss of immunological self-tolerance causes the immune system to attack host tissue, mediated by autoantibodies and autoreactive T-cells. Examples: rheumatoid arthritis (joint synovium), Type-1 diabetes (pancreatic beta cells), systemic lupus erythematosus (multi-organ), Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Genetic susceptibility is largely HLA-linked; management uses immunosuppressants and targeted biologics such as anti-TNF monoclonal antibodies.

## Conclusion

The arc from Jenner’s cowpox lymph to mRNA and DNA platforms is a progressive substitution of precision for crudeness -less pathogen, more targeting, faster design. India’s contribution has been to convert that science into scale and affordability. The remaining challenge is neither scientific nor manufacturing but behavioural and logistical: reaching zero-dose children in tribal, migrant and peri-urban pockets, as Andhra Pradesh learned when seven measles outbreaks were reported between January and March 2025 - six in Alluri Sitarama Raju district and one in Vizianagaram - traced to immunity gaps from dropout children, prompting statewide Measles-Rubella special drives under the national MR elimination campaign 2025-26 (WHO-India/NPSN, 2025-26).

256. What is an antibody? Discuss the advancements in the field of immunodiagnostics with suitable examples. (TGPSC, 2016)

An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped glycoprotein secreted by plasma cells derived from B-lymphocytes. Two heavy and two light chains form a variable region that binds one specific epitope with extraordinary precision, and a constant (Fc) region that determines class (IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD) and recruits effector functions. It is this two-part architecture that makes antibodies not merely defensive molecules but the most versatile reagents in medicine: the variable region supplies specificity, and the constant region provides a convenient handle to attach enzymes, dyes or gold particles for signal generation.

## Reproducible infographic - the generational ladder of immunodiagnostics
- **Generation** — Technique · What it added · Indian example
- **1st - Visual** — Agglutination, precipitation (Widal, blood grouping) · Simplicity, no equipment · Widal test for typhoid
- **2nd - Enzymatic** — ELISA, Western blot · Quantification and high throughput · NACO HIV screening; ICMR dengue/JE/chikungunya IgM kits
- **3rd - Monoclonal** — Hybridoma-derived mAbs, lateral-flow strips · Reproducibility, batch-to-batch uniformity · Pregnancy kits, malaria and COVID rapid antigen tests
- **4th - Automated** — CLIA, flow cytometry, immunofluorescence · Sensitivity and multiplexing · Leukaemia immunophenotyping; CD4 counts under NACP
- **5th - Point-of-care** — Immunosensors, microfluidics, lab-on-chip · Portability, near-patient testing · Hub-and-spoke diagnostics under Ayushman Bharat HWCs

1. From polyclonal serum to monoclonal precision The Khler-Milstein hybridoma technique (1975) allowed a single B-cell clone to be immortalised, producing an unlimited, identical antibody supply. This solved the reproducibility problem that had made serological tests unreliable, and is why every modern rapid test strip works the same way in Vizag as in Delhi. The same technology now yields therapeutic monoclonals - anti-TNF for rheumatoid arthritis, trastuzumab for HER2 breast cancer - making immunodiagnostics and immunotherapy a shared technology base.

2. Multiplexing and automation raised the ceiling Flow cytometry can tag several surface markers simultaneously, enabling leukaemia sub-typing and CD4/CD8 monitoring for people living with HIV under the National AIDS Control Programme. Chemiluminescence immunoassays pushed detection limits low enough to measure cardiac troponin, thyroid hormones and tumour markers routinely.

3. Miniaturisation moved the laboratory to the patient Immunosensors and microfluidic cartridges deliver laboratory-grade results in minutes at a health-and-wellness centre, addressing rural India’s real bottleneck - not the absence of tests but the distance to a laboratory.

4. Indian self-reliance - the current record At the India MedTech Expo 2025, ICMR licensed nine health technologies to Indian firms, including IgM-detection ELISA kits for Japanese encephalitis, dengue and chikungunya, the AFuPEPLISA kit for Aspergillus fumigatus antibodies, and a colorimetric LAMP assay for monkeypox (PIB, 2025). Separately, DBT, BIRAC, ICMR and AIIMS reviewed indigenously developed HPV test kits for cervical cancer screening (PIB, 2025). (Note: LAMP is a nucleic-acid amplification method, not an immunoassay - a distinction examiners look for.)

5. Andhra Pradesh anchor The AP MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam, spread over 270 acres, provides shared capital-intensive facilities - component testing, EMI laboratory, sterilisation and radiation testing - that cut device manufacturing costs sharply for small firms. It houses the DBT-supported Kalam Institute of Health Technology (KIHT), which conducts health-technology assessment and market intelligence, and the Bio Valley Incubation Council, making Visakhapatnam India’s principal cluster for diagnostic-device manufacture.

## Conclusion

Each generation of immunodiagnostics solved the previous one’s binding constraint - first reproducibility, then sensitivity, then portability. The frontier now is affordability at the last mile, where lateral-flow and microfluidic formats meet the Ayushman Bharat network of health and wellness centres. For India the strategic question is no longer whether it can invent these assays but whether it can manufacture them domestically at scale; institutions such as ICMR’s technology-licensing route and AMTZ Visakhapatnam are the answer being constructed.

257. (a) Enumerate the mechanism of the humoral immunity system and the usefulness of antibodies. (b) Give an account of the adverse effects of passive immunisation. (APPSC, 2012)

Humoral immunity is the antibody-mediated arm of adaptive immunity, executed by B-lymphocytes and effective chiefly against extracellular pathogens and their toxins circulating in blood, lymph and mucosal fluids - the complement of cell-mediated immunity, which handles intracellular threats. Passive immunisation short-circuits this process by transferring ready-made antibodies, buying immediate protection at the cost of durability and, occasionally, safety.

## (a) Mechanism of the humoral response

## Reproducible infographic - linear flowchart

Antigen entry -> B-cell receptor binding -> antigen processing and MHC-II display -> CD4+ helper T-cell recognition + cytokine release -> clonal proliferation -> differentiation into plasma cells (antibody factories) + memory B-cells -> antibody secretion and pathogen elimination -> affinity maturation and class switching (IgM -> IgG/IgA)

- Antigen recognition: surface immunoglobulin on a naive B-cell binds its specific epitope; the antigen is internalised and re-displayed on MHC-II.
- T-cell help: a matching CD4+ helper T-cell releases interleukins that license the B-cell to divide - which is why HIV, by depleting CD4 cells, cripples antibody responses as well.
- Effector phase: plasma cells secrete thousands of antibody molecules per second; germinal-centre affinity maturation progressively improves binding strength.
- Memory: long-lived memory B-cells persist for years to a lifetime, producing the rapid, high-titre secondary response that vaccination is designed to install.

Usefulness of antibodies - five functions - Neutralisation: blocking viral attachment (anti-spike antibodies preventing SARS-CoV-2 from binding ACE2) or toxin binding (diphtheria and tetanus antitoxin). - Opsonisation: coating pathogens so macrophage Fc receptors can grip and phagocytose them. - Agglutination and precipitation: clumping microbes and soluble antigens for clearance - also the basis of blood grouping and the Widal test. - Complement activation: the classical pathway culminating in the membrane attack complex and bacterial lysis. - Practical utility: memory-based vaccine protection, diagnostics (ELISA, rapid kits), and therapeutic monoclonals.

## (b) Adverse effects of passive immunisation - with mechanism
- Serum sickness (Type-III hypersensitivity): heterologous (usually equine) serum proteins form antigen-antibody immune complexes that deposit in joints, kidneys and skin, producing fever, urticaria, arthralgia and proteinuria 7-14 days after administration. This is the classic hazard of equine anti-snake venom (ASV) and equine anti-rabies serum.
- Anaphylaxis (Type-I hypersensitivity): IgE-mediated, immediate, potentially fatal - the reason ASV and rabies immunoglobulin must be administered only where adrenaline and resuscitation facilities exist, a requirement embedded in MoHFW’s National Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Snakebite Envenoming (NAPSE, 2024), which targets halving snakebite deaths by 2030 and is directly relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s high rural snakebite burden.
- Interference with active immunisation: passively transferred IgG neutralises live vaccine virus before it can replicate; hence measles vaccination must be deferred after immunoglobulin administration, and maternal antibody explains why measles vaccine is given at nine months, not at birth.
- No immunological memory and short protection: transferred IgG has a half-life of about three weeks, so protection wanes and repeat exposure needs repeat treatment - with rising risk of sensitisation each time.
- Transmission and quality risk: blood-derived products carry a residual, though now very small, risk of blood-borne infection; this drove the shift from equine to human immunoglobulin and now to recombinant monoclonal antibodies, which eliminate animal protein and batch variability entirely.

## Conclusion

Humoral immunity is the body’s own precision-guided system, slow to build but self-renewing through memory; passive immunisation is a borrowed shield - instant, indispensable in emergencies such as snakebite, rabies exposure and tetanus-prone wounds, but transient and immunologically foreign. The correct policy posture, therefore, is to reserve passive immunisation for post-exposure emergencies while investing in active immunisation coverage and in recombinant monoclonal alternatives that carry the benefit without the hypersensitivity burden.

258. (a) What are the organs of the immune system? Give a schedule of immunisation for new-born children. (b) Write a short note on the adverse consequences of vaccination. (APPSC, 2012)

The immune system is an organ-and-cell network that distinguishes self from non-self and eliminates pathogens. Its anatomy is functionally divided into primary lymphoid organs, where lymphocytes are generated and educated, and secondary lymphoid organs, where they encounter antigen and mount responses. Immunisation deliberately loads this system with harmless antigen; in India this is delivered through the Universal Immunisation Programme, which achieved 98.4% full immunisation coverage by January 2026 (PIB, March 2026) while reducing zero-dose children to 0.06% of the child population (2024).

- **14 weeks** — Pentavalent-3, OPV-3, Rotavirus-3, fIPV-2, PCV-2 · As above
- **9-12 months** — Measles-Rubella-1, JE-1*, PCV booster, Vitamin-A 1st dose · Measles, rubella, Japanese encephalitis
- **16-24 months** — MR-2, JE-2*, DPT booster-1, OPV booster · Consolidation of immunity
- **5-6 years** — DPT booster-2 · Long-term protection
- **10 and 16 years** — Td · Tetanus and adult diphtheria

*JE vaccine only in endemic districts. Td doses at 10 and 16 years now draw on the indigenous Td vaccine from CRI Kasauli, launched 21 February 2026 (PIB, 2026).

## (c) Adverse consequences of vaccination - the WHO causality framework

An Adverse Event Following Immunization (AEFI) is any untoward medical occurrence after vaccination, which need not be caused by it. India classifies AEFIs into five causal categories, and this framing - rather than a bare list of symptoms - is what distinguishes a strong answer:

- Vaccine product-related: the true pharmacological reaction - mild fever, injection-site pain and swelling (very common, self-limiting); rarely, anaphylaxis (roughly 1-2 per million doses) or febrile seizure.
- Vaccine quality defect-related: a manufacturing or batch fault, addressed through CDSCO lot-release testing.
- Immunisation error-related (programme error): contaminated diluent, wrong reconstitution, reuse of syringes -the largest preventable category, tackled through auto-disable syringes and vaccinator training.
- Immunisation anxiety-related: fainting, hyperventilation and dizziness triggered by fear, especially in adolescent school-based campaigns; not a vaccine effect at all.
- Coincidental: an unrelated illness occurring by chance in the same window - historically the largest category, and the main driver of media-fuelled vaccine hesitancy.

Surveillance architecture: AEFIs are reported through SAFE-VAC, integrated with the U-WIN platform for routine immunisation, investigated by District Immunisation Officers, and causality-assessed by State and National AEFI Committees under the National AEFI Surveillance and Response Operational Guidelines, 2024 (MoHFW), with technical support from the National AEFI Technical Collaborating Centre at Lady Hardinge Medical College.

## Conclusion

The immune system’s architecture explains both why vaccines work and why they occasionally misfire: the same antigen-processing machinery that confers protection can produce inflammatory or hypersensitivity reactions. The correct public health response is not to minimise adverse events but to detect, investigate and communicate them transparently - which is precisely what AEFI surveillance exists to do. Andhra Pradesh’s experience is instructive: seven measles outbreaks in early 2025, concentrated in Alluri Sitarama Raju and Vizianagaram districts, arose not from vaccine risk but from dropout children in tribal and peri-urban pockets, and were answered with statewide Measles-Rubella special drives. The lesson is that the danger from not vaccinating remains vastly larger than the danger from vaccinating.

Institutional map: MoHFW/Immunization Division -> NHM State Immunisation Cells -> District Immunisation Officer -> ANM/ASHA at Village Health and Nutrition Days; NTAGI advises on vaccine introduction; CDSCO regulates; ITSU provides technical support. - Terminology: cold chain, open-vial policy, auto-disable syringe, zero-dose child, causality assessment, herd immunity, catch-up round. - SDG linkage: SDG-3.2 (neonatal and under-5 mortality), SDG-3.8 (UHC), SDG-3.b (access to vaccines), SDG-10.2 (reaching marginalised tribal populations).

259. Define immunity. Discuss the concept of vaccination and explain how the vaccine for OPT is produced conventionally. (APPSC, 2011)

Immunity is the capacity of a host to recognise, resist and neutralise pathogens and their toxins through cellular and antibody-mediated defence. Vaccination converts this natural capacity into a planned public-health instrument. Its scale in India is striking: full immunisation coverage rose from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026, while zero-dose children fell to 0.06% of the population in 2024 (MoHFW/PIB, March 2026).

- **Type** — Basis · Nature · Example
- **Innate** — Present from birth · Non-specific, no memory · Skin, mucosa, phagocytes, complement
- **Acquired - Active** — Antigen exposure · Specific, memory formed · Natural infection; OPV, Td vaccine
- **Acquired - Passive** — Ready-made antibodies transferred · Immediate but short-lived · Maternal IgG; anti-snake venom, anti-tetanus serum

Concept of vaccination. Vaccination deliberately introduces an attenuated, killed or fractionated antigen so that memory B and T cells form without the disease. This matters because on re-exposure the anamnestic response is faster and larger than the primary response. Beyond the individual, coverage above the threshold produces herd immunity, which protects the unvaccinated - the mechanism behind India’s polio-free certification by the WHO in March 2014.

Conventional production of the “OPT” vaccines(read as Oral Polio + Tetanus toxoid of the triple antigen):

- Oral Polio Vaccine (Sabin, live attenuated): the three poliovirus serotypes are attenuated by serial passage at low temperature; propagated in primary monkey-kidney (later Vero) cell culture; harvested, filtered, titrated, blended and stabilised with magnesium chloride. Given orally, it induces mucosal IgA in the gut - the reason it interrupts wild-virus transmission, not merely disease.
- Tetanus toxoid:Clostridium tetani is grown in fermenters; the exotoxin is harvested and detoxified with formaldehyde into a non-toxic but immunogenic toxoid; purified and adsorbed onto aluminium phosphate/hydroxide adjuvant to prolong antigen release; blended into DPT/Td. In February 2026, CRI Kasauli launched India’s first indigenously manufactured Td vaccine, supplying 55 lakh doses to the UIP by April 2026 (PIB, 2026).

AP linkage: Andhra Pradesh delivers UIP doses through its eVIN-enabled cold-chain network and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, and joined the nationwide HPV vaccination rollout on 28 February 2026 along with all States and UTs (PIB, 2026).

## Conclusion

Immunity is the biological foundation; vaccination is the public-health architecture built upon it. The conventional OPV and tetanus toxoid routes - attenuation and chemical detoxification respectively - remain textbook illustrations of how immunological principle becomes industrial process. Sustaining near-universal coverage, closing the residual zero-dose pocket, and expanding indigenous manufacturing are now the operative priorities.

- U-WIN platform (pan-India rollout 2024): 11.87 crore children and 3.96 crore pregnant women registered as of March 2026; creates portable, permanent digital immunisation records (PIB, 2026).
- UIP scale: reaches 2.9 crore pregnant women and 2.54 crore newborns annually, free of cost - among the world’s largest programmes.
- India’s elimination record: smallpox eradicated; polio eradicated (WHO certification, March 2014); maternal and neonatal tetanus and yaws eliminated.
- HPV vaccination (Feb 2026): single-dose Gardasil-4 for ~1.15-1.2 crore girls aged 14; India joins 160+ countries with HPV in the national schedule.
- Regulatory standing: India has achieved WHO Maturity Level 3 in global benchmarking of regulatory systems (PIB, 2026).
- Mission Indradhanush (Dec 2014) -> IMI 5.0 (2023), which extended coverage from under-2s to under-5s and piloted U-WIN nationally.
- SDG linkage: SDG 3.2 (end preventable newborn/under-5 deaths) and SDG 3.8 (universal health coverage).

260. Medicinal and Aromatic Plants could contribute immensely to the National Health and Wealth. Critically analyse its role on impacting rural livelihood and empowering women involved in the same. (TGPSC, 2024)

Medicinal and Aromatic Plants (MAPs) are species yielding bioactive compounds used in medicine, perfumery, cosmetics and nutraceuticals. India documents 1,178 medicinal plant species in trade, of which 242 are traded above 100 MT per annum, against an annual domestic demand of roughly 5,12,000 metric tonnes (NMPB study cited by Ministry of Ayush/PIB, 2026). This places MAPs at the intersection of health security, export earnings and forest-fringe livelihoods.

Conservation (MPCDA / MPCA) -> Quality Planting Material (RCFCs) -> Cultivation (NAM subsidy) -> Primary processing (VDVK / SHG) ->

Market (e-CHARAK, buy-back MoUs)Leakage arrow downward at stages 3-4: wild over-harvest, adulteration, distress sale to intermediaries.

1. National health and wealth. MAPs are the raw-material base of the AYUSH systems, which the WHO estimates serve roughly 80% of the world’s population through traditional medicine. Government support is structured: the NMPB Central Sector Scheme for Conservation, Development and Sustainable Management of Medicinal Plants carries an outlay of Rs. 322.41 crore for 2021-22 to 2025-26, while the National AYUSH Mission subsidises cultivation of 140 prioritised species at 30%, 50% or 75% of cost and has supported over 56,000 hectares (Ministry of Ayush/PIB).

2. Rural livelihood. Because species such as Ashwagandha, Aloe vera, Mentha and Lemongrass tolerate marginal and rainfed land, they diversify income where cereals give thin returns. The constraint has always been the market, which is why NMPB’s e-CHARAK portal (with C-DAC) and buy-back MoUs with AYUSH industry bodies at pre-agreed price and volume matter more than subsidy alone - they convert a subsistence collection activity into a contracted supply relationship.

3. Women’s empowerment - the Andhra Pradesh instance. Nursery raising, drying, grading and distillation are low-capital, near-home operations, which is why women dominate them. In AP, the Girijan Co-operative Corporation (GCC), Visakhapatnam - which holds exclusive minor forest produce procurement rights across the state’s tribal tracts - has had 415 Van Dhan Vikas Kendras sanctioned with Rs. 36.04 crore released, covering 1,24,500 tribal members, with honey processing units alone generating over Rs. 250 lakh in 2024-25 (Ministry of Tribal Affairs knowledge repository, 2026). Under this framework, Chenchu women of the Nallamala forest converted Nannari (Decalepis hamiltonii) roots into a processed medicinal juice enterprise, moving from wage collection to first-generation entrepreneurship.

4. The critical half. Three constraints blunt the promise. First, most high-volume trade still relies on wild collection, so demand growth translates into resource depletion - Himalayan species such as Saussurea costus are already CITES Appendix-I listed. Second, adulteration and variable bioactive content depress buyer confidence; the Quality Council of India’s Voluntary Certification Scheme for Medicinal Plant Produce (VCSMPP) remains, as its name says, voluntary. Third, benefit-sharing under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 is mediated through Biodiversity Management Committees whose capacity in tribal AP is uneven, so value often accrues downstream rather than to the gatherer.

## Conclusion

MAPs link health security to livelihood sustainability, but the link holds only where cultivation replaces extraction and where women’s collectives capture processing margin rather than raw-material price. The AP model - GCC procurement at MSP-aligned rates plus VDVK-based value addition - shows the institutional form this can take. Scaling it requires enforceable quality certification, functioning benefit-sharing, and forward market contracts rather than one-time subsidy.

- NMPB (Ministry of Ayush) implements: MPCDAs for in-situ conservation, herbal gardens for ex-situ conservation, livelihood linkages through JFMCs/BMCs/SHGs, IEC and R&D, and marketing promotion.
- Regional-cum-Facilitation Centres (RCFCs) supply Quality Planting Material; AP received support under the “Forward and Backward Linkage in Supply Chain of Medicinal Plants” component in FY 2023-24 (PIB, 2026).
- e-CHARAK - NMPB + C-DAC portal and mobile app connecting growers to buyers.
- VCSMPP (QCI) - voluntary certification on Good Agricultural Practices and Good Field Collection Practices; 4,408 farmers trained across 76 programmes.
- Pradhan Mantri Van Dhan Yojana (TRIFED) and PM-JANMAN VDVKs for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups - 73 VDVKs covering 6,162 PVTG beneficiaries in AP.
- Legal frame: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (access and benefit sharing); Forest Rights Act, 2006 (community rights over MFP).
- SDG linkage: SDG 1 (poverty), SDG 3 (health), SDG 5 (gender equality), SDG 15 (life on land).

261. What is recombinant DNA? Draw a schematic to show the process of creating rDNA and explain the roles of restriction enzymes and vectors in this process. Give an example of rDNA technology. (APPSC, 2020)

Recombinant DNA is artificially constructed DNA formed by joining segments from two different sources, so that a host cell expresses a gene it never possessed. Since Boyer and Cohen’s 1973 demonstration, this single technique has underwritten modern biopharmaceuticals and transgenic agriculture. Its economic footprint in India is now substantial: the bioeconomy reached USD 195.3 billion in 2025, contributing about 4.8% of GDP, with biopharma the second-largest sub-sector (India BioEconomy Report 2025, DBT-BIRAC).

Donor organism DNA                    Vector (plasmid pBR322)           |                                        |    [ EcoRI cuts GAATTC ]  <-- same enzyme -->  [ EcoRI cuts ]           |                                        |    Gene with STICKY ENDS  ------------------>  Open vector                           \                  /                         [ DNA LIGASE seals ]                                  |                     RECOMBINANT VECTOR (chimeric DNA)                                  |         Transformation into host (E. coli / yeast)         via CaCl2 heat-shock or electroporation                                  |         Selection: antibiotic resistance marker /         insertional inactivation of reporter gene                                  |         Bioreactor culture -> Downstream processing                                  |                      PURIFIED PRODUCT (e.g. insulin)

Role of restriction enzymes. Restriction endonucleases scan double-stranded DNA for a palindromic recognition sequence - EcoRI recognises 5’-GAATTC-3’ - and cut off-centre between the same two bases on both strands. This off-centre cut is the whole point: it leaves single-stranded overhangs, or sticky ends, that hydrogen-bond with any complementary fragment cut by the same enzyme. Precision matters because the gene must be excised without damaging its coding sequence; over 900 such enzymes from 230+ bacterial strains give the engineer a wide choice of cut sites.

Role of vectors. A vector is the delivery vehicle and must carry three features to work: an origin of replication (so the insert is copied), a selectable marker such as ampR (so transformed cells can be identified against a background of untransformed ones), and unique recognition sites for cloning. Plasmid pBR322 and bacteriophage lambda serve bacterial hosts; the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens serves plants - the route by which Bt genes enter crops.

Examples and the Indian context.Humulin (1982) was the first recombinant therapeutic. The Hepatitis B vaccine in India’s UIP is a recombinant surface-antigen product expressed in yeast - proof that rDNA reaches routine public health, not just premium medicine. In agriculture, Bt cotton expresses the cry1Ac toxin gene from Bacillus thuringiensis.

AP linkage: Cotton is grown across Guntur, Kurnool, Prakasam, Krishna and Anantapur under all four cultivated Gossypium species (AICRP-Cotton, ANGRAU). ANGRAU’s Regional Agricultural Research Station, Lam (Guntur) now runs a dedicated biotechnology laboratory and has developed a public-sector Bt cotton variety - significant because, unlike proprietary hybrids, a variety allows farmers to save and reuse seed (ANGRAU, 2026).

Regulatory layer: the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM) under DBT clears laboratory and confined trials; the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) under MoEFCC, constituted under the Rules of 1989 framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, approves environmental release.

## Conclusion

Recombinant DNA technology converted genetics from a descriptive science into a manufacturing platform. Restriction enzymes supply the precision and vectors supply the delivery; together they make a human gene expressible in a bacterium. India’s task now is less scientific than institutional - predictable biosafety clearance, indigenous vectors and cell lines, and public-sector varieties like ANGRAU’s that keep the benefit with the farmer.

- Five tools of rDNA technology: restriction endonucleases, DNA ligase, polymerases (PCR), vectors, and a competent host.
- Palindrome: a sequence reading identically 5’->3’ on both strands - the structural basis of sticky-end generation.
- Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size on an agarose matrix; smaller fragments migrate farther toward the anode.
- Downstream processing - separation, purification, formulation and quality control - typically dominates the cost of a recombinant product.
- BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment), 2024 - DBT; six thematic sectors including precision biotherapeutics and climate-resilient agriculture; India’s first Biomanufacturing Institute at Mohali and a National Biofoundry Network.
- Biopharma SHAKTI (Union Budget 2026-27): Rs. 10,000 crore over five years for biologics and biosimilars.
- AP institutional map: ANGRAU-Lam biotechnology laboratory (Guntur); Institute of Frontier Technologies, RARS Tirupati (biotechnology, bioinformatics, nanotechnology, biocontrol).

262. Describe the medicinal qualities of mushrooms. (APPSC, 2017)

Medicinal mushrooms are macrofungi whose fruiting bodies or mycelia yield compounds with demonstrable pharmacological activity, used in Ayurveda and East Asian medicine long before their chemistry was known. India is now roughly the fourth-largest producer globally, output having risen from about 1 lakh tonnes a decade ago to approximately 3.5 lakh tonnes, with white button mushroom accounting for the dominant share (ICAR-Directorate of Mushroom Research, Solan, 2024).

- **Bioactive compound** — Representative species · Therapeutic action
- **Beta-glucans (polysaccharides)** — Lentinula edodes, Pleurotus spp. · Immunomodulation - bind Dectin-1 and CR3 receptors on macrophages
- **Triterpenoids (ganoderic acids)** — Ganoderma lucidum (Reishi) · Anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective, antioxidant
- **Cordycepin** — Cordyceps militaris · Antioxidant, anti-tumour activity in preclinical models
- **Lovastatin** — Pleurotus ostreatus · Cholesterol-lowering (HMG-CoA reductase inhibition)
- **Ergothioneine, ergosterol** — Agaricus bisporus · Antioxidant; UV exposure converts ergosterol to Vitamin D2
- **Lectins, antimicrobial peptides** — Volvariella, Calocybe spp. · Antibacterial and antifungal activity

Why the immunological effect matters. Beta-glucans act as biological response modifiers: rather than killing a pathogen directly, they prime innate immune cells so the host responds faster. This is the mechanistic reason mushroom polysaccharides are studied as adjuncts to chemotherapy - to reduce treatment-associated immunosuppression rather than to replace the cytotoxic agent.

Nutritional-therapeutic value. Mushrooms are high in protein and dietary fibre, low in fat, cholesterol-free, and among the few non-animal dietary sources of Vitamin D2 and selenium. Their low glycaemic index makes them useful in diabetic diets - relevant where India’s diabetes prevalence stands at 11.4% (ICMR-INDIAB, 2023).

The necessary caveat. Most anticancer and antiviral claims rest on in vitro and animal studies; large randomised human trials are few, and extract standardisation is weak, so potency varies batch to batch. In India, mushroom preparations are regulated as nutraceuticals and health supplements under the FSSAI regulations, which permit nutritional claims but not disease-treatment claims. An exam answer that omits this reads as uncritical.

Livelihood dimension and AP linkage. Mushroom cultivation converts agricultural waste into protein, needs little land or water, and yields within weeks - ideal for small, marginal and landless households, with support available under the Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH). Coastal Andhra’s paddy belt in the Krishna-Godavari delta supplies abundant straw substrate for paddy straw mushroom (Volvariella volvacea), traditionally grown under coconut and mango shade. Dr. YSR Horticultural University, Venkataramannagudem runs mushroom cultivation as a formal skill module through its KVKs - including the tribal KVK at Pandirimamidi - and a tribal woman farmer trained under this programme received ICAR’s Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Antyodaya Krishi Puraskar (Dr. YSRHU, 2021).

## Conclusion

Mushrooms occupy an unusual position - simultaneously a food, a nutraceutical and a candidate pharmacological source. Their beta-glucans and triterpenoids give a genuine immunomodulatory and metabolic rationale, and their cultivation economics make them a rare crop that suits the landless. Realising the medicinal promise, however, requires standardised extracts and clinical validation; realising the livelihood promise requires cold chain and market linkage, which is where AP’s horticultural extension system can decisively intervene.

- ICAR-Directorate of Mushroom Research, Solan - the country’s only dedicated mushroom research institute; Solan was designated “Mushroom City of India” in 1997; it coordinates the All India Coordinated Research Project on Mushroom (launched 1984) across coordinating and cooperating centres in 27 states.
- ICAR-DMR has standardised 42 mushroom-based value-added products - powders, capsules, snacks, beverages.
- Species grown commercially in India: white button (temperate/controlled houses), oyster, paddy straw, milky mushroom (tropical and sub-tropical).
- Growing conditions for white button mushroom: 24 +/- 2 deg C for spawn run, 16-18 deg C for fruiting, 80-90% relative humidity with ventilation.
- High-value species:Cordyceps commands prices upward of Rs. 1 lakh per kg; Morchella (gucchi) is wild-collected in the Himalaya.
- Circular economy angle: mushrooms valorise paddy straw - directly relevant to stubble-burning mitigation and to Mission LiFE’s sustainable consumption pillar.
- SDG linkage: SDG 2 (zero hunger, nutrition), SDG 3 (health), SDG 12 (responsible consumption).

263. Give an account on chemicals and drugs produced from animals. (APPSC, 2017)

Animal tissues, glands, blood and secretions have supplied medicine with hormones, enzymes, anticoagulants, antisera and vaccine substrates for over a century. Many remain irreplaceable - polyvalent antivenom still cannot be made without hyperimmunised horses - even as biotechnology progressively substitutes recombinant equivalents for the rest.

- **Category** — Product · Animal source · Therapeutic use
- **Hormones** — Insulin (historical), Thyroxine, Adrenaline, Cortisone · Porcine/bovine pancreas, thyroid, adrenal glands · Diabetes, hypothyroidism, anaphylaxis, inflammation
- **Enzymes** — Trypsin, Pepsin, Hyaluronidase · Pancreas, gastric mucosa, bovine testes · Digestive aids; dispersion of injected drugs
- **Anticoagulant** — Heparin · Porcine intestinal mucosa, bovine lung · Thrombosis prophylaxis, dialysis, surgery
- **Antisera** — Polyvalent anti-snake venom, anti-rabies and anti-tetanus serum · Hyperimmunised horse plasma · Passive immunisation - immediate protection
- **Excipients** — Gelatin · Bone and hide collagen · Capsule shells, vaccine stabiliser
- **Others** — Chitosan, cod liver oil, bile salts, conjugated oestrogens · Crustacean shell, fish liver, ox bile, equine urine · Wound dressing, nutrition, digestion, hormone therapy

Case 1 - Anti-snake venom. Venom is milked, injected in graded sub-lethal doses into horses, and the resulting hyperimmune plasma is fractionated into immunoglobulin. India’s polyvalent ASV is raised against the “Big Four” - cobra, Russell’s viper, common krait and saw-scaled viper - and is effective in roughly 80% of envenomation cases. The residual 20% reflects species and regional venom variation, which is precisely the gap the National Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Snakebite Envenoming (NAPSE), launched by MoHFW in March 2024, addresses through a One Health approach: strengthening Regional Venom Centres, ASV quality and distribution, and district-level training, with the target of halving snakebite deaths by 2030.

Case 2 - Heparin. Still extracted from porcine intestinal mucosa because its complex sulphated polysaccharide structure resists economical synthesis. This makes global supply hostage to pig-farming cycles and to contamination events - the rationale for pharmacopoeial tightening and for low-molecular-weight and synthetic alternatives.

Limitations. - Zoonotic and prion risk - bovine-derived materials carry theoretical BSE transmission risk, which is why sourcing is geographically restricted and certified. - Immunogenicity - equine sera can provoke anaphylaxis or delayed serum sickness, requiring pre-medication and monitored administration. - Batch variability and supply constraint -biological sources cannot be scaled on demand, and potency varies between lots. - Ethical and regulatory limits - animal use is governed by the CPCSEA under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, with Institutional Animal Ethics Committee clearance mandatory.

The recombinant transition, with AP linkage. Human insulin, the yeast-derived Hepatitis B vaccine and recombinant clotting factors have already displaced their animal-derived predecessors, and monoclonal antibody antivenoms are in research. Biopharma SHAKTI (Union Budget 2026-27, Rs. 10,000 crore over five years) explicitly supports the shift toward human-relevant testing systems and away from animal models. Andhra Pradesh sits directly on this transition: the AP Bulk Drug Park at Nakkapalli (Anakapalli district) and Jawaharlal Nehru Pharma City, Parawada provide the fermentation and API base for recombinant substitutes, while Sri Venkateswara Veterinary University, Tirupati anchors veterinary biologicals research in the state.

## Conclusion

Animal-derived chemicals built the foundations of modern pharmacology and, in antivenom and heparin, still hold positions no synthetic route has matched. But the direction of travel is unmistakable: recombinant expression offers greater purity, consistent potency, freedom from zoonotic risk and ethical defensibility. India’s policy architecture - CPCSEA on one side, Biopharma SHAKTI on the other - is now aligned to accelerate that substitution while safeguarding the products that cannot yet be replaced.

Venom-derived drugs (a high-yield list for any biotechnology question):

- Captopril - Brazilian pit viper venom; antihypertensive (ACE inhibitor).
- Exenatide - Gila monster saliva; type-2 diabetes.
- Ziconotide - cone snail venom; severe chronic pain.
- Eptifibatide - pygmy rattlesnake venom; antiplatelet in acute coronary syndrome.
- Batroxobin - South American pit viper; defibrinogenating agent.
- Tozuleristide - scorpion venom-derived; intraoperative brain tumour imaging.

Institutional and policy map:

- CPCSEA (Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals) - statutory oversight of animal experimentation.
- NAPSE, 2024 - MoHFW; One Health approach; halve snakebite deaths by 2030; ASV listed as an essential drug procured under NHM.
- Central Research Institute, Kasauli and Haffkine Institute - historic public-sector sera and vaccine producers.
- SDG linkage: SDG 3.3 (neglected tropical diseases, including snakebite envenoming) and SDG 3.8.

264. Elucidate a low volume high value product giving the example of insulin. Mention the role of Indian companies for its production. (APPSC, 2011)

Low-Volume High-Value (LVHV) bioproducts are manufactured in small physical quantities yet command disproportionate economic value because of their technological complexity, R&D intensity and regulatory burden. Insulin is the classic case: a few kilograms of purified protein serve millions of patients. The demand base is enormous - the ICMR-INDIAB study (2023) estimates 10.1 crore Indians with diabetes, a prevalence of 11.4%, with a further 15.3% prediabetic.

- **Parameter** — LVHV (insulin, interferons, mAbs) · HVLV (paracetamol, urea, bulk APIs)
- **Output volume** — Kilograms per year · Thousands of tonnes
- **Value per unit mass** — Very high · Low
- **Process** — Fermentation, chromatography, cold chain · Chemical synthesis
- **Entry barrier** — Very high (IP, know-how, capex) · Moderate

Why insulin is LVHV - four factors. 1. Biomanufacturing complexity: it is a folded protein, not a small molecule. Recombinant E. coli or Pichia pastoris fermentation, inclusion-body recovery, refolding and multi-step chromatography cannot be reverse-engineered from a chemical formula. 2. Regulatory intensity: every batch is validated against CDSCO/DCGI norms, and export requires USFDA or EMA clearance under biosimilar comparability guidelines - a cost that only high unit value can absorb. 3. Cold-chain dependence: the product must move at 2-8 deg C from fermenter to patient, embedding logistics cost in every vial. 4. Chronic, non-substitutable demand: a type-1 diabetic needs insulin for life, giving predictable volumes but no price elasticity - the structural reason it stays under NLEM price control.

Production schematic (draw as a linear chain):Human insulin gene -> cloned into plasmid -> transformed into E. coli /

yeast -> fermentation -> cell lysis and inclusion body recovery -> refolding -> enzymatic cleavage of C-peptide -> chromatographic

purification -> crystallisation -> formulation and fill-finish -> cold chain

Role of Indian companies.Biocon Biologics (Bengaluru) is the anchor firm - the first Indian company to obtain approval in both the US and EU for an insulin glargine biosimilar, and a supplier to over 100 countries, giving India presence in a segment historically dominated by three multinationals. Wockhardt manufactures the full recombinant insulin range and filed for Insulin Aspart in 2024. Zydus Lifesciences, Lupin and Panacea Biotec operate in analogues and licensing partnerships across Africa and Latin America. The strategic significance is affordability: Indian biosimilar entry has been the principal mechanism by which insulin analogue prices fell in low- and middle-income markets.

Policy architecture. The National Biopharma Mission - Innovate in India (i3) (DBT, implemented by BIRAC, USD 250 million with 50% World Bank co-funding) built shared GCLP, GLP and cGMP facilities that MSMEs could not have financed alone. The BioE3 Policy, 2024 added biofoundries and biomanufacturing hubs. Most decisively, Biopharma SHAKTI, announced in the Union Budget 2026-27 with Rs. 10,000 crore over five years, targets 5% of the global biopharmaceutical market, a network of over 1,000 accredited clinical trial sites, and three new NIPERs (PIB, February 2026).

AP linkage. Andhra Pradesh is positioned to capture part of this. The AP Bulk Drug Park at Nakkapalli, Anakapalli district is one of only three parks approved nationally under the Department of Pharmaceuticals’ Rs. 3,000 crore scheme (PIB, 2022), planned as an integrated pharma zone within the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor. Together with Jawaharlal Nehru Pharma City, Parawada, it gives the state fermentation, API and utilities infrastructure on which biologics capacity can be layered.

Constraints. Dependence on imported cell lines, culture media and single-use bioprocess consumables inflates cost; biosimilar approval timelines remain long; and cold-chain reliability in rural districts limits last-mile access even where the product is affordable.

## Conclusion

Insulin demonstrates that in biotechnology, value is decoupled from volume - complexity, regulation and irreplaceability, not tonnage, determine worth. India has moved from importing insulin to exporting biosimilars to over a hundred countries, and Biopharma SHAKTI signals the next transition, from generic manufacturing to biologics innovation. For Andhra Pradesh, the Nakkapalli park converts a national policy opportunity into a state industrial one, provided skilled bioprocess manpower and indigenous input supply chains keep pace.

- Biopharma SHAKTI - Strategy for Healthcare Advancement through Knowledge, Technology and Innovation; Rs. 10,000 crore over five years from FY 2026-27; objectives: advanced biomanufacturing infrastructure, 1,000+ accredited clinical trial sites, three new NIPERs and upgrading seven existing ones, and a skilled bioprocess workforce.

- Other LVHV bioproducts: interferons, monoclonal antibodies, erythropoietin, human growth hormone, clotting factors, therapeutic enzymes.
- Affordability instrument: insulin is listed under the National List of Essential Medicines, bringing it under DPCO price control.

## Introduction

Bio-pesticides are pest-control agents derived from living organisms or natural products — bacteria, fungi, viruses, plant extracts and pheromones — regulated in India under the Insecticides Act, 1968 and registered by the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC). The question concedes their agronomic weaknesses, and they are real. The case for shifting to them is therefore not that they act faster, but that speed is the wrong metric: chemical pesticides deliver quick kill while transferring their true costs to human health, ecosystems, export earnings and the next season’s pest pressure. Bio-pesticides internalise those costs.

Comparison — reproduce this compact table:

Aspect Bio-pesticides Conventional pesticides

Origin Living organisms and natural products Synthetic chemicals

Speed of action Slow (3-7 days); acts by infection, repellence or growth disruption

Rapid knockdown

Persistence and residue Short-lived; negligible residue Persistent; measurable residues, some bioaccumulative

Specificity Narrow-spectrum; spares natural enemies and pollinators

Broad-spectrum; kills non-target and beneficial organisms

Resistance risk Low — multiple modes of action High — single-target-site selection pressure

Cost profile Higher per unit initially; falls with on-farm production

Cheap upfront; externalised health and ecological costs

Why the shift is nonetheless necessary:

1. The chemical treadmill — resistance and resurgence. Single-target-site chemicals impose intense selection pressure, so resistance evolves rapidly; the collapse of pink bollworm control in Bt cotton and repeated brown planthopper resurgence in paddy are Indian illustrations. Broad-spectrum sprays also destroy natural enemies such as Trichogramma and coccinellid predators, releasing secondary pests from control. A fast pesticide that stops working in five seasons is slower, in effect, than a bio-pesticide that keeps working. 2. Human health externalities. Farm-worker poisoning during application is a recurring public-health event in India, and residues in food are a chronic exposure pathway. The Government’s ongoing review of hazardous molecules and the re-issued draft Pesticide Management Bill (Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, January 2026) reflect recognition that the 1968 Act’s framework predates modern toxicological knowledge. 3. Export competitiveness — the strongest commercial argument. Maximum Residue Limits set by the EU, Japan and Codex now determine market access for Indian chilli, grapes, basmati, tea and shrimp. Consignment rejections on residue grounds cost far more than the pesticide saved. This is directly an Andhra Pradesh issue: AP is India’s largest chilli producer, and the Guntur chilli and coastal aquaculture economies both live or die by residue compliance. Bio-pesticides leave negligible residue and are therefore an export-enabling technology, not merely an ecological preference. 4. Soil biology and ecosystem services. Repeated broad-spectrum application suppresses soil microflora, earthworms and mycorrhizae, degrading the nutrient-cycling capacity that determines long-run yield, and harms pollinators on which a significant share of horticultural output depends. Bio-pesticides preserve this natural capital. 5. Policy pull is now substantial. The National Mission on Natural Farming, approved in November 2024 with an outlay of Rs. 2,481 crore (Centre Rs. 1,584 crore, States Rs. 897 crore), targets 1 crore farmers, 15,000 clusters and 7.5 lakh hectares, with 10,000 Bio-Input Resource Centres and an incentive of Rs. 4,000 per acre per year for two years (PIB, November 2024). By July 2025, over 10 lakh farmers had enrolled and 1,100 model farms were established (Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, PIB). PKVY and MOVCDNER supply the organic-certification route. 6. Andhra Pradesh — the world’s largest live demonstration.Andhra Pradesh Community-Managed Natural Farming (APCNF), run by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha under the State Department of Agriculture since 2015-16, has reached 8,168 gram panchayats, over 1.77 million farmers and about 0.92 million hectares, with reported gains of 38-66 per cent in farmer incomes, up to 50 per cent water savings and up to 46 per cent lower greenhouse gas emissions per acre (Government of Andhra Pradesh, 2026). It is the largest agroecology transition anywhere, and it works precisely because bio-inputs are produced locally by women’s self-help groups, removing the cost and shelf-life problems that hold bio-pesticides back elsewhere. 7. The weaknesses are manageable — and this is the marks-winning paragraph. Slow action is addressed by using bio-pesticides prophylactically and at low pest density rather than as rescue treatments; UV sensitivity by evening application and UV-protectant, oil-based or encapsulated formulations; short shelf life by decentralised, just-in-time production at Bio-Input Resource Centres; and variable efficacy by quality control under CIB&RC registration. Nano-formulations — such as the ICAR nano-formulation from Myrothecium verrucaria for powdery mildew in tomato and grape — are closing the efficacy gap directly. Infographic suggestion — a cause-effect loop diagram:Chemical treadmill: heavy spray --> natural enemies killed + resistance --> pest resurgence --> heavier spray against Biological loop: bio-input + natural enemies conserved --> pest suppressed below threshold --> lower cost, no residue

## Conclusion

The trade-off in the question is real but wrongly framed: chemical pesticides are fast only in the season of application and expensive across the decade, once resistance, health damage, soil degradation and export rejections are counted. Bio-pesticides are best deployed not as one-to-one substitutes but as the core of Integrated Pest Management, with need-based chemical use retained as a last resort. Given the residue-driven realities of India’s agri-export basket and the scale already demonstrated by APCNF, the shift is now an economic and trade imperative as much as an ecological one — and directly serves SDG 2.4 and SDG 12.4.

## Value addition
- Four regulatory categories of bio-pesticides:microbial (Bacillus thuringiensis, Trichoderma, NPV, Beauveria); biochemical (azadirachtin from neem, pheromones, plant growth regulators); plant-incorporated protectants (Bt cotton’s Cry proteins); macrobials / natural enemies (Trichogramma, Chrysoperla, predatory mites).
- Analytical point on Indian pesticide use: India’s average per-hectare pesticide consumption is well below the global average, but this national average is misleading — use is concentrated in cotton, paddy, chilli and vegetables, and in a handful of States, so local intensity and residue risk are far higher than the aggregate suggests. Making that distinction shows examination-level judgement.
- Kisan-Kavach: India’s first anti-pesticide protective bodysuit, developed with DBT support, addressing applicator exposure — a useful example that pesticide harm is an occupational-safety issue, not only a residue issue.
- Institutional map: CIB&RC and the Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage (Faridabad) for registration and IPM; ICAR-NBAIR, Bengaluru as the national bureau for agricultural insect resources and biocontrol agents; State biocontrol laboratories for mass multiplication; Krishi Vigyan Kendras and Farmer Field Schools for extension.
- International anchors: Codex Alimentarius MRLs govern trade; the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants and the Rotterdam Convention (prior informed consent for hazardous chemicals) frame global phase-out; SDG 12.4 targets sound chemical management and SDG 2.4 sustainable food production systems.
- Scheme shortlist for any bio-input question: National Mission on Natural Farming (2024), Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana, MOVCDNER, Soil Health Card, and the Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation for precision application.

India’s innovation standing has improved steadily - its Global Innovation Index rank rose from 66th in 2019 to 38th in 2025 (Economic Survey 2025-26), and domestic patent filings nearly tripled from 24,326 in 2020-21 to 68,176 in 2024-25 (PIB, November 2025). Yet the absolute number of patents granted remains a fraction of China’s or America’s. The paradox is explained not by inventiveness but by the size of the research base that feeds the patent pipeline and by the institutional capacity that processes it.

1. The input problem is decisive. Patents are an output of R&D spending, and India spends 0.6-0.7% of GDP on R&D against roughly 2% or more in China and over 3% in the US. Crucially, India’s private sector funds only about 36% of GERD, whereas in China, Korea and the US the private share exceeds 70% (PIB, February 2026). Since corporate R&D is the single largest source of patent filings worldwide, a small private research base mechanically produces a small patent base.

2. Examination capacity was historically the bottleneck. A patent application must be examined before it can be granted; India’s patent office had a sanctioned strength of just 431 in 2014, expanded 233% to 1,433 by 2024 (PIB, 2025). The consequence was a large pendency backlog whose clearance produced the dramatic single-year jumps in grants - which is why quoting a “149.4% increase in grants” without the absolute base overstates the position.

3. Legal filters deliberately restrict grants.Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970 bars patents on new forms of known substances lacking enhanced efficacy - upheld by the Supreme Court in Novartis v. Union of India (2013) on the Glivec application. This is a conscious public-health choice protecting India’s generic industry, and it legitimately lowers the grant count relative to jurisdictions with permissive incremental patenting.

4. Patent culture and weak industry-academia linkage. Indian academic incentives reward publication, not disclosure; many inventions are published before filing, destroying novelty. Simultaneously, weak linkage means fewer inventions are industry-relevant, so applicants abandon prosecution or lapse on renewal fees. Only about 13,000 of India’s 2 lakh-plus DPIIT-recognised startups work in deep-tech areas such as AI, IoT and robotics (Economic Survey; PIB), narrowing the patentable pool.

5. Andhra Pradesh’s corrective attempt. State-level capacity gaps mirror the national ones. AP’s response - the AP Innovation Society-NRDC Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre and the WIPO-supported TISC at Sunrise Incubation Hub, Visakhapatnam - targets exactly the missing step: helping MSMEs and university researchers conduct prior-art searches and draft specifications before publishing.

## Conclusion

India’s rising GII rank measures innovation potential; patent grants measure converted, protected and prosecuted innovation - and the gap between the two is a funding and institutional gap, not a talent gap. The correction is already visible in the near-tripling of filings since 2020-21 and the 233% expansion of examiner strength. The Rs. 1 lakh crore RDI Scheme (November 2025), aimed squarely at raising private R&D, addresses the root cause. Until private research spending approaches global norms, however, India’s patent grants will continue to trail China and the US regardless of how high its innovation ranking climbs.

## Value addition
- Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024: introduced a Certificate of Inventorship, reduced the deadline for filing Request for Examination, simplified working-statement requirements (Form 27, now triennial) and eased pre-grant opposition -framed under Section 159 of the Patents Act, 1970 (PIB, March 2024).
- Comparative anchors: India ranked 6th globally in patent applications and features in the global top 10 for patents, trademarks and industrial designs (WIPO, World Intellectual Property Indicators 2024, via PIB).
- Overall IP filings: rose 44% from 4,77,533 in 2020-21 to 6,89,991 in 2024-25; sector growth led by GI (+380%), Designs (+266%) and Patents (+180%) (PIB, July 2025).
- Reform levers to cite: examiner recruitment and AI-assisted prior-art search * mandatory TTOs in funded institutions * a Bayh-Dole style ownership statute * patent-box style tax treatment of licensing income * strengthened IP valuation profession.
- Terminology: pendency * pre-grant and post-grant opposition * evergreening * working of patents * patent-to-GDP ratio * deep-tech.
- SDG linkage: SDG-9.5 (R&D spending and researchers per million population) - India’s researcher density remains well below the OECD average.

## Introduction

Commercialisation converts a legal right into revenue. India now generates IP at scale - total IP filings rose 44% from 4,77,533 in 2020-21 to 6,89,991 in 2024-25 (PIB, July 2025) - but a large share of granted rights are never licensed, valued or renewed. Closing this “valley of death” between grant and market requires a defined toolkit, which the Cell for IPR Promotion and Management (CIPAM) under DPIIT was created to assemble as the single point of reference for the National IPR Policy, 2016.

## Reproducible Infographic - The IP Commercialisation Chain (draw as a left-to-right pipeline)

## Stage Tool Required Institution / Scheme

1. Identification and audit. Firms cannot commercialise what they have not catalogued. IP audits and freedom-to-operate opinions determine whether a product can be launched without infringing others’ rights - the step at which most MSMEs fail. Technology and Innovation Support Centres (TISCs), set up with WIPO and DPIIT, provide free access to patent and non-patent literature for exactly this purpose.

2. Valuation and financing - India’s binding constraint. Banks lend against factories, not patents, because India lacks accepted IP valuation standards and a liquid secondary market for rights. Consequently, IP-backed lending is negligible. The Rs. 1 lakh crore RDI Scheme (launched 3 November 2025), providing long-tenor, low-interest and largely unsecured financing with TDB and BIRAC as Second-Level Fund Managers, is the first serious attempt to price innovation risk rather than collateral (PIB, 2025-26).

3. Technology transfer machinery. The NRDC licenses publicly funded inventions to industry; institutional TTOs in IITs, CSIR laboratories and agricultural universities negotiate royalties and milestone payments. Without professional TTOs, faculty inventors negotiate alone and typically undervalue their rights.

4. Procedural simplification - CIPAM’s clearest contribution. CIPAM coordinated e-filing, expedited examination for startups and small entities, and reduced timelines; the Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024 further compressed the Request-for-Examination window and introduced a Certificate of Inventorship. Startup-specific support flows through the Scheme for Facilitating Start-ups Intellectual Property Protection (SIPP, 2016), under which the government bears the professional fees of empanelled IP facilitators, now extended to educational institutions using TISC services (PIB, 2025).

5. Awareness and GI market linkage. Awareness is delivered principally through the National Intellectual Property Awareness Mission (NIPAM), launched in December 2021 and implemented by CGPDTM, which has run about 9,500 programmes across all 28 states and 8 UTs, reaching over 25 lakh students and faculty (PIB, July 2025). CIPAM’s distinct contribution lies in GI branding and market linkage - exhibitions, e-marketing and authorised-user enrolment, which lifted authorised GI users from 365 to about 29,000 in a decade (PIB, January 2025). In Andhra Pradesh this directly benefits Etikoppaka lacquer toys (GI 2017), Kondapalli Bommalu (GI 2006), Araku Valley Arabica coffee, Bandar Laddu and Dharmavaram sarees, where GST on toys was also cut from 12% to 5% to widen the market (PIB, September 2025).

## Conclusion

The tools of IP commercialisation form a chain, and a chain fails at its weakest link - in India, valuation and IP-backed finance, not awareness or filing. CIPAM has demonstrably strengthened the earlier links: simpler procedures, startup facilitation and, most visibly, GI branding that has converted community heritage into market income for artisans in Anakapalli and Araku. The next step is institutional rather than promotional: accepted valuation standards, mandatory TTOs in publicly funded institutions, and an ownership statute for public-funded IP, so that RDI Scheme capital finances licensed technologies rather than dormant certificates.

## Introduction

Global agriculture today produces enough dietary energy for every person on earth, yet the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 (FAO-IFAD-UNICEF-WFP-WHO, July 2026) estimates that about 645 million people faced hunger in 2025 (7.8% of humanity), while roughly 2.7 billion could not afford a healthy diet. This divergence between abundance and deprivation is the empirical core of the statement. It echoes Amartya Sen’s entitlement insight that famines occur not because food is absent but because people lose the ability to command it. The proposition is therefore diagnostically sound — but its therapeutic conclusion, that GM crops are a “bad answer,” overstates the case.

PRODUCTION  --> yield gap, degraded soil, unreliable irrigation         |     HARVEST    --> threshing/handling losses         |    STORAGE     --> pest damage, absent cold chain         |    TRANSPORT   --> spoilage, market fragmentation         |    MARKET/PDS  --> exclusion errors, leakage         |    HOUSEHOLD   --> intra-household inequity, affordability         |    ABSORPTION  --> sanitation, disease, hidden hunger         |    NUTRITION SECURED    [GM/GE crops act ONLY at the first and last stages]

1. Farming inefficiency is a real and binding constraint. Low yields in developing agriculture stem from degraded soils, unreliable irrigation, poor seed replacement rates and fragmented holdings rather than from any genetic ceiling. India’s policy response has been to attack precisely these variables: the Soil Health Card Scheme for nutrient-specific fertiliser use, Per Drop More Crop under PMKSY for micro-irrigation, and the Pradhan Mantri Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana announced in the Union Budget 2025-26, which targets 100 low-productivity agricultural districts and is expected to benefit about 1.7 crore farmers through productivity, diversification and post-harvest support. That the state chooses these instruments over seed technology is itself evidence for the first half of the statement. 2. Distribution and post-harvest loss are where food actually disappears. A study conducted by NABARD Consultancy Services (NABCONS) for the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, covering 2020-22, valued India’s annual harvest and post-harvest losses at approximately Rs. 1,52,790 crore. Globally, the UNEP Food Waste Index Report 2024 recorded about 1.05 billion tonnes of food wasted in 2022. Losses of this magnitude cannot be engineered away in the seed; they are a cold-chain, road, market and governance problem — which is why India’s answer has been the Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana for cold chain and processing infrastructure, and eNAM for market integration. 3. Access is an entitlement question, settled by law and not by biology. The National Food Security Act, 2013 extends subsidised grain to about 81.35 crore persons, and free foodgrain distribution under PMGKAY was extended for five years from 1 January 2024. India simultaneously holds buffer stocks well above norms and hosts a large undernourished population — the clearest possible demonstration that production is not the operative bottleneck. 4. Where the statement overreaches — GM and GE crops solve problems redistribution cannot. Pest pressure, salinity, drought and micronutrient deficiency are biological constraints, not logistical ones. Bt cotton (GEAC-approved, 2002) remains India’s only commercially cultivated GM crop and now covers over 90% of cotton area. More decisively, in May 2025 ICAR released the world’s first genome-edited rice varieties — DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) from ICAR-IIRR Hyderabad and Pusa DST Rice 1 from ICAR-IARI — delivering, per ICAR, a 19% yield gain, about 20% lower greenhouse gas emissions and an estimated saving of 7,500 million cubic metres of irrigation water. Biofortification similarly targets “hidden hunger,” which a perfectly efficient PDS distributing nutrient-poor grain would leave untouched.

Andhra Pradesh anchor: Both genome-edited rice varieties are built on Andhra Pradesh genetics — Kamala is derived from Samba Mahsuri (BPT 5204), bred at the ANGRAU station at Bapatla, and Pusa DST Rice 1 from Cotton Dora Sannalu (MTU 1010), bred at the ANGRAU Regional Agricultural Research Station, Maruteru, West Godavari (ICAR, May 2025). Both are recommended for Zone VII, which includes Andhra Pradesh. AP thus supplies the germplasm base for India’s precision-breeding frontier while simultaneously suffering the distribution problem — its horticulture-heavy cropping pattern in Kuppam, Chittoor and the Godavari delta makes it acutely vulnerable to cold-chain gaps.

## The statement is RIGHT that… The statement is WRONG that…

Hungercoexistswithsurplusstocks GMaddresses“thewrongproblem”

Hunger coexists with surplus stocks GM addresses the wrong problem

Losses are logistical (Rs. 1.52 lakh cr, NABCONS) Pest/salinity/micronutrient gaps are biological

PDS reform yields faster gains Genome editing cuts water and emissions too

Technology alone cannot buy purchasing power Nutrition security needs biofortified seed

## Conclusion

The proposition is half-right and therefore half-misleading. It correctly identifies that the world’s food shortage is a shortage of entitlement, infrastructure and governance rather than of calories — and to that extent GM crops are indeed an inadequate answer if offered as the answer. But framing seed technology and system reform as rival prescriptions is a false binary. India’s own trajectory — a genome-edited rice programme running alongside NFSA, PMGKAY and PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana — demonstrates that precision breeding is best understood as a complement to distributive justice, not a substitute for it. The real error would be to invest in either alone.

## Value addition
- Conceptual anchor: Amartya Sen’s Poverty and Famines (1981) — famines arise from collapse of exchange entitlements, not food availability decline. This is the single highest-value framing for any food-security answer.
- SDG linkage:SDG 2 (Zero Hunger, Targets 2.1 and 2.2) and SDG Target 12.3, which seeks to halve per-capita food waste and reduce post-harvest losses by 2030. SOFI 2025 projected that on current trends about 512 million people could still face hunger in 2030, nearly 60% of them in Africa.
- Hidden hunger: ICAR has released a large portfolio of biofortified varieties (iron-rich pearl millet, zinc-rich wheat and rice, quality protein maize); the Poshan Abhiyaan and fortified-rice distribution through PDS attack the same deficit from the consumption side.
