## Introduction

Weather monitoring and forecasting convert an unavoidable hazard into a manageable risk. Their value is demonstrable rather than theoretical: India’s cyclone mortality has fallen from around 10,000 deaths in the 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone to double or single digits in comparably severe recent cyclones — achieved almost entirely through better forecasting, communication and evacuation rather than through any change in the hazard itself. ISRO’s satellite infrastructure underpins this capability, and the NISAR mission, launched in July 2025, substantially extends it.

SMS, sirens) --> ACT (evacuation) , noting that the chain is only as strong as its weakest link — usually the last.

## Why monitoring and forecasting are crucial
- Lives saved through lead time. Evacuation requires warning hours to days in advance. Cyclone Fani (2019) saw over a million people evacuated in Odisha; Cyclone Biparjoy (June 2023) saw around a lakh evacuated in Gujarat, with minimal loss of life. Lead time is the entire mechanism.
- Agriculture. India’s monsoon-dependent agriculture requires seasonal and short-range forecasts for sowing, irrigation, spraying and harvest decisions — delivered through the Gramin Krishi Mausam Sewa and Meghdoot app.
- Economic protection. Aviation, shipping, fisheries, power scheduling (increasingly critical with variable renewables), and construction all depend on forecasts.
- Water and disaster resource management. Reservoir operation, flood forecasting and drought declaration all rest on meteorological and hydrological data.
- Climate adaptation. Long-term monitoring establishes the baselines against which change is detected and adaptation planned.

## ISRO’s role — and how it differs from IMD’s

A distinction worth stating: ISRO builds and operates the observation platforms; IMD (Ministry of Earth Sciences) runs the forecasting models and issues warnings. ISRO supplies the eyes; IMD supplies the judgement.

- Meteorological satellites.INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR carry a six-channel Imager and a nineteen-channel Sounder, providing vertical profiles of temperature and humidity and imagery at intervals as short as 15 minutes during cyclone watch. INSAT-3DS, launched in February 2024, continues the series. During Cyclone Amphan (2020), rapid-scan imagery enabled continuous tracking that underpinned evacuation of over three million people across West Bengal and Odisha.
- Ocean and atmospheric observation.Oceansat/EOS-06 for ocean colour and winds; SCATSAT-1 for wind vectors, directly used in cyclone intensity estimation; Megha-Tropiques (with CNES) for tropical water cycle studies.
- Data platforms.MOSDAC (Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre, SAC Ahmedabad) disseminates weather and ocean products; Bhuvan (NRSC) hosts disaster applications; Bhoonidhi provides satellite data access.
- Disaster Management Support (DMS) Programme. ISRO’s dedicated programme provides near-real-time support for floods, cyclones, drought,

landslides, forest fires and earthquakes — including flood inundation mapping using radar (which sees through cloud), damage assessment, and hazard-vulnerability-risk mapping for NDMA and State authorities. The National Database for Emergency Management (NDEM) is the geospatial backbone.

- Forest fire alerts. The Forest Survey of India’s near-real-time alert system uses satellite detections to push SMS alerts to field staff — an example of observation converted directly into field action.
- Landslide and deformation monitoring. Cartosat and RISAT imagery mapped ground deformation at Joshimath (2023), supporting evacuation and building-safety decisions.
- Navigation and communication in disasters.NavIC messaging delivers cyclone alerts to fishermen beyond mobile coverage — directly relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s 1,053-km coastline; INSAT-based Disaster Warning System receivers serve coastal villages.

## Note on Mission NISAR
- What it is. The NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar satellite, launched on 30 July 2025 aboard GSLV-F16 from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota — the first joint ISRO-NASA Earth observation mission and the world’s first satellite carrying dual-frequency SAR: NASA’s L-band and ISRO’s S-band, on a shared 12-metre unfurlable mesh reflector antenna. Mass about 2,392 kg, in a sun-synchronous orbit near 747 km.
- Why radar matters for India specifically. Optical satellites cannot see through cloud — and India’s floods and cyclones occur precisely when cloud cover is total. SAR images day or night, through cloud and rain, which makes it the only observation type usable during the event rather than only before and after.
- Capability. Complete global coverage every 12 days, and detection of surface deformation of less than one centimetre.
- Applications: flood inundation mapping during monsoon and cyclone events; earthquake and landslide deformation; subsidence monitoring in cities and mining regions; infrastructure integrity monitoring for dams, bridges and embankments; soil moisture and crop growth through the kharif season; glacier dynamics and biomass estimation.
- Its disaster management significance: NISAR shifts India from post-event assessment toward during-event observation and pre-event deformation detection — identifying slope movement or ground subsidence before failure occurs.

## Remaining challenges

Integration of satellite, Doppler radar and ground-station data; forecast downscaling to village level; communicating probabilistic forecasts to the public without either alarm fatigue or false reassurance; and last-mile dissemination. Mission Mausam (2024), with an outlay of about Rs. 2,000 crore, addresses observation network density, computing capacity and forecast accuracy.

## Conclusion

Monitoring and forecasting have delivered India’s most measurable disaster management achievement — the near-elimination of mass cyclone mortality — and ISRO’s satellite infrastructure is the observational foundation of that achievement. NISAR extends it decisively by allowing observation during cloud-covered events and detection of ground movement before failure. The remaining constraint is no longer observation but the last mile: converting an accurate forecast into timely action by the household that must move.

## Introduction

Generative AI can now produce audio, images and video that a reasonable observer cannot distinguish from authentic recordings. India’s law now names this category: the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, notified on 10 February 2026 and effective from 20 February 2026, define “synthetically generated information” (SGI) as content that appears reasonably authentic but is artificially or algorithmically generated or altered. With over 970 million registered voters and among the world’s highest social-media usage, India is uniquely exposed to its misuse.

## Impact on privacy
- Synthetic media appropriates a person’s likeness and voice without consent, severing the link between identity and its representation. The harm is asymmetric: non-consensual sexual deepfakes overwhelmingly target women, and voice cloning enables impersonation fraud against elderly relatives.
- The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing, but a deepfake may be generated from publicly available images without any “data breach” in the conventional sense — which is precisely the gap the 2026 SGI framework was created to fill.

## Impact on democracy
- Fabricated speech attributed to candidates can circulate faster than any rebuttal, and the window before an election is too short for correction to matter. The 2024 general election saw documented circulation of manipulated audio and video involving political figures, prompting Election Commission advisories to parties on the use of synthetic content in campaigning.
- The deeper harm is the “liar’s dividend” — once the public knows convincing fakes exist, genuine evidence of wrongdoing can be dismissed as fabricated. Deepfakes corrode trust in authentic recordings as much as they create false ones.
- Micro-targeted synthetic content in multiple Indian languages can deliver different, mutually inconsistent messages to different communities, fragmenting the shared factual basis democratic debate requires.

## Impact on national security
- Information warfare: hostile actors can fabricate statements by military or political leadership to provoke unrest or market panic; in a crisis, minutes of confusion have strategic value.
- Communal escalation: synthetic video depicting fabricated incidents can trigger violence before verification is possible — the reason internet shutdowns remain a blunt but frequently used response.
- Fraud and social engineering: cloned voices of senior officials have been used in “digital arrest” and financial fraud schemes, which the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) tracks.
- Public health: synthetic content on vaccines and treatments propagates the “infodemic” the WHO named during COVID-19.

## Solutions
- Legal — the current framework. The IT Amendment Rules, 2026 require that SGI be clearly and prominently labelled (visual labels for visual content, audio disclosures for audio), that intermediaries embed permanent provenance metadata where feasible, that users be barred from stripping such labels, and that flagged unlawful content be removed within sharply reduced timelines. Compliance is tied to safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act, which gives platforms a real incentive. Existing provisions under the IT Act, the DPDP Act 2023 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita on impersonation and obscenity supplement this.
- Technical — provenance over detection. Detection tools degrade as generators improve, so the durable approach is content provenance: cryptographically signing authentic media at the point of capture so that the absence of provenance becomes the signal. Research support runs through IITs, IIITs, C-DAC and CERT-In.
- Platform accountability: significant social media intermediaries must deploy filtering technology, honour takedown timelines, maintain grievance officers, and enable traceability of first originators for specified offences under the 2021 Rules.
- Media and information literacy: Election Commission voter-awareness programmes, the Press Information Bureau Fact Check Unit, and school-level digital literacy — because in a country of India’s scale, verification cannot be centralised and citizens are the first filter.
- Institutional capacity: I4C and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal for redress; forensic capability in State police cyber cells, where the constraint is trained personnel rather than law.
- International cooperation: India hosted the India AI Impact Summit 2026 in New Delhi (16-21 February 2026), the first global AI summit in the Global South, which adopted the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact, endorsed by 92 countries and international organisations and structured around three Sutras — People, Planet and Progress. The New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments were signed by 13 leading model developers, placing obligations upstream on those who build the models rather than only on those who host the output.

## Conclusion

AI-manipulated media attacks the three foundations of a functioning polity simultaneously: the individual’s control over their own likeness, the citizen’s ability to know what a leader actually said, and the state’s monopoly on authoritative information in a crisis. India’s response has matured from advisories to a binding labelling-and-provenance regime under the 2026 Rules, backed by international commitments secured at the New Delhi Summit. The remaining challenge is enforcement at the speed at which synthetic content actually travels — and doing so without the takedown machinery becoming an instrument of legitimate-speech suppression.

## Value addition
- IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026: notified 10 February 2026, effective 20 February 2026; first legal definition of synthetically generated information; mandatory prominent labelling and provenance metadata; users prohibited from removing labels; sharply reduced takedown timelines; obligations weighted toward Significant Social Media Intermediaries (over 50 lakh users).
- India AI Impact Summit 2026: Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, 16-21 February 2026; first global AI summit hosted in the Global South; three Sutras — People, Planet, Progress; New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact endorsed by 92 countries and international organisations across seven pillars; New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments by 13 frontier model developers; expansion of sovereign compute beyond the 38,000+ GPUs already provisioned under the IndiaAI Mission.
- Earlier global milestones for context: the Bletchley Declaration (November 2023, UK AI Safety Summit) — the first international agreement on frontier AI safety, signed by 28 countries and the EU, including India; the Seoul and Paris summits followed.
- Institutional machinery in India: CERT-In (incident response); Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal; PIB Fact Check Unit; the IndiaAI Safe & Trusted AI pillar.
- Concepts worth naming:liar’s dividend; content provenance and the C2PA-style signing approach; GANs and diffusion models; cheapfakes (crudely edited, not AI-generated — often more widespread than true deepfakes).
- The balancing argument to include: overbroad takedown obligations and mandatory labelling raise concerns about compelled speech, prior restraint and over-removal of legitimate satire and commentary. A complete answer notes that the regulatory challenge is calibration, not merely stringency.

## Introduction

Coastal erosion is the wearing away and landward retreat of the shoreline through the removal of sediment by waves, currents, tides and wind. The essential concept is the sediment budget: a coast is stable when sediment supplied equals sediment removed; erosion is a budget deficit and accretion a surplus. India’s coastline of about 7,500 km is under sustained pressure, and the National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR), which conducts national shoreline change assessment, has recorded that roughly a third of the mapped Indian coastline is under erosion, with a comparable share accreting and the remainder stable.

## Factors causing coastal erosion

Natural factors - Wave action and energy — the primary driver. Hydraulic action, abrasion and attrition dislodge and transport sediment, with high-energy storm and monsoon waves doing disproportionate work. - Longshore drift — the along-shore movement of sediment driven by waves striking the coast obliquely. Where drift is interrupted, erosion occurs immediately downdrift — the mechanism behind most structure-induced erosion. - Tidal currents and their range, and rip currents removing sediment offshore. - Sea-level rise — thermal expansion and meltwater bringing wave energy further inland; India’s coast is experiencing rise at roughly 3 mm per year on average, with local variation. - Cyclones and storm surge — episodic events that can remove in hours what accumulates over years. - Geomorphology — soft unconsolidated sediment erodes readily; hard rock resists. - Land subsidence in deltas, from sediment compaction, increasing relative sea-level rise.

Human-induced factors - Dams and barrages upstream — the most consequential. They trap sediment that would otherwise reach the coast, starving the shoreline of its supply. Delta starvation is the result, and it operates hundreds of kilometres from the dam. - Ports, harbours, breakwaters and groynes interrupting longshore drift, causing accretion updrift and erosion downdrift — protection at one point transferring the problem to the next. -Sand mining from beaches, dunes and river mouths, removing sediment directly from the budget. - Destruction of mangroves, coral reefs and dunes, which dissipate wave energy naturally. A degraded mangrove belt is a removed defence. - Coastal construction within the active zone, and dredging of navigation channels. - Aquaculture conversion of mangrove and intertidal land.

## Why the East coast erodes more than the West coast

This is the question’s core, and it requires four distinct reasons:

- 1. Cyclone frequency and energy — the dominant reason. The Bay of Bengal generates the large majority of India’s severe cyclones, at several times the frequency of the Arabian Sea, because of higher sea surface temperature, greater freshwater influx creating a stable warm surface layer, and favourable atmospheric conditions. Each cyclone brings storm surge and high-energy waves that remove large volumes of sediment. Andhra Pradesh and Odisha are therefore the most cyclone-exposed stretches in India.
- 2. Geomorphology — soft deltaic sediment versus hard rock. The east coast is an emergent, depositional coast built of the soft alluvium of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery deltas — unconsolidated sand, silt and clay that erode readily. The west coast is a submergent coast backed closely by the Western Ghats, with resistant basalt, laterite and rocky headlands, and pocket beaches sheltered between them.
- 3. Continental shelf gradient. The east coast has a wider, gentler shelf, which allows storm surge to build higher and travel further inland — amplifying erosive energy at the shore. The west coast shelf is narrower and steeper in most stretches, dissipating surge more quickly.
- 4. Sediment starvation from dams on east-flowing rivers. The major east-flowing peninsular rivers — Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery — are extensively dammed, trapping sediment upstream. Their deltas, which depend on continuous sediment delivery to keep pace with subsidence and sea-level rise, are consequently starved. West-flowing rivers are shorter, steeper, less extensively dammed, and discharge into a narrower shelf.

Two supporting factors: the east coast has a higher density of major ports and harbours interrupting longshore drift; and its deltaic subsidence raises relative sea level beyond the eustatic rate.

AP illustration — the case to name.Uppada, in the Kakinada region of Andhra Pradesh, is among India’s most severely eroding stretches, with documented loss of shoreline and repeated relocation of the coastal road and settlements. It combines every factor above: soft deltaic sediment, high cyclone exposure, reduced Godavari sediment delivery, and structures interrupting drift.

## Remedial measures
- Soft (preferred, ecosystem-based):mangrove restoration under MISHTI — mangroves attenuate wave energy and trap sediment simultaneously; dune stabilisation with vegetation; beach nourishment (replenishing sand); coral and seagrass protection.
- Hard (site-specific, use with care): seawalls, groynes, breakwaters, offshore reefs — effective locally but frequently transferring erosion downdrift, so they require cell-level rather than point design.
- Planning and regulation:Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019 restricting construction; Integrated Coastal Zone Management (ICZM) Project; Shoreline Management Plans based on NCCR’s erosion-accretion mapping; setback lines and no-development zones.
- Sediment management: regulation of sand mining; sediment release from reservoirs and catchment management to restore supply.
- Monitoring: NCCR shoreline change assessment; satellite-based monitoring through Bhuvan; NISAR, launched July 2025, detecting deformation below one centimetre.

## Conclusion

Coastal erosion is a sediment budget deficit, and the east coast runs a larger deficit than the west for four converging reasons: it faces the great majority of India’s cyclones, it is built of soft deltaic sediment, its wider shelf amplifies storm surge, and its rivers are extensively dammed, starving the deltas of replenishment. Uppada in Andhra Pradesh shows all four operating together. The durable response is therefore not more seawalls — which move the problem downdrift — but restoring the sediment budget and the natural defences of mangroves and dunes.

## Value addition
- The sediment budget framing: erosion = removal exceeding supply. This single concept explains why upstream dams cause coastal erosion and why groynes shift rather than solve the problem.
- Institutions:National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR), Chennai, for national shoreline change assessment; NCSCM for coastal zone management; INCOIS for ocean state; Survey of India for coastal mapping; Bhuvan for geospatial monitoring.
- Why the Bay of Bengal generates more cyclones: higher sea surface temperature; large freshwater influx from the Ganga-Brahmaputra and peninsular rivers creating a stable warm surface layer that resists mixing; a shallow, wide shelf amplifying surge; and a funnel-shaped northern coastline.
- Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019: CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive, including mangroves, corals, turtle nesting and the intertidal zone); CRZ-II (developed municipal areas); CRZ-III (rural, with No Development Zone); CRZ-IV (water area to 12 nautical miles); administered through National and State Coastal Zone Management Authorities.
- Ecosystem-based defence: mangroves measurably attenuate wave height and storm surge; MISHTI (Budget 2023-24) for mangrove restoration; coral reefs and seagrass performing the same function offshore.
- The downdrift problem to name: a groyne or breakwater traps sediment updrift and starves the coast immediately downdrift — which is why shoreline protection must be planned at the scale of a littoral cell, not a single village.
- AP-specific:Uppada (Kakinada region) as a severe erosion hotspot; the 1,053-km coastline; Coringa mangroves as natural defence; Godavari and Krishna delta subsidence and sediment starvation; ports at Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Krishnapatnam and Gangavaram interrupting drift.

## Introduction

Technology has been the decisive variable in environmental degradation not because it is inherently destructive, but because it dissolves the natural limits that once constrained human impact. Pre-industrial societies damaged their environments; they simply could not do so quickly enough to outpace regeneration. Mechanisation removed that constraint, converting a question of physical capacity into a question of choice and governance.

1. Extraction: removing the limits of scale and reach

- Mechanised extraction. Draglines, deep-sea drilling rigs and mechanised felling accomplish in hours what once took seasons. Bottom trawling clears areas of seabed and destroys benthic habitat in a single pass — the clearest illustration that the damage is a function of rate, not intent.
- Access to the previously inaccessible. Technology opens deep ocean, polar and deep-crustal resources that were physically beyond reach, extending the frontier of exploitation rather than merely intensifying it within an existing one.
- Indian instance: open-cast coal mining in the Jharkhand-Odisha-Chhattisgarh belt causes deforestation, overburden dumping and particulate pollution at a scale underground mining never achieved; iron-ore mining in Goa and Karnataka led to Supreme Court intervention and mining bans.

2. Production: new substances and new persistence

- Synthetic chemistry created materials nature cannot process. Plastics, persistent organic pollutants and synthetic pesticides do not simply add to the waste stream — they add a permanent waste stream, since no decomposition pathway evolved for them. The problem is qualitative, not merely quantitative.
- Fertiliser and the nitrogen cascade. The Haber-Bosch process roughly doubled the reactive nitrogen circulating in the biosphere. It fed billions, and simultaneously caused nitrate contamination of groundwater, eutrophication of water bodies and nitrous oxide emissions — the single clearest case of a technology being both indispensable and destabilising.
- Indian instance: groundwater nitrate contamination in Punjab and Haryana; pesticide residue issues; industrial effluent in the Ganga and Yamuna basins.

3. Distribution: separating consumption from its consequences

Containerised shipping, refrigeration and aviation created supply chains in which the consumer never sees the extraction site. This is environmentally significant because it removes the feedback that historically restrained local overuse: a community that depletes its own forest observes the result, whereas one importing timber from another continent does not. Globalised logistics therefore weaken the informational basis for restraint while multiplying emissions from transport itself.

4. Disposal: obsolescence as a design feature

- E-waste. Rapid product cycles generate a waste stream carrying lead, mercury, cadmium and brominated flame retardants. In India a large majority is handled informally through open burning and acid leaching, contaminating soil and exposing workers — governed now by the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022.
- Greenhouse gas emissions. The core technologies of modern life — coal-fired generation and petroleum-fuelled transport — are the principal drivers of climate change.
- New waste streams from clean technology: solar modules and lithium batteries will generate large end-of-life volumes, addressed by the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 and the inclusion of solar PV modules in the 2022 e-waste rules.

## The counter-argument — necessary for a balanced answer

Technology is also the primary instrument of environmental remediation. Satellite monitoring detects deforestation and forest fires in near-real time through the Forest Survey of India’s alert system; PARIVESH makes environmental clearances auditable; continuous emission monitoring transmits stack readings directly to pollution control boards; and renewables now displace fossil generation on cost. The determining variable is therefore governance and incentive structure, not technology itself.

AP instance: the Real Time Governance Society’s AWARE platform integrates satellite, drone and sensor data for environmental and disaster monitoring — the same technological capability that enables extraction being turned to detection and early warning.

## Conclusion

Technology became a medium of environmental destruction by removing the physical constraints that once made restraint automatic — of scale in extraction, of persistence in materials, of distance in consumption, and of volume in disposal. But the same capabilities now underpin monitoring, enforcement and clean generation. The question is therefore not whether to have technology but which incentives direct it: a circular economy, stringent enforcement and full-cost pricing of environmental damage determine whether the next generation of technology repairs or repeats.

## Introduction

The Paris Agreement (2015) commits parties to holding warming “well below 2deg C” while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5deg C above pre-industrial levels. The IPCC’s Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5deg C (2018) established why the half-degree matters. A crucial clarification: 2024 was the first calendar year with global average temperature above 1.5deg C (WMO), but the Paris threshold refers to a multi-decadal average, so a single exceeding year is a warning signal rather than a formal breach — though it indicates how little margin remains.

## Why the threshold is non-linear — the key idea

Climate impacts do not scale smoothly with temperature. Between 1.5deg C and 2deg C, several outcomes change by far more than the 0.5deg C interval suggests, because ecological and physical systems have thresholds. This is why the half-degree is treated as a policy boundary rather than an arbitrary number.

## Amplified extreme weather
- Heatwaves become more frequent, longer and hotter; at 2deg C, extreme heat events that were once rare become routine, with sharply higher heat-related mortality — a first-order concern for India, where outdoor and agricultural labour is a large share of employment.
- Heavy precipitation intensifies (a warmer atmosphere holds roughly 7% more moisture per degree), while drought frequency rises in already dry subtropical regions.
- Compound events — heat plus drought, or storm surge plus riverine flood — increase disproportionately and overwhelm response systems designed for single hazards.

## Ecosystems and biodiversity
- Coral reefs decline by 70-90% at 1.5deg C, and by more than 99% at 2deg C (IPCC SR1.5) — the starkest single illustration of non-linearity. India’s reefs at the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andamans are directly affected, with consequences for fisheries and coastal protection.
- Species lose climatically suitable range; the proportion of insects, plants and vertebrates losing over half their range roughly doubles or triples between 1.5deg C and 2deg C.
- Ocean warming and acidification alter marine food chains and reduce fish catch potential, undermining protein security for coastal populations.

## Cryosphere, sea level and tipping points
- Sea-level rise by 2100 is about 10 cm higher at 2deg C than at 1.5deg C — which, at the margin, exposes roughly ten million additional people to inundation risk.
- Arctic summer sea-ice-free conditions shift from about once a century at 1.5deg C to roughly once a decade at 2deg C.
- Tipping elements — Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, permafrost carbon release, Amazon dieback, and weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation — become more probable. Their defining feature is irreversibility on human timescales: once crossed, reducing emissions does not restore the prior state.

## Food, water and human systems
- Yield reductions in wheat, rice and maize, most severe in tropical regions; heat stress during grain-filling is particularly damaging in the Indo-Gangetic plain.
- Water stress intensifies; hundreds of millions more people face scarcity at 2deg C than at 1.5deg C, and Himalayan glacial retreat affects the perennial flow of rivers on which northern India depends.
- Health: expanded range of vector-borne disease, heat mortality, and worsened air quality.
- Economic loss, displacement and migration — concentrated in the tropics and among low-income populations, which is why the threshold question is inseparable from climate justice.

## India-specific exposure

A 7,500-km coastline with dense delta populations; the monsoon’s variability affecting a large agricultural workforce; Himalayan glacial retreat and glacial lake outburst flood risk; and intensifying cyclones on the eastern seaboard — including Andhra Pradesh’s 1,053-km coast, among the most cyclone-exposed stretches in the world.

## The carbon budget

The remaining carbon budget for a reasonable chance of limiting warming to 1.5deg C is now small relative to current annual emissions — which is what converts the threshold from a distant target into an immediate constraint on the pace of the energy transition.

## Conclusion

Crossing 1.5deg C does not produce a single catastrophic event; it shifts the entire probability distribution of harm — more frequent extremes, more reef loss, faster sea-level rise, and a higher chance of triggering irreversible tipping elements. The fact that 2024 already exceeded 1.5deg C in a single year signals how narrow the remaining margin is. Even if the long-term threshold is overshot, every fraction of a degree avoided still reduces harm — which makes mitigation a continuing imperative rather than a pass-or-fail test.

## Value addition
- IPCC SR1.5 (2018) contrasts to quote: coral reefs decline 70-90% at 1.5deg C versus over 99% at 2deg C; sea-level rise about 10 cm lower at 1.5deg C by 2100; Arctic ice-free summers once per century versus once per decade; species range loss roughly doubles for vertebrates and triples for insects.
- The threshold’s definition: the Paris goal refers to a long-term (multi-decadal) average, not a single year. 2024 was the first calendar year above 1.5deg C (WMO), and the last decade comprises the warmest years in the instrumental record.
- Tipping elements: Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets; permafrost carbon; Amazon dieback; AMOC weakening; coral reef die-off; monsoon shifts. Defined by hysteresis — reversing the forcing does not reverse the outcome.
- Paris architecture: Nationally Determined Contributions on a five-year ratchet cycle; the Global Stocktake (first concluded at COP28, 2023, which called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels”); the Loss and Damage Fund operationalised at COP28.
- India’s commitments:Panchamrit (COP26) — 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, 50% of energy requirements from renewables, one billion tonnes of avoided emissions, 45% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels, net zero by 2070. India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years early.
- Concepts:carbon budget; overshoot and drawdown; climate sensitivity; committed warming; adaptation limits — the point beyond which adaptation is no longer possible, only loss.

## Introduction

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger in which records are grouped into cryptographically linked blocks, validated by consensus across multiple nodes and effectively immutable once written. Its value lies in creating a single, tamper-evident version of the truth among parties who do not trust one another — which describes Indian agriculture’s supply chain precisely, with its many intermediaries, disputed weights and grades, and delayed payments.

## Applications in agriculture
- Traceability and provenance. Recording each transfer of custody from farm to retail allows a buyer to verify origin, and allows a farmer to claim a premium for verified quality. This matters most for exports, where a single consignment rejection for pesticide residue can trigger a blanket restriction on an entire region’s produce — traceability localises the problem to one grower rather than one State.
- Certification integrity. Organic, Geographical Indication and residue-free certificates are today paper claims that are easy to forge. Anchoring them on a ledger makes the claim verifiable, which protects both the honest farmer and the GI itself — relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s registered GIs such as Banaganapalle mango, Guntur Sannam chilli and Araku Valley Arabica coffee.
- Smart contracts for assured payment. Payment can be released automatically when defined conditions — delivery, weight, quality grade — are recorded, removing the discretionary delay that is farmers’ most common grievance against traders and even procurement agencies.
- Input and subsidy tracking. The GNFC fertiliser pilot tracked shipments and invoices on a ledger, enabling real-time subsidy claims and reducing diversion — the most concretely demonstrated Indian use case to date.
- Warehouse receipts and credit. Tokenised, verifiable warehouse receipts allow produce in storage to serve as collateral, giving farmers an alternative to distress sale immediately after harvest.

## Government scaffolding
- National Blockchain Framework (NBF) and the Vishvasya stack (MeitY): offers Blockchain-as-a-Service with smart contracts, interoperability and sandbox environments, hosted on geographically distributed NIC data centres at Bhubaneswar, Pune and Hyderabad.
- blockchain.gov.in: the national portal providing technical standards, pilot support and capacity building.
- NITI Aayog’s “Blockchain: The India Strategy” identifies agriculture as a high-potential sector, specifically for reducing intermediaries and creating transparent records.
- Digital Agriculture Mission and AgriStack: approved in 2024, building the Farmers’ Registry, Geo-referenced Village Maps and Crop Sown Registry, along with the Krishi Decision Support System. This is the precondition — a ledger is only as good as the identity and land records it links to, so AgriStack determines whether agricultural blockchain becomes usable or remains pilot-stage.
- e-NAM integration for recording mandi transactions and reducing disputes.
- AP instance: Andhra Pradesh’s Revenue One platform is digitising land and revenue records with over 19,000 revenue officials using it, and the State’s RTGS data architecture consolidates departmental data into a single layer — the digitised land-record base without which farmer identity cannot be reliably linked to a plot, and therefore to any traceability ledger.

## Challenges and constraints
- The garbage-in problem. A blockchain guarantees that a record has not been altered; it cannot guarantee the record was true when entered. Where produce quality is assessed by a human at a mandi gate, the ledger merely makes a possibly wrong entry permanent. This is the single most important limitation and stating it demonstrates real understanding.
- Digitisation and connectivity gaps in land records, farm boundaries and rural bandwidth.
- Interoperability with AgriStack, Aadhaar, UPI and State land-record systems.
- Cost and capacity: infrastructure, energy and skilled personnel, against small per-transaction values.
- Governance and privacy: who controls the nodes, how disputes are resolved, and how farmer consent over data is secured under the DPDP Act, 2023.

## Conclusion

Blockchain addresses a real and specific failure in Indian agriculture — the absence of a trusted shared record among parties with conflicting interests — and its clearest wins are in traceability, certification and assured payment. But it is a doorway rather than the destination: its usefulness depends entirely on the quality of data entering it, which makes AgriStack, land-record digitisation and sensor-based grading the actual prerequisites. Deployed on that foundation, with farmer-centric governance, blockchain can make agricultural markets measurably fairer.

## Value addition
- National Blockchain Framework (MeitY): technology stack comprising distributed infrastructure, core framework, smart contracts and API gateway, security-privacy-interoperability layers, and application development; offers Blockchain-as-a-Service (BaaS); supports permissioned blockchain platforms; hosted at NIC data centres in Bhubaneswar, Pune and Hyderabad.
- Digital Agriculture Mission (2024): builds AgriStack — Farmers’ Registry, Geo-referenced Village Maps, Crop Sown Registry — plus the Krishi Decision

Support System and Soil Profile Mapping; the data layer for all agri-tech including blockchain.

- Key distinction to make:public/permissionless blockchains (open, energy-intensive, used for cryptocurrency) versus private/permissioned blockchains (restricted validators, low energy, used for enterprise and government). India’s NBF uses permissioned platforms — noting this pre-empts the “blockchain is environmentally costly” objection.
- Other Indian blockchain applications beyond agriculture: land-record pilots in several States; academic certificate verification; e-stamping; drug supply-chain traceability; and the RBI’s Digital Rupee (CBDC) pilots, which use distributed-ledger concepts.
- AP Geographical Indications for the certification argument: Banaganapalle mango, Guntur Sannam chilli, Araku Valley Arabica coffee, Tirupati laddu, Bandar laddu, Machilipatnam Kalamkari, Kondapalli toys, Uppada Jamdani saree.
- SDG linkage: SDG 2 (zero hunger) and SDG 12.3 (reducing food loss along supply chains) — traceability shortens the chain and reduces spoilage attributable to opaque handoffs.

## Introduction

The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), opened for signature in 1968 and in force from 1970, rests on three pillars — non-proliferation, disarmament, and peaceful uses of nuclear energy. With 191 states parties, it is among the most widely adhered-to treaties; India, Pakistan, Israel and South Sudan remain outside it, and North Korea withdrew in 2003. India’s refusal is grounded not in opposition to non-proliferation but in objection to how the treaty defines it.

discriminatory definition | unfulfilled Article VI | technology denial .

## Reasons for India’s opposition
- The discriminatory cut-off — the core objection. The NPT defines a Nuclear Weapon State as one that manufactured and exploded a nuclear device before 1 January 1967, legitimising the arsenals of five states while permanently prohibiting all others. India characterises this as “nuclear apartheid” — a treaty that freezes an existing hierarchy rather than establishing a universal norm.
- Unfulfilled disarmament obligation.Article VI obliges all parties to pursue negotiations toward nuclear disarmament in good faith. India’s position is that the nuclear-weapon states have not honoured this, so the bargain — non-proliferation by the many in exchange for disarmament by the few — has not been kept.
- National security compulsions.China’s nuclear test in 1964, following the 1962 conflict, and subsequent proliferation in India’s neighbourhood, convinced Indian policymakers that external security guarantees were unreliable and that an independent deterrent was necessary.
- Restrictions on peaceful uses. Signing as a non-nuclear-weapon state would have required full-scope safeguards and abandonment of the weapons capability, while technology denial regimes constrained even civilian access — directly affecting the three-stage programme (PHWR –> Fast Breeder –> thorium) built around India’s limited uranium and large thorium reserves.
- Strategic autonomy. India’s consistent position is that it will accept universal, non-discriminatory and verifiable disarmament, but not an unequal permanent arrangement.

## Impact of the civil nuclear agreement and the NSG waiver on power generation
- Access to fuel — the decisive change. The India-US Civil Nuclear Agreement (123 Agreement, 2008), the India-specific IAEA safeguards agreement, and the NSG waiver of September 2008 ended three decades of nuclear isolation dating from 1974. India could now import uranium from Russia, Kazakhstan, France, Canada, Australia and Uzbekistan.
- Immediate operational effect. Before the waiver, Indian PHWRs ran at low capacity factors because of a domestic uranium shortage. Imported fuel raised utilisation substantially — the fastest and largest generation gain the agreement produced, achieved without building a single new reactor.
- Separation of civil and military facilities. India placed a specified list of reactors under IAEA safeguards while keeping others outside, preserving the strategic programme — the arrangement’s essential architecture.
- Capacity expansion.Kudankulam units with Russian VVER reactors, further units under construction, and the proposed Jaitapur project with France. Domestic capacity stands at about 8.78 GW (MNRE, March 2026) across roughly 25 reactors, with 22,480 MW targeted by 2031-32.
- Freeing domestic uranium for the three-stage programme. Imported fuel for safeguarded reactors allowed indigenous uranium to be reserved for unsafeguarded reactors and for the Fast Breeder Reactor programme — the PFBR at Kalpakkam marking India’s entry into Stage II.
- Strategic legitimacy — with a precise qualification. The waiver enabled India’s entry into the MTCR (2016), the Wassenaar Arrangement (2017) and the Australia Group (2018). India is not, however, a member of the NSG, where membership continues to be blocked on the ground that India has not signed the NPT. The 2008 waiver permitted trade with the NSG; it did not confer membership of it.
- The current legislative shift: the SHANTI Act, 2025, enacted in December 2025, repealed the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Civil Liability for

Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, opening the sector to private and foreign participation. This addresses the supplier-liability concerns that had stalled foreign reactor investment since 2010 — the single largest obstacle to realising the 2008 agreement’s commercial promise.

## Conclusion

India’s objection to the NPT is structural rather than opportunistic: it rejects a permanent two-tier order while accepting universal, verifiable disarmament. The 2008 waiver resolved the practical consequence of that stand by restoring fuel access, lifting reactor utilisation and freeing domestic uranium for the breeder programme — though NSG membership remains outstanding. With the SHANTI Act, 2025 removing the liability barrier, the framework created in 2008 may finally translate into the reactor construction it was intended to enable.

## Value addition
- NPT essentials: drafted 1968, in force 1970, indefinitely extended 1995; three pillars — non-proliferation, disarmament (Article VI), peaceful uses (Article IV); NWS defined by the 1 January 1967 cut-off; 191 states parties; non-parties India, Pakistan, Israel and South Sudan; North Korea announced withdrawal in 2003.
- The 2008 architecture: India-US 123 Agreement; India-specific IAEA safeguards agreement; Separation Plan dividing civilian and strategic facilities; NSG waiver (September 2008).
- Export control regime membership — state it precisely: India is in the MTCR (2016), Wassenaar Arrangement (2017) and Australia Group (2018); India is not in the NSG.
- Related treaties and India’s position:CTBT — India has not signed but maintains a voluntary testing moratorium; FMCT — India supports negotiation at the Conference on Disarmament but seeks coverage of existing stockpiles; TPNW — India is not a party.
- Uranium suppliers to name: Russia, Kazakhstan, France, Canada, Australia, Uzbekistan and Namibia.
- AP relevance: the Tummalapalle mine in Kadapa district, in the Cuddapah Basin, is among the world’s larger uranium deposits and a key domestic source; Kovvada in Srikakulam district is earmarked for a nuclear power project under international cooperation.

## Introduction

E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment containing both valuable materials — gold, silver, copper, palladium, rare earths — and toxic substances — lead, mercury, cadmium, brominated flame retardants. India is among the world’s largest e-waste generators, with volumes rising rapidly alongside digitalisation. The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, effective from 1 April 2023, replaced the 2016 Rules with a stronger Extended Producer Responsibility regime.

## E-waste recycling practices in India
- The formal system. CPCB-authorised recyclers follow controlled processes — collection, segregation, dismantling, shredding, mechanical and hydrometallurgical metal recovery, and disposal of residues. Facilities are concentrated in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Telangana. Producers operate take-back and buy-back schemes, and Producer Responsibility Organisations aggregate collection.
- Informal sector dominance — and why. A large majority of India’s e-waste is handled informally, using open burning to recover copper, acid leaching for gold, and manual stripping without protective equipment. This causes soil and air contamination and exposes workers, including children, to heavy metals and dioxins. The reason this persists is economic, not merely regulatory: informal operators pay households more for old devices than formal recyclers can, because they bear no compliance, safety or environmental cost and recover only the high-value fractions. Formalisation therefore requires making the formal channel financially competitive — through EPR financing — not merely making the informal one illegal. This is the analytical point that distinguishes a strong answer.
- Institutional and awareness initiatives: collection drives by urban local bodies, corporate take-back programmes, and integration of waste-pickers into formal collection in some cities.

## Highlights of the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022
- Strengthened Extended Producer Responsibility. Producers must meet annual recycling targets through registered recyclers, discharged via EPR certificates generated on the CPCB portal. Targets are 60% (2023-25), rising to 70% (2025-27) and 80% (2027-28 onwards) of the quantity placed on the market in a defined earlier year.
- Mandatory registration and digital tracking. Manufacturers, producers, refurbishers and recyclers must register on the CPCB online portal; unregistered entities cannot operate, and registered entities may not transact with them. Filing of returns and digital traceability of collection and recycling are required.
- Wider coverage. The schedule expanded to 106 categories of electrical and electronic equipment, and now includes solar photovoltaic modules, panels and cells — a forward-looking inclusion given India’s solar expansion, since modules installed today become waste in the 2040s.
- Environmental safeguards. Reduction of hazardous substances (lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium and specified flame retardants) with verification by CPCB; environmental compensation for non-compliance; and a Steering Committee chaired by the CPCB Chairman to oversee implementation.
- Deregulation of intermediaries. The 2022 Rules removed the separate categories of dismantler and collection centre from the earlier regime, consolidating obligations on registered recyclers — intended to simplify, though it has been criticised for weakening intermediate oversight.

## Subsequent amendments
- Second Amendment Rules, 2023: added a clause on the safe and accountable management of refrigerants used in refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment.
- Amendment Rules, 2024: empowered the Central Government to create dedicated platforms for trading EPR certificates, with CPCB fixing a price band — a maximum of 100% and a minimum of 30% of the environmental compensation applicable for non-compliance. This addresses certificate price collapse, which had undermined recycler viability.

## The implementation gap

Rules have improved reporting but not yet decisively shifted volumes from informal to formal channels. The binding constraints are the price differential described above, limited formal recycling capacity relative to generation, weak enforcement at the household and scrap-dealer interface, and the absence of a large-scale transition pathway for informal workers.

## Conclusion

The 2022 Rules represent a substantial tightening — mandatory registration, escalating targets, digital traceability and the inclusion of solar modules — and the 2024 price-band amendment addresses a real market failure. But e-waste formalisation is fundamentally a pricing problem: as long as informal operators can outbid formal recyclers for used devices, volumes will follow the money. Sustainable progress requires channelling EPR finance into collection prices and creating a livelihood transition for informal workers.

## Value addition
- EPR target trajectory: 60% (2023-25), 70% (2025-27), 80% (2027-28 onwards); discharged through EPR certificates on the CPCB portal; 2024 amendment allows certificate trading with a CPCB-fixed price band (30-100% of applicable environmental compensation).
- Coverage:106 EEE categories under the 2022 Rules, including solar PV modules, panels and cells — significant because India’s solar fleet will generate a large module waste stream from the 2040s.
- Related waste rules to cite together:Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended, with EPR and the single-use plastic ban of July 2022); Battery Waste Management Rules 2022; Construction and Demolition Waste Rules 2016; Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016; Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016; Solid Waste Management Rules 2016. All now follow a common EPR architecture.
- Recoverable value — the circular economy argument: e-waste contains gold, silver, copper, palladium and rare earths at concentrations often exceeding natural ore. Urban mining — recovering metals from waste rather than ore — is directly relevant to India’s National Critical Mineral Mission (2025), which explicitly includes recycling as a source of supply.
- Health effects to name: lead (neurological damage, especially in children), mercury (kidney and neurological), cadmium (renal), and dioxins from open burning of PVC and flame retardants.
- International framework: the Basel Convention on transboundary movement of hazardous wastes, and its Ban Amendment prohibiting exports of hazardous waste from developed to developing countries — the reason e-waste import into India is restricted.

## Introduction

At COP26 (Glasgow, November 2021), two voluntary pledges were launched outside the formal UNFCCC negotiating track: the Global Methane Pledge, committing signatories to a collective 30% reduction in methane emissions from 2020 levels by 2030, and the Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration on Forests and Land Use, committing signatories to halt and reverse forest loss and land degradation by 2030. India joined neither, while simultaneously announcing its most ambitious climate commitments to date — the Panchamrit.

## Why India did not join the Global Methane Pledge
- The composition of India’s methane emissions is fundamentally different. In most developed economies, methane comes predominantly from fossil fuel operations — leakage from oil and gas extraction, processing and distribution — which can be reduced through engineering fixes at limited cost. In India, methane arises overwhelmingly from enteric fermentation in livestock and from flooded paddy cultivation. These are the emissions of subsistence agriculture, not of an extractive industry.
- The equity argument that follows. A blanket 30% reduction would fall on small and marginal farmers and livestock keepers — a population with among the lowest per-capita emissions in the world and the least capacity to absorb cost. India’s position is that agricultural methane from smallholder food production is survival emissions, distinguishable in principle from emissions arising from industrial or luxury consumption.
- Livestock’s economic role. India has the world’s largest cattle population, and livestock is a critical income source for landless and marginal households, particularly women. Reducing herd size is not, in India’s assessment, an available policy lever.
- Concerns about trade and future conditionality — that a collective target could become the basis of border measures or conditions on agricultural exports.
- Preference for the formal UNFCCC track. India has consistently held that climate commitments should be negotiated within the UNFCCC framework, governed by CBDR-RC, rather than through plurilateral pledges outside it that may later be treated as norms.
- Technical uncertainty in measuring agricultural methane at national scale, and the absence of proven mitigation options for smallholder systems at the time.

## Why India did not join the Glasgow Forests Declaration
- Concerns over land-use sovereignty — that commitments framed around halting land-use change could constrain a developing country’s decisions on infrastructure, mining and agricultural land use, which are matters of national policy.
- Definitional and equity concerns about how forest loss and degradation are defined and measured across very different forest types and tenure systems.
- India’s existing commitments were considered sufficient. India already had a domestic target under its NDC of creating an additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through additional forest and tree cover by 2030, and had reported increasing forest and tree cover — 25.17% of geographical area in ISFR 2023, up 1,445 sq km over 2021. India’s position was that it was already delivering on forests through domestic policy.
- Trade-related concerns regarding provisions linking forest protection to agricultural commodity supply chains.

## The common underlying principle

Both refusals rest on the same foundation: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC) and the associated argument for carbon space — that developing countries with low per-capita emissions and a large development deficit should not accept the same absolute obligations as historical emitters, particularly through instruments negotiated outside the UNFCCC.

## The counter-arguments — required for balance
- Methane is the most effective near-term lever. It has a much higher warming potential than CO2 over twenty years but a short atmospheric lifetime, so reducing it produces faster cooling than any other intervention — which is why the pledge exists.
- Mitigation options in Indian agriculture are available and beneficial:Alternate Wetting and Drying in paddy reduces methane while saving water; improved feed and fodder quality raises livestock productivity while reducing enteric methane per unit of milk. These are win-win rather than sacrificial.
- Reputational and negotiating cost — declining plurilateral pledges can limit influence in the forums where norms are formed.
- India’s own programmes already move in this direction — the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, SRI and AWD promotion, and APCNF, which reports emission reductions of up to 46% per acre across 1.77 million farmers in Andhra Pradesh.

## What India did commit to at COP26 — the essential balancing point

At the same conference India announced the Panchamrit: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50% of energy requirements from renewables; reduction of projected emissions by one billion tonnes by 2030; reduction of emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels; and net zero by 2070. India also launched Mission LIFE and, with the UK, the Green Grids Initiative — One Sun One World One Grid. India has since crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of target (MNRE).

## Conclusion

India declined the two pledges for distinguishable reasons — the methane pledge because its own methane arises from subsistence agriculture rather than fossil operations, and the forests declaration on land-use sovereignty and the sufficiency of existing domestic commitments — united by the principle that obligations should reflect differentiated responsibility and be negotiated within the UNFCCC. The position is defensible on equity grounds, though methane’s short lifetime makes it the most efficient near-term mitigation lever available, and several Indian agricultural practices already reduce it while delivering water and productivity gains. India’s simultaneous Panchamrit announcement indicates that the refusals reflected a view about instrument and equity, not a reluctance to commit.

## Value addition
- The two pledges, precisely:Global Methane Pledge — collective 30% reduction in methane from 2020 levels by 2030, launched by the US and EU at COP26; Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration on Forests and Land Use — halt and reverse forest loss and land degradation by 2030, endorsed by countries covering the large majority of the world’s forests. India joined neither; China and Russia also stayed out of the methane pledge.
- Methane’s properties — why it matters: roughly 28 times the warming potential of CO2 over 100 years but far higher over 20 years, with an atmospheric lifetime of about a decade. Its short lifetime means reducing it produces faster temperature benefit than CO2 reduction — the scientific basis of the pledge.
- India’s methane profile: dominated by enteric fermentation (livestock) and rice cultivation, with waste and fossil operations smaller — in contrast to developed economies where fossil operations dominate.
- Panchamrit (COP26): 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50% of energy requirements from renewables; one billion tonnes reduction in projected emissions; 45% cut in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels; net zero by 2070.
- Win-win mitigation options in Indian agriculture:Alternate Wetting and Drying and System of Rice Intensification (methane reduction plus water saving); improved feed and fodder (lower enteric methane per litre of milk); APCNF in Andhra Pradesh reporting up to 46% emission reduction per acre.
- India’s principled position:CBDR-RC; carbon space and per-capita equity; preference for the UNFCCC track over plurilateral pledges; climate justice; Mission LIFE as the demand-side contribution; and the Green Grids Initiative — One Sun One World One Grid launched with the UK at COP26.
- Forest data supporting India’s argument: forest and tree cover 25.17% of geographical area (ISFR 2023), an increase of 1,445 sq km over 2021; NDC commitment of an additional 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2e carbon sink by 2030.

## Introduction

A Gene Sanctuary is an area set aside for the in-situ conservation of the entire gene pool of a target plant species in its natural habitat — typically a crop wild relative or a landrace-rich zone — so that its genetic variability continues to exist, and to evolve, where it arose. It differs fundamentally from a wildlife sanctuary: the object of protection is not a species population as such but the genetic variation within it, held as raw material for future crop improvement. The concept operationalises Article 8 of the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), which places in-situ conservation ahead of ex-situ methods.

## Legal and Institutional Basis
- Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023):Section 37 empowers State Governments, in consultation with local bodies, to notify Biodiversity Heritage Sites — the operative statutory vehicle for such areas. The three-tier machinery of NBA –> State Biodiversity Boards –> Biodiversity Management Committees administers access and benefit sharing.
- ICAR-NBPGR is the nodal agency for plant genetic resources, running the National Gene Bank which conserves 4,71,561 accessions of 2,157 species (PIB, March 2025) — the world’s second largest.
- Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Biosphere Reserve programme (MoEFCC) provide the habitat-level protection within which gene sanctuaries sit.

## Indian Examples
- Citrus Gene Sanctuary, Nokrek Biosphere Reserve, Garo Hills, Meghalaya — India’s flagship, conserving Citrus indica (“Indian wild orange”), a progenitor of cultivated citrus and a source of resistance to citrus canker and tristeza virus.
- Sikkim — gene sanctuary areas for Rhododendron species and large cardamom wild relatives.
- Western Ghats — in-situ areas for wild pepper, mango and cardamom relatives.
- AP anchor — Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve (notified 2010; 4,756 sq km across Chittoor and Kadapa), Andhra Pradesh’s first biosphere reserve, holds the world’s only natural population of Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus), along with endemics such as Cycas beddomei, Syzygium alternifolium and Shorea tumbuggaia. The ICFRE-Institute of Forest Biodiversity, Hyderabad has assessed the genetic structure of natural red sanders populations using cpDNA markers and established a Gene Conservation Stand carrying 500 germplasm accessions drawn from eight distinct populations — a textbook demonstration of gene-pool conservation in the Eastern Ghats.

## How They Actually Protect Genetic Diversity
- They halt genetic erosion at source. Green Revolution monocultures displaced thousands of landraces; a gene sanctuary preserves the wild and traditional variation that formal breeding never captured.
- They keep evolution running — the decisive advantage. A seed bank is static: an accession frozen in 1985 still carries 1985’s resistance genes. A gene sanctuary is dynamic — wild populations continue to co-evolve with local pathogens, pests and a warming climate, so the gene pool keeps generating new useful variation. This is why in-situ and ex-situ are complements, not substitutes.
- They supply traits that rescue cultivated crops. The classic proof: Oryza nivara, a wild rice from Odisha, supplied the single gene conferring grassy stunt virus resistance to IR36 — a trait found in no cultivated variety worldwide.
- They conserve the whole ecological context. Pollinators, mycorrhizal fungi, soil microbiota and dispersal agents are conserved along with the plant, which no gene bank can replicate.
- They protect associated traditional knowledge and enable benefit sharing, since local Biodiversity Management Committees maintain People’s Biodiversity Registers under the Act.

## Conclusion

Gene sanctuaries convert conservation from an act of storage into an act of stewardship: they keep the raw genetic material of agriculture alive, evolving and in its own ecological context, which is precisely what a warming climate and narrowing crop base will require. Their present limitation is legal — India has no distinct statutory category called a “gene sanctuary,” and such areas rely on the Biodiversity Heritage Site route or biosphere-reserve status. Strengthening this would mean notifying priority crop-wild-relative habitats in the Eastern and Western Ghats, activating Biodiversity Management Committees, and funding complementary conservation — a live sanctuary in the Seshachalam hills alongside a duplicate accession in the National Gene Bank.

## Value addition
- Gene bank / germplasm bank: a facility conserving seeds, pollen, tissue and DNA under long-term cold or cryogenic storage. India’s National Gene Bank (ICAR-NBPGR, New Delhi) holds 4,71,561 accessions of 2,157 species, with 12 regional stations — including a Regional Station at Hyderabad serving the South-Eastern Coastal zone covering Andhra Pradesh.
- Budget 2025-26 announced a Second National Gene Bank with capacity for 10 lakh germplasm lines — a doubling of India’s conservation capacity.
- Crop Wild Relatives (CWR): wild species genetically close to cultivated crops; the principal trait donors for disease resistance, drought and salinity tolerance. India is a Vavilov Centre of origin/diversity for rice, sugarcane, brinjal, mango, pepper, turmeric and several millets.
- Related conservation categories to distinguish: Biosphere Reserve (MoEFCC/UNESCO-MAB) | National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary (WLPA, 1972) | Biodiversity Heritage Site (BD Act, Sec. 37) | Conservation and Community Reserves (WLPA amendment, 2002) | Sacred Groves (community-conserved).
- International anchors:CBD (1992) Article 8 (in-situ) and Article 9 (ex-situ); International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (ITPGRFA), 2001 — the multilateral system and Farmers’ Rights; Nagoya Protocol (2010) on access and benefit sharing; Svalbard Global Seed Vault as the global backup.
- AP-specific conservation names to drop: Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve (2010); Sri Venkateswara National Park; Papikonda National Park; Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary (mangrove genetic diversity); Kolleru Lake and Coringa (Ramsar sites); ANGRAU, Bapatla and ICAR-IIOR/CTRI Rajahmundry for crop germplasm work.
